**What a plateau feels like.** Months of work and no sense of improvement. You are not learning new grammar, the words you look up do not stick, and your speech sounds the same as it did in the spring. The natural conclusion is that you have stopped progressing.

**What is actually happening.** Three things, all of them normal:

**1. The gains have changed form.** In stages 1 to 6 progress was new knowledge — a tense a week, visible and countable. From stage 8 progress is the **same** knowledge becoming faster and more automatic, which is invisible from inside. You cannot feel yourself getting fluent.

**2. The frequency curve has flattened.** The first two thousand words cover perhaps 80 per cent of ordinary text; the next two thousand add maybe 8 per cent. **So the same effort now yields a quarter of the visible result**, not because you are learning more slowly but because each word is rarer.

**3. There are no more levels to clear.** A1 to B1 happens in months and feels like flying. B1 to C1 takes years, because the distance is larger and the steps are smaller.

**The honest numbers**, so that the expectation is right:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A1 to A2** | perhaps 100 hours |
| **A2 to B1** | perhaps 200 more |
| **B1 to B2** | perhaps 300 more |
| **B2 to C1** | perhaps 400 more |
| **C1 to C2** | as long as you like |

**So the plateau is not a plateau. It is the shape of the curve.**

**What to do about it, concretely:**

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| **Nothing feels new** | change the material, not the method — a new genre, a harder podcast, a different century |
| **Speech has stalled** | more output. The usual cause is reading a lot and speaking never. |
| **Comprehension has stalled** | harder listening, with transcripts. Usually the cause is only ever listening to one speaker. |
| **The deck feels pointless** | prune it. Delete the leeches and card from your own gaps instead. |
| **Everything feels pointless** | read the journal from six months ago |
| **You have stopped** | do five minutes. The habit matters more than the session. |

**That last row is the real advice.** The danger of a plateau is not slow progress — it is quitting, and the defence against quitting is a floor so low you cannot fail to clear it. Five minutes of the daily saint on a bad day keeps the chain alive.

**And the thing to hold on to**, in his own word: *ad astra*. There is no level at which this finishes, so there is no level at which falling short of it is a failure. The only question each day is whether there was some Greek in it.

**Practice.** Read your journal from as far back as it goes. Then write down one thing you can do now that you could not do when you started this stage. Then do five minutes of Greek, whatever happens today.
Making a Greek environment:
Immersion without leaving York: arranging your surroundings so that Greek happens to you rather than being scheduled.

**The idea.** An hour of study a day is an hour. An environment that produces Greek in the gaps — on the phone, on the wall, in the car, in the kitchen — adds another hour without any willpower. **The environment is the cheapest hours in this curriculum.**

**The interface switches, which cost ten minutes once:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The phone's language** | Greek. Twenty encounters a day with the same fifty words, meaning already known. |
| **The browser and the desktop** | Greek. Omarchy, Hyprland and the GTK apps all take `LANG=el_GR.UTF-8`. |
| **Search in Greek** | searching for a Greek phrase surfaces Greek pages |
| **YouTube and Spotify's region and language** | changes what gets recommended, permanently |
| **The keyboard layout** | already set up in stage 1 — keep it one key away |

**The ambient listening, for dead time:**

- **The commute, the walk, the washing up** — a podcast. Extensive, 60 per cent, no guilt.
- **The kitchen** — a Greek cooking channel while you cook.
- **The background, honestly assessed**: music counts, because the words go in. Radio you are not attending to does not, as the input lesson said — but it costs nothing either.

**The physical environment:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Labels on things** | the old trick, and it works for a month, which is long enough |
| **A Greek icon with its inscription** | which you can now read |
| **A wall calendar of the Greek church year** | the saint of the day, in Greek, where you will see it |
| **Books left out** | the one you are reading, face up, where you sit |
| **The daily saint on the phone's home screen** | saint.gr, bookmarked |

**The social environment, which matters most and is the next lesson's subject**: the parish is a Greek environment you already attend weekly, and arriving fifteen minutes early is fifteen minutes of Greek a week that you are not currently taking.

**The one-day experiment, worth doing once a month: a Greek day.** From waking to sleeping, everything you can control is in Greek — the phone, the music, the reading, the thinking, the self-talk, the shopping list, the prayers you say privately. It is tiring and it reveals exactly where your gaps are, which is the point.

**What not to do**: do not switch anything you need to use urgently and cannot navigate — banking, work tools, anything medical. The environment should produce Greek, not risk.

**And the measure of whether it is working**: Greek should appear in your day without your having planned it. If all your Greek happens in a scheduled block, the environment is not pulling its weight.

**Practice.** Switch the phone and the desktop to Greek today. Bookmark saint.gr on the home screen. Then pick one dead-time slot — the commute, the washing up — and put a podcast in it permanently.
Dictionaries and tools, used properly:
Which tool for which question, and the rule about when to use any of them.

**The rule first: at this level, look up less than you want to.** Every lookup breaks the reading, and the context usually teaches the word better than the entry does. **The discipline is to look up a word only when the sentence has collapsed without it.**

**With that said, the tools:**

| Tool | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| **Triantafyllidis dictionary** (greek-language.gr) | **the authority.** A Greek-to-Greek dictionary with full inflection tables, etymology and real examples. The one to grow into. |
| **Neurolingo Lexiscope** | *what form is this?* — paste any inflected word and get its lemma and its full table. Free, capped daily. |
| **WordReference, Lexilogos** | quick Greek–English, with forum threads on the hard cases |
| **Greek Wiktionary** | declension and conjugation tables, free, patchy |
| **Google Translate** | gist of a whole paragraph only. Never for producing Greek. |
| **Linguee / Reverso Context** | **a word in twenty real sentences**, with translations. The best tool for *how is this actually used?* |
| **Forvo** | a word pronounced by native speakers, several accents |
| **Corpus tools** (greek-language.gr) | *is this phrase actually said?* — frequency in real Greek |

**The move to a Greek-to-Greek dictionary is the real step of this stage.** An English gloss gives you an approximation; **ευγενικός: που δείχνει ευγένεια, καλοί τρόποι** gives you the word's own shape, and reading the definition is more Greek input. Start using Triantafyllidis for words you half know, and keep the bilingual for words you do not know at all.

**The three questions and their tools:**

| Question | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| **What does this word mean?** | bilingual first, then Triantafyllidis |
| **What form is this?** | Lexiscope |
| **How is this word actually used?** | Reverso Context or the corpus |
| **Is this sentence I wrote correct?** | none of them. A person, or a corpus search of the phrase. |

**That last row matters.** No dictionary will validate your own Greek. The honest options are: search the exact phrase in quotes and see whether Greeks write it, ask a person, or post it where Greeks will correct it.

**And the warning about machine translation, specifically.** It is useful for reading a paragraph you cannot face and useless for writing, because it produces Greek that is grammatical and not Greek — the wrong register, the wrong idiom, the wrong preposition. **Anything you write in stage 9 must be assembled from frames you have read**, which is why the imitation lesson exists.

**The lookup workflow that keeps reading moving:**

1. **Sentence collapsed?** If not, keep going.
2. **If yes, guess first.** Say what you think it means before you look.
3. **Look it up, read only the first sense**, and move on.
4. **Tick the three-tick list.**
5. **Do not read the whole entry** unless you have stopped reading anyway.

**Step two is worth insisting on**: guessing before looking is how you learn to infer, and inference is what lets you read at volume.

**Practice.** Take ten words from today's reading. Guess each one, then check it in Triantafyllidis rather than a bilingual. Then paste one inflected word into Lexiscope and read its full table.
Keeping the spoken side alive:
The one thing input cannot do for you, and the lesson that keeps this stage from producing a reader who cannot talk.

**The risk is specific.** A stage spent reading and listening will raise comprehension fast and leave speech where stage 7 left it. Six months of that, and the gap becomes uncomfortable enough to avoid speaking, which widens it further.

**The defence is small and regular**: some speech every week, with a person, however brief.

**Where the people are, in your actual circumstances:**

**1. The parish, which is the reason for the curriculum.** Fifteen minutes before and after the service. The Greeks there will switch to English the moment you hesitate — that is kindness, not judgement — so the move is to **ask in Greek and keep going in Greek**. Three exchanges a week is a real practice.

**The openers that work**, from stage 5 and 7: **Ποιος άγιος γιορτάζει σήμερα; · Πώς πάει η δουλειά; · Τι έγινε με…; · Πού είναι ο πατέρας; · Μπορώ να βοηθήσω;**

**2. One person who will be your Greek.** The single most effective arrangement available: one person at the parish who agrees to speak only Greek with you. It costs them nothing and it gives you a relationship in which English is not an option.

**How to ask**: **Μπορούμε να μιλάμε μόνο ελληνικά; Θέλω να μάθω.** People say yes, and they are usually pleased.

**3. Language exchange, free.** Tandem, HelloTalk, ConversationExchange — a Greek learning English, half an hour each way. It is unglamorous, it works, and it costs nothing.

**4. Online Greek rooms.** Discord servers and Clubhouse-style rooms where Greeks talk. Listening in is free, joining in is optional, and both are useful.

**5. Yourself.** Self-talk and retelling, from the output lesson. Not a substitute for people, and better than nothing on the weeks when nothing happens.

**6. The phone.** Calling a Greek shop or a monastery guest house to ask a real question is a genuine, terrifying, ninety-second practice. The absence of gesture makes it hard, which makes it valuable.

**The weekly minimum**, repeated because it is the whole lesson: **ten minutes of conversation with a person.** Not an hour, not a lesson, not a course. Ten minutes, weekly, for a year, is enough to keep production growing alongside comprehension.

**What to do with the hard moments**, all from stage 7 and worth rehearsing until automatic:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| Συγγνώμη, πώς το λένε αυτό; | sorry, what do you call this? |
| Δεν ξέρω τη λέξη, αλλά είναι σαν… | I don't know the word, but it's like… |
| Πιο αργά, σε παρακαλώ. | more slowly, please |
| Πώς το λες στα ελληνικά; | how do you say it in Greek? |
| Είμαι ξένος — ακούω και μαθαίνω. | I'm a foreigner — I'm listening and learning |
| Διόρθωσέ με, σε παρακαλώ. | correct me, please |

**That last one changes the dynamic**, and almost nobody says it. Asking to be corrected turns a polite conversation into a lesson.

**And the thing worth knowing about Greeks and your Greek**: the reaction to a foreigner speaking Greek is disproportionate pleasure. It is a small language that nobody learns, and the fact that you have bothered is read as respect. **You will be forgiven everything and encouraged for less than you deserve** — which is an advantage, so use it.

**Practice.** This week, have three exchanges in Greek at church and do not switch to English. Then ask one person the only-Greek question. Then set up one language-exchange account.
Measuring progress honestly:
What to measure in a stage with no lessons to tick, so that you can tell the difference between a plateau and a stall.

**What not to measure:** words known, cards reviewed, days on a streak, hours logged. All of them go up whether or not your Greek does.

**What to measure, six things, quarterly:**

**1. Reading speed on known material.** Take a page you can read and time it. Pages per hour, recorded. This number moves steadily and is the cleanest evidence of progress there is.

**2. Comprehension on a fixed recording.** Keep one podcast episode as a benchmark. Every three months, listen to the same three minutes and write down the percentage you caught. The material is constant, so the change is you.

**3. The dictionary rate.** How many lookups per page? Count on one page, quarterly. It should fall.

**4. Time without stopping.** How long can you read before you need a break or a lookup? Minutes, recorded.

**5. A written paragraph, kept.** Once a quarter, write ten sentences on the same topic — say, *why I am learning Greek* — and keep them all in one file. Rereading last quarter's is the most convincing evidence available, because errors you have outgrown are visible in your own hand.

**6. A spoken minute.** Once a quarter, speak for one minute on a set topic. Keep nothing — **he does not record himself** — but note immediately afterwards: did you hesitate more or less than last time? Did you find the words? That judgement, written down, is the measure.

**The quarterly sheet:**

| | Mar | Jun | Sep | Dec |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pages per hour | | | | |
| Benchmark comprehension % | | | | |
| Lookups per page | | | | |
| Minutes without stopping | | | | |
| Books finished | | | | |
| Conversations this quarter | | | | |

**Four entries a year, five minutes each.** That is the whole measurement system, and it is enough.

**The external check**, which is the next lesson: an Ellinomatheia past paper, once a year. It is free, it is graded, and **no exam is taken** — it is used as a thermometer and nothing else.

**What good progress looks like in this stage**, so you know what to expect:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year one of stage 8** | from two novels a year to one a month; podcasts from 60 to 85 per cent |
| **Year two** | television without subtitles; an essay read without the dictionary |
| **Year three** | literature; the news as background rather than exercise |

**And the comparison to avoid**: not against other learners, not against native speakers, and not against the imaginary version of yourself who should be further along. **Against your own March.** That is the only comparison that contains information.
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper:
Once a year, a graded external measure of where your Greek actually is — taken at home, marked by you, and never sat as an exam.

**His ruling, restated:** the Ellinomatheia levels are the skeleton of this curriculum because they are an honest external description of what each level means and because the material is free. **No exam is ever taken.** The paper is a thermometer.

**What Ellinomatheia is.** The Certificate of Attainment in Greek, run by the Centre for the Greek Language in Thessaloniki, at six levels A1 to C2. Its past papers and the matching audio are published free at **ellinomatheia.gr** and on the Centre's site.

**What a paper contains**, which is why it is a good diagnostic:

| Part | What it tests |
| --- | --- |
| **Κατανόηση γραπτού λόγου** | reading comprehension — several texts, multiple choice and short answer |
| **Χρήση γλώσσας** | grammar and vocabulary in context — gap-fill, transformation |
| **Κατανόηση προφορικού λόγου** | listening, with the audio provided |
| **Παραγωγή γραπτού λόγου** | writing — two tasks, one practical, one extended |
| **Παραγωγή προφορικού λόγου** | speaking — the prompts are published, so you can do them alone |

**The four written parts mark themselves** from the published answer keys. The writing and speaking you judge against the published criteria, which are specific about what each level requires.

**The method, once a year:**

1. **Choose the level you think you are at**, then do the one below it as well.
2. **Time yourself properly.** The timings are published, and working against the clock is part of the diagnosis.
3. **Mark the objective sections honestly.** Pass is normally around 60 per cent per section.
4. **Do the writing tasks** and compare them against the criteria.
5. **Do the speaking prompts aloud**, alone, and judge whether you managed the task.
6. **Record the result in the quarterly sheet** and move on.

**What the levels mean, in plain terms**, so the result tells you something:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | survival: greetings, numbers, basic needs |
| **A2** | everyday transactions, simple past and future, familiar topics |
| **B1** | the independent user: following a conversation, handling the unexpected, expressing an opinion simply |
| **B2** | arguing a position, following a discussion between natives, reading a newspaper, writing a structured text |
| **C1** | fluent and nearly effortless — implicit meaning, register control, literature |
| **C2** | functionally like an educated native |

**Where this stage should land you.** Stage 7 finished at a solid B1. **Stage 8's work takes you to B2**, and the end-of-stage marker is a B2 paper passed comfortably in the reading and listening sections. Stage 9 does the writing half.

**Where it is likely to be uneven**, and that is normal: your reading will outrun your writing by a level, and your writing will outrun your speaking unless you have been doing the ten minutes a week. The paper's value is showing you which one is lagging.

**And the thing not to do with it**: do not study for it. Practising past papers raises your score and not your Greek, which defeats the only purpose it has here.

**Practice.** Download one B1 paper and one B2 paper from ellinomatheia.gr. Do the B1 reading and listening sections today, timed, and mark them. Then put the B2 one away for the end of this stage.
A week of stage 8, written out:
The whole stage reduced to a timetable, so there is no decision to make each day.

**The principle, from the first lesson: an hour a day, mostly input, with output weekly.** Everything below is one way of spending it; the shape matters more than the particulars.

| | Reading | Listening | Output | Tracks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mon** | 30 min novel + the daily saint | 20 min podcast | retelling | deck |
| **Tue** | 30 min novel + news | 20 min podcast | retelling, 5 mined sentences | deck, Spelling |
| **Wed** | 20 min intensive paragraph | 20 min intensive, 2 min four passes | retelling | deck |
| **Thu** | 30 min novel + the daily saint | 20 min podcast | retelling, substitution exercise | deck, Forms |
| **Fri** | 30 min non-fiction + news | episode of a series, Greek subtitles | retelling, 5 lines from the episode | deck |
| **Sat** | 20 min read aloud, copying | a song, all six steps | **conversation, 10 min** | deck |
| **Sun** | **church** — notices, today's saint | the sermon | **three exchanges in Greek** | journal |

**The daily non-negotiables, if the week collapses:**

1. **The daily saint.** Four minutes. The floor.
2. **The deck.** Ten minutes.
3. **One retelling.** Thirty seconds.

**Fifteen minutes. On the worst day, that is the day's Greek, and the chain holds.**

**The weekly non-negotiables:**

- **Ten minutes of conversation** with a person.
- **One journal entry.**
- **One intensive session**, reading or listening.
- **Some pages of a book**, so that books get finished.

**Sunday is the best-value day in the week** and it is the one most easily wasted: the service, the notices, the sermon, the people, the fifteen minutes before and after. Arriving early and staying late converts church into the single largest block of real Greek you have.

**The monthly additions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One Greek day** | everything you control, in Greek |
| **Finish a book** | or abandon one honestly |
| **Prune the deck** | delete the leeches |

**And the quarterly ones**: the six measurements, and a paragraph written and kept.

**The annual ones**: an Ellinomatheia paper, and a read back through the journal.

**On the tracks.** Spelling and Forms run alongside this stage and should finish inside it — Spelling 4 and 5, Forms 4 and 5. Two sessions a week, one each, twenty minutes. By the end of stage 8 both tracks are done and the reference material is yours.

**The one adjustment to make if something is wrong:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Falling behind on the hour** | cut the intensive work first, never the extensive |
| **Comprehension not moving** | more listening, harder material, with transcripts |
| **Speech not moving** | the ten minutes a week is not happening. Fix that first. |
| **Bored** | change the material. Not the method. |
| **Stopped entirely** | do the fifteen-minute floor today |

**Practice.** Write out your own version of the week, with your actual commitments in it. Put the fifteen-minute floor somewhere you will see it. Then do tomorrow's.
The long game:
What this stage is actually for, and the shape of Greek for the rest of your life.

**The honest frame.** Stages 1 to 7 were a course: finite, ordered, with a thing to learn each day. **Stage 8 is not a course. It is the beginning of the permanent arrangement** — a language you use rather than study.

**That is the transition this stage makes**, and it is a change in kind rather than in degree. There is no last lesson. *Ad astra* was his word for it from the beginning.

**What "using it" looks like at steady state:**

- A book on the go, in Greek, always.
- A podcast in the dead time.
- The daily saint with the morning.
- The news, some of it, in Greek.
- Conversation at church, in Greek, by default.
- The deck, ten minutes, fed by what you read.
- No study block at all, eventually.

**The point at which the curriculum stops being needed** is the point at which Greek is one of the languages you live in rather than a subject. Stages 9, 10 and 11 exist to close the remaining gaps — writing, Cyprus, literature — but they are additions to a practice that is already running.

**And then the second curriculum.** Classical Greek moving into theological and liturgical Greek: the Liturgy, the hymnography, the Fathers, the Septuagint and the New Testament in their own language. **That is the thing this was for**, by his own answer to the first question, and the modern language is the road to it rather than a detour from it.

**What stage 8 contributes to that**, specifically:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Several thousand words** | most of which have ancient ancestors you will recognise |
| **The sound system** | so the hymns are pronounceable |
| **The case system** | which Koine uses, with more cases and more endings |
| **Reading stamina** | the ability to sit with a text for an hour |
| **The Church's modern vocabulary** | the bridge: ανάστασις / ανάσταση, εκοιμήθη / κοιμήθηκε |
| **The people** | who will explain the Liturgy to you, in Greek |

**That last one is worth stating plainly.** The reason the order was modern-first was not pedagogy. It was that the Greek people at church can teach you what the Liturgy means, and to be taught by them you have to be able to talk to them. **The modern language buys you the teachers.**

**The years, honestly estimated:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Stages 1–7** | perhaps a year, at an hour a day |
| **Stage 8** | two to three years to B2 and beyond, and it never ends |
| **Stages 9–11** | alongside, not after |
| **The classical curriculum** | begin it whenever stage 8 has become comfortable — there is no gate |

**And there is no requirement to wait.** Nothing stops you opening the classical curriculum the week it exists. The only claim this one makes is that it will be easier with a few thousand modern words already in place.

**The last thing.** The measure of this stage is not a level. It is whether, in five years, there is Greek in your ordinary week without your having arranged it — a book by the chair, a voice in the kitchen, a conversation after the service that nobody switched out of. **That is what fluency is, and it is built four minutes at a time.**

**Practice.** Write down what you want your Greek week to look like in five years. Then look at this week's. Then do the next lesson.
Review: stage 8:
Thirty lessons on method rather than material, and the stage that converts a course into a practice.

**The method**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Input at volume** | an hour a day, mostly understood, in quantity |
| **90–95 per cent comprehension** | the learning zone; 3–5 unknown words per hundred |
| **Nine parts extensive, one intensive** | volume for acquisition, precision for noticing |
| **The hundred-word and two-minute tests** | thirty seconds to judge any material |
| **Comprehensible beats difficult** | the children's book you finish beats the novel you abandon |

**The material**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The news** | fifteen minutes daily, closed vocabulary, headline grammar |
| **Podcasts and radio** | best hours per effort; interviews are the sweet spot |
| **Television and film** | Greek audio, **Greek** subtitles, five lines an episode |
| **The internet** | YouTube, the parish's Facebook, the comments, the phone in Greek |
| **Your first novel** | short, known, dialogue-heavy — the modern-Greek Gospel is a real candidate |
| **Literature** | the map, for recognition now and reading in stage 11 |
| **The Church's modern Greek** | **the best material available to you**, because you can predict the content |
| **The daily saint** | four minutes, formulaic, 365 texts a year |
| **Non-fiction** | the school history books; the register stage 9 needs |
| **Children's and YA** | authentic and easy, the only material that is both |
| **Song** | stixoi.info, six steps, one a week |
| **Audiobooks** | text plus audio; three modes, ending cold |

**The practices**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reading aloud** | twenty minutes; pronunciation, accent, fluency and parsing at once |
| **The three-tick list** | card a word on its third encounter, not its first |
| **The reading journal** | one page a week; the gap list is the best card source you have |
| **Retelling** | thirty seconds after everything, immediately and badly |
| **Imitation** | copy, transform, substitute, summarise — the road into stage 9 |
| **Ten minutes of conversation** | weekly, with a person, non-negotiable |
| **The environment** | the phone, the desktop, the dead time, the calendar on the wall |

**The honesty**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The plateau is the curve** | gains change form; the frequency curve flattens; nothing is wrong |
| **The fifteen-minute floor** | saint, deck, retelling. The chain matters more than the session. |
| **Six measurements, quarterly** | pages per hour, benchmark comprehension, lookups, stamina, a kept paragraph, a spoken minute |
| **One Ellinomatheia paper a year** | free, graded, **never sat** |
| **Compare against your own March** | nothing else contains information |

**Where you are.** B1 going into B2. You can read a novel, follow a podcast, watch a series with Greek subtitles, read the Church's modern Greek comfortably, hold a conversation, and keep going when it gets hard. The remaining gaps are **writing**, which stage 9 takes, and **production under pressure**, which only people give you.

**The checkpoint, honestly:**

1. **Have you finished a book in Greek?** If not, that is the stage's one real task.
2. **Is there Greek in your week that you did not schedule?**
3. **Did the ten minutes of conversation happen most weeks?**
4. **Are the tracks finished** — Spelling 1–5, Forms 1–5?
5. **Does the journal go back six months?**

**If the answer to the first is no, stay here.** Stage 9 does not require more comprehension; it requires a reading habit that is already running.

**What stage 9 does.** Writing, argument and register: the practical texts you will actually need, then structured argument, then the register choices — formal and informal, spoken and written, and where the learned forms are unavoidable. Thirty lessons, and the output half of B2. The reading of this stage is its raw material: **you will write by imitating what you have read**, which is why imitation came before composition.

**And the tracks.** Both should be finished by now. If they are not, finish them inside stage 9 — Spelling 5 and Forms 5 are reference material that stage 9's writing uses constantly.

**Practice.** Answer the five checkpoint questions in the journal. Then do the B2 reading and listening paper you put away. Then start stage 9 — or stay here another six months, which is also the right answer.
What stage 9 is: producing Greek:
The output stage. Everything until now has been understanding Greek or saying it; this is making it, deliberately, in writing, where there is nowhere to hide.

**Why writing earns a stage of its own.** Speech is forgiving: you can gesture, hesitate, repeat, and your listener helps you. Writing is not. The spelling is visible, the accents are visible, the agreement is visible, the register is visible, and nothing moves on until you have committed to a form. **So writing is where you find out what you actually know**, which is why it comes after a stage of reading rather than before.

**And why it comes after stage 8.** You write by imitating what you have read. A learner who writes before reading at volume produces English sentences in Greek words; a learner who has read a few hundred thousand words of Greek has frames to borrow. **Stage 8 was the raw material for this stage** — that is what the imitation lesson was for.

**What this stage covers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanics** | handwriting at speed, spelling under pressure, punctuation in full |
| **The sentence** | from short and correct to long and controlled |
| **The paragraph** | and how Greek organises a text |
| **Register** | the four levels, and choosing one deliberately |
| **The written-Greek apparatus** | the passive, impersonals, nominalisation, participles, the unavoidable learned forms |
| **The practical texts** | a message, an email, a letter, a form, a notice, a CV |
| **The four modes** | describing, narrating, explaining, arguing |
| **The Church's own forms** | how to address a priest, a bishop, a monastery |
| **The discipline** | editing yourself, and being corrected |

**What it does not cover.** The learned register in full — his ruling, and it belongs to the later classical curriculum. Where a learned form is unavoidable in modern written Greek this stage names it, teaches you to read it, and teaches the handful you should actually produce. **Recognise, do not reproduce**, except where a notice or a letter genuinely requires it.

**The level.** Stage 8 took comprehension to B2. This stage takes production there: writing a structured text, arguing a position, adapting the register to the reader. That is the output half of B2, and it is the half most self-taught learners never do.

**How the stage works.** Almost every lesson ends in a text you write — short, two hundred words or fewer, on something real. **Write it, leave it a day, edit it against the checklist, then keep it.** The file of everything you wrote in this stage is the measure of the stage.

**The one rule, stated at the start**: write what you can say. Do not reach for a construction you have never read, and never assemble a sentence from a dictionary and hope. **Every sentence you write should be a sentence you have seen the shape of.** That is not a restriction on ambition — it is where good writing in a second language comes from.

**Practice.** Write two hundred words, in Greek, on why you are learning Greek. Do it now, before the stage teaches you anything, and keep it. You will read it again at the end.
Handwriting at speed:
Writing Greek by hand, fast, legibly, with the accents in place — which is a different skill from forming the letters, and the Spelling track's hand lesson is its foundation.

**Why it still matters.** Forms are filled in by hand, notes are taken by hand, a card or a letter is written by hand, and — the real reason — **writing by hand is the only mode that forces every accent and every ending through your fingers.** Typing lets you half-know a spelling. The hand does not.

**The joins, which are what speed is made of.** Greek cursive joins differently from Latin:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **α, ε, ι, ο, υ** | join in and out freely — the backbone of any join |
| **γ, η, μ, ρ, φ, χ, ψ** | descend below the line; the next letter starts from the baseline, not from the tail |
| **σ** | joins out from the top; **ς** does not join at all, because it ends a word |
| **θ, δ, λ, ξ, ζ** | the awkward ones. Practise them between vowels: **αθα, αδα, αλα, αξα, αζα**. |
| **τ, π** | cross or join at the top, which is where the hand loses time |

**The accent is the thing that slows people down**, and the fix is mechanical: **write the word, then the accent, as one movement at the end of the word** — not as you pass the vowel. Trying to place it mid-word breaks the stroke and costs more than it saves.

**The specific confusions to drill out**, all of them real in a fast hand:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ν against υ** | the ν is pointed, the υ is round-bottomed. In a hurry they merge. |
| **θ against ο with a bar** | keep the θ's bar short and inside |
| **ζ against ξ** | the ξ has two bellies, the ζ one and a tail |
| **γ against ψ** | both descend; the ψ has the fork above the line |
| **μ against υ** | a hurried μ loses its first leg |
| **ς against σ** | only at the end of a word. A ς inside a word is a visible error. |

**The drills, fifteen minutes, three times a week:**

1. **A line of each awkward join** — αθα, αδα, αλα, αξα, αζα, ανα, αυα.
2. **Copy a paragraph** from whatever you are reading, at normal speed, accents included. From stage 8's imitation lesson: this is the cheapest spelling drill there is.
3. **Write from dictation** — play two sentences of a podcast and write them. **This is the single best combined test of listening, spelling and hand** in the whole curriculum.
4. **Write a paragraph of your own**, by hand, at speed, then read it back and mark your own slips.

**The dictation drill deserves the emphasis.** It catches the *i*-spellings you have been guessing at, the final **-ν** you have been dropping, and the accents you have been placing by feel. Nothing else in the curriculum exposes those three at once.

**The practical note on capitals.** A word in all capitals takes no accents — **ΚΑΛΗΜΕΡΑ** — and a capital at the start of a word keeps its accent: **Άννα, Όλγα, Έλληνας**. Forms and headings are full of both.

**And the signature.** Decide how you write your name in Greek letters and write it the same way every time. It goes on forms, and consistency is the whole point of a signature.

**Practice.** Do the four drills. Then write a dictation of two sentences from a podcast, check it against the transcript, and count your errors by type: *i*-spellings, accents, final -ν, endings. That count is what the next lesson is about.
Spelling under pressure:
The errors you will actually make when writing at speed, listed so that the editing checklist has something to look for.

**The honest frame.** You will misspell Greek for years, and so do Greeks — the *i* problem is a national one, and **ορθογραφικά λάθη** are a standing joke about other people's writing. The goal is not perfection. It is to know your own error list and check for those six things.

**The six errors, in order of frequency for an English speaker:**

**1. The *i* spellings.** Which of **ι η υ ει οι** a word takes. This is the main memory burden of the language and the Spelling track exists for it.

**The leverage, repeated from the track**: the **endings** are regular even when the roots are not.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-ει** | third person singular of a verb — **γράφει, μιλάει** |
| **-η** | feminine nouns, and the subjunctive third singular — **η νίκη, να γράφη** is wrong; **να γράφει** |
| **-οι** | masculine plural — **οι άνθρωποι, οι καλοί** |
| **-η** | feminine singular — **η καλή** |
| **-ι** | neuter singular — **το παιδί, το σπίτι** |
| **-ι / -οι in adjectives** | **καλοί** men, **καλή** woman, **καλό** thing |

**So most *i* decisions are grammar, not memory**, which is the single most useful fact in Greek spelling.

**2. The accent.** Missing it, or putting it on the wrong syllable. Missing accents are the most visible error a foreigner makes in writing, because Greeks read them.

**The mechanical check**: every word of two syllables or more has exactly one accent. Count them.

**3. Final -ν.** Kept or dropped, by the rule from the Spelling track:

- **Always kept** on the article **τον, την**, on **δεν**, **μην**, and on **έναν** — before a vowel or a stop (**κ π τ, μπ ντ γκ, τσ τζ, ξ ψ**).
- **Dropped** before the other consonants: **τη γυναίκα, δε θέλω**.
- **Always kept** in the neuter: **το παιδί** has no -ν, but **ένα, κανένα** follow the article rule.

**In practice: when in doubt, keep it.** Keeping a final -ν where it could be dropped is a mild formality; dropping one where it is required is an error.

**4. Double consonants.** **άλλος** with two λ, **θάλασσα** with two σ, **γράμμα** with two μ — and **μέλι** with one. There is no sound difference. It is a fact about the word, and it is a card.

**5. ο against ω.** Both say *o*. The endings help again: **-ω** is the first person of a verb (**γράφω**), **-ο** is neuter singular (**το βιβλίο**), **-ος** masculine. The roots must be learned.

**6. ε against αι.** Both say *e*. Mostly a root fact, but **-ε** is a verb ending (**γράφε, έγραψε**) and **-αι** appears in **ναι**, **και**, **είναι** and the passive endings (**γράφεται**).

**The written check, which takes two minutes on two hundred words:**

1. **Count the accents.** One per polysyllabic word.
2. **Read every *i* and ask: is it an ending?** If it is, the grammar decides it.
3. **Check the final -ν on every τον, την, δεν, μην.**
4. **Check the verb endings**: **-ω** first person, **-ει** third person, **-ετε** second plural, **-εται** passive.
5. **Check agreement** — article, adjective and noun in the same gender, number and case.
6. **Read it aloud.** Half your errors are audible.

**That checklist is the editing lesson in miniature** and it will catch most of what you get wrong.

**Practice.** Take the two hundred words you wrote in the first lesson of this stage and run all six checks on it. Count the errors by type. The largest category is where your spelling study should go for the next month.
Punctuation in full:
Greek punctuation, which is mostly like English and differs in exactly the places that will make you look careless.

**The four differences that matter:**

**1. The question mark is a semicolon.** **;** — not **?**.

> **Πού πηγαίνεις;** — *Where are you going?*

**On a Greek keyboard it is the **q** key.** Writing **?** in Greek is a visible foreignism.

**2. The semicolon's job is done by the άνω τελεία, a raised dot.** **·**

> **Ήρθε αργά· δεν τον περίμενε κανείς.** — *He came late; nobody was expecting him.*

It is on **alt gr + w** on the standard layout. In practice many Greeks use a comma or a full stop instead, and that is acceptable in informal writing.

**3. Quotation marks are guillemets.** **« »**

> **Είπε: «Θα έρθω αύριο».**

**And the full stop goes outside the closing mark** — the opposite of the American convention. English-style double quotes are common online and in some publishing; the guillemets are standard.

**4. The apostrophe marks elision**, which is far more common in Greek than in English:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **σ' το λέω** | σε + το |
| **απ' τη δουλειά** | από + τη |
| **παρ' όλα αυτά** | παρά + όλα |
| **μ' αρέσει** | μου + αρέσει |
| **τ' αυτοκίνητο** | το + αυτοκίνητο |
| **κι εγώ** | και + εγώ — **and this one has no apostrophe**, because κι is its own form |

**The rest, which behave as you expect:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τελεία .** | full stop |
| **κόμμα ,** | comma |
| **δύο τελείες :** | colon |
| **θαυμαστικό !** | exclamation mark |
| **αποσιωπητικά …** | ellipsis — **three dots, no more**, and Greeks use it heavily in informal writing |
| **παύλα —** | dash, including for dialogue |
| **παρένθεση ( )** | brackets |
| **ενωτικό -** | hyphen |

**The comma, which is where learners actually go wrong.** Greek commas are **not** placed by breath, and the rules differ from English:

- **No comma before ότι, να, or an indirect question.** **Ξέρω ότι ήρθε** — no comma. English would tempt you into one.
- **A comma before a relative clause only when it is non-defining** — the same principle as English, applied more loosely in practice.
- **A comma after a leading adverbial**: **Χθες, πήγα στην εκκλησία** — optional, and common.
- **Commas around a vocative**: **Πάτερ, μπορώ να σας ρωτήσω κάτι;** — **required**, and the one most often dropped.
- **No comma between a subject and its verb**, however long the subject.

**Dialogue, which looks unfamiliar.** Greek novels mark speech with a dash at the start of the line:

> **— Πού ήσουν;**
> **— Στην εκκλησία.**

**And the one piece of typography worth knowing**: an all-capitals word takes no accents, so headings, signs and official forms look accent-free. That is correct, not sloppy.

**Practice.** Rewrite a paragraph of your own with every Greek convention: **;** for questions, **« »** for quotes, the apostrophes for elision, and a comma around every vocative. Then find a page of a Greek novel and check how its dialogue is marked.
The sentence: from short to long:
How to build a long Greek sentence that holds, rather than a long English sentence in Greek.

**The starting rule, and keep it as a floor**: a short correct sentence beats a long broken one. Three short sentences are always an acceptable answer to a complicated thought.

**But B2 writing requires some length**, because a text made only of short sentences reads as a list. The skill is controlled extension.

**The five ways Greek extends a sentence**, all of them from stages 3 to 6:

**1. Coordination** — **και, αλλά, όμως, ή, ούτε**.

> **Πήγα στην εκκλησία και μετά μίλησα με τον πατέρα.**

The cheapest extension, and the one to use least: strings of **και** read as a child's writing.

**2. Subordination with a conjunction** — **ότι, επειδή, αν, όταν, αφού, ενώ, μολονότι**.

> **Δεν πήγα, επειδή ήμουν άρρωστος.**

**3. A relative clause** — **που**, or **ο οποίος** in formal writing.

> **Ο άνθρωπος που μου μίλησε ήταν ο ψάλτης.**
> **Η απόφαση, η οποία ανακοινώθηκε χθες, άλλαξε τα πάντα.** — formal

**4. A participle, which replaces a whole clause.** This is the written register's main device:

> **Φτάνοντας στην εκκλησία, άκουσα τον ψάλτη.** — *Arriving at the church, I heard…*
> **Έχοντας διαβάσει το βιβλίο, κατάλαβα γιατί.** — *Having read the book, I understood why.*

**5. Nominalisation** — turning a clause into a noun phrase, which is the next lesson but one.

> **Μετά την ανακοίνωση της απόφασης…** rather than *after they announced the decision*

**The structural difference from English, and it is the one to internalise.** English builds long sentences by **stacking clauses to the right**. Greek can do that, and it also puts weight at the **front** — a participle, an adverbial, a subordinate clause — before the main verb arrives:

> **Παρά τις δυσκολίες, και έχοντας υπόψη όσα είχαν συμβεί, η επιτροπή αποφάσισε να προχωρήσει.**

**Front-loading is the single most characteristic move of written Greek**, and imitating it is what makes your prose read as Greek rather than translated.

**The three ways a learner's long sentence breaks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The verb never arrives** | too much front-loading. Count: one main verb per sentence, and make sure it is there. |
| **The agreement drifts** | a subject at the front and a verb thirty words later. Check back. |
| **The participle has the wrong subject** | **Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, η πόρτα ήταν ανοιχτή** is wrong — the door did not arrive. The participle's subject must be the main clause's subject. |

**That third one is the error to watch**, because English makes it too and Greek makes it more visible.

**The exercise that builds the skill — sentence combining:**

Take three short sentences and write them as one, four different ways.

> **Πήγα στην εκκλησία. Ήταν γεμάτη. Δεν βρήκα θέση.**
>
> **1.** Πήγα στην εκκλησία, αλλά ήταν γεμάτη και δεν βρήκα θέση.
> **2.** Επειδή η εκκλησία ήταν γεμάτη, δεν βρήκα θέση.
> **3.** Φτάνοντας στην εκκλησία, που ήταν γεμάτη, δεν βρήκα θέση.
> **4.** Λόγω του πλήθους στην εκκλησία, δεν βρήκα θέση.

**Four registers, from spoken to formal, from one set of facts.** That range is what this stage is for.

**Practice.** Take three short sentences of your own and write them as one in four ways, as above. Then take the longest sentence from today's reading, count its main verbs, and find where its weight sits.
The connective inventory:
The words that hold a text together, in one list, by job — because a B2 text is judged largely on these.

**Why they matter more than vocabulary.** A reader forgives an unknown word; they do not forgive not being able to follow the argument. **The connectives are the signposts**, and using the right one tells the reader what kind of sentence is coming.

**Adding:**

| Greek | English | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **και** | and | all |
| **επίσης** | also | all |
| **επιπλέον** | furthermore, in addition | written |
| **εξάλλου** | besides, after all | all |
| **αφ' ενός… αφ' ετέρου…** | on the one hand… on the other… | formal |
| **πρώτον, δεύτερον** | firstly, secondly | written |

**Contrasting:**

| Greek | English | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **αλλά** | but | all |
| **όμως** | however | all — and it can come second in the clause |
| **ωστόσο** | nevertheless | written |
| **εντούτοις** | nevertheless | formal, learned |
| **αντίθετα** | on the contrary | written |
| **από την άλλη** | on the other hand | spoken and written |
| **ενώ** | while, whereas | all |
| **μολονότι, παρόλο που** | although | written / all |

**Causing:**

| Greek | English | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **γιατί** | because | spoken |
| **επειδή** | because | all |
| **καθώς** | as, since | written |
| **αφού** | since (with the present) | all |
| **λόγω + genitive** | due to | written |
| **εξαιτίας + genitive** | because of | written |
| **δεδομένου ότι** | given that | formal |

**Concluding:**

| Greek | English | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **άρα** | so, therefore | all |
| **λοιπόν** | so, then | spoken |
| **επομένως** | therefore | written |
| **συνεπώς** | consequently | written |
| **συνεπώς και** | and consequently | formal |
| **ως εκ τούτου** | hence | formal, learned |
| **συμπερασματικά** | in conclusion | written |

**Exemplifying and explaining:**

| Greek | English | Register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **δηλαδή** | that is, I mean | all — the workhorse |
| **για παράδειγμα, π.χ.** | for example | all |
| **όπως** | such as | all |
| **με άλλα λόγια** | in other words | all |
| **συγκεκριμένα** | specifically | written |

**Sequencing:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **πρώτα, μετά, έπειτα, στη συνέχεια** | first, then, next, subsequently |
| **τέλος, τελικά** | finally, in the end |
| **εν τω μεταξύ** | meanwhile |
| **αρχικά** | initially |

**Qualifying, which is the B2 marker:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ίσως, πιθανόν** | perhaps, possibly |
| **φαίνεται ότι** | it seems that |
| **κατά τη γνώμη μου** | in my opinion |
| **σε γενικές γραμμές** | broadly speaking |
| **μέχρι ενός σημείου** | up to a point |
| **ειδικά, κυρίως** | especially, mainly |

**The three cautions:**

1. **Do not over-signpost.** A short text with a connective in every sentence reads as an exam answer. One or two per paragraph.
2. **Match the register.** **ως εκ τούτου** in a text message is absurd; **λοιπόν** in a formal letter is wrong. The register lesson is three ahead.
3. **όμως moves.** Unlike English *however*, it commonly sits second or third in its clause: **Δεν ήρθε όμως.**

**Practice.** Take a paragraph you wrote and replace every **και** and **γιατί** with a more precise connective. Then take a Kathimerini essay and list every connective in it, with the job each one does.
Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga:
Above the sentence: how a Greek text is shaped, which differs from English conventions enough to notice.

**The paragraph, as Greek uses it.** Longer than modern English journalism, which has trained people to a paragraph a sentence. A Greek paragraph in a newspaper, an essay or a letter is typically four to eight sentences and carries one idea developed.

**The shape of a paragraph:**

1. **The idea, stated.**
2. **Developed** — explained, qualified, or given a reason.
3. **Illustrated** — an example, a case, a quotation.
4. **Closed**, or turned towards the next paragraph.

**That is a convention, not a law**, and it is what you will see in the essays you read.

**The shape of a whole text, in the Greek essayistic tradition:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πρόλογος** | the introduction: the subject, why it matters, and often a question |
| **Κύριο μέρος** | the body: the argument in two to four paragraphs, each one point |
| **Επίλογος** | the conclusion: the position stated, and a closing thought |

**The introduction's job, in Greek convention**, is to establish that the subject matters before saying anything about it — more preamble than English would use. And the conclusion is expected to **state a position**, not merely summarise. A conclusion that only restates reads as evasive.

**The useful formulas, which Greek school writing teaches explicitly** and which the Ellinomatheia writing paper expects:

| Greek | Job |
| --- | --- |
| **Τα τελευταία χρόνια…** | the standard opening: *in recent years…* |
| **Το θέμα που θα μας απασχολήσει είναι…** | the subject before us is… |
| **Αξίζει να σημειωθεί ότι…** | it is worth noting that… |
| **Από την άλλη πλευρά…** | on the other side… |
| **Όσον αφορά…** | as regards… |
| **Εν κατακλείδι / Συμπερασματικά…** | in conclusion… |
| **Κλείνοντας, θα έλεγα ότι…** | in closing, I would say that… |

**Those are formulaic and they are expected.** Greek written convention is more tolerant of set phrases than English, where they would read as padding.

**What marks a paragraph boundary visually**: an indent in print, a blank line online. Greek does not use both.

**The cohesion devices**, which are what makes a text read as one thing rather than a pile:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The connectives** | from the last lesson |
| **Pronouns and the article** | **αυτό, το ζήτημα αυτό, η εν λόγω απόφαση** referring back |
| **Repeating a key noun** | which Greek does more readily than English, where it reads as clumsy |
| **Demonstratives pointing forward** | **Το εξής:** *the following:* |
| **Nominalising the previous sentence** | *they announced it* → **η ανακοίνωση αυτή** |

**That last one is the most Greek device of the set**, and it is the next lesson but one: a clause becomes a noun phrase, and the noun phrase becomes the subject of the next sentence. That is how Greek expository prose moves.

**Practice.** Take an essay from Kathimerini and mark its πρόλογος, κύριο μέρος and επίλογος. Count the sentences per paragraph. Then write one paragraph of your own in the four-part shape, on anything.
Register: the four levels:
Choosing how to sound, deliberately — which is the real content of B2 writing and the thing that marks a learner who has read from one who has only studied.

**The four levels you need**, which is a simplification and a workable one:

**1. Intimate and online.** Family, friends, messages, comments.

- **εσύ** throughout, diminutives, **ρε**, abbreviations, no accents sometimes, English words.
- **Τι κάνεις ρε; Θα 'ρθεις το βράδυ;**

**2. Everyday neutral.** Most speech, most ordinary writing, a note, a friendly email.

- Standard grammar, **εσύ** or **εσείς** as the relationship requires, no slang, no learned forms.
- **Καλημέρα. Θα ήθελα να ρωτήσω κάτι για την Κυριακή.**

**3. Formal.** A letter, an official email, a notice, anything institutional.

- **εσείς** always, no contractions, the passive and impersonal, nominalisation, **παρακαλώ** and the polite conditional, and some learned vocabulary.
- **Σας παρακαλώ να με ενημερώσετε σχετικά με τη διαδικασία.**

**4. Learned and ecclesiastical.** Church documents, legal texts, academic writing, inscriptions.

- Katharevousa survivals, ancient datives, participles doing clause work, **όστις**-type relatives, archaic vocabulary.
- **Recognise it. Do not write it** — except the fixed forms of address, which the lesson on writing to the Church teaches, because there you must.

**His ruling, which this stage respects**: the learned register is skipped and remembered for the later classical curriculum. So level 4 is a reading skill here, with one exception, and that exception is church correspondence.

**The markers that move a text up or down, in a table you can actually use:**

| Feature | Informal | Formal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Address** | εσύ, σου | εσείς, σας |
| **Greeting** | Γεια σου, Καλημέρα | Αξιότιμε Κύριε, Αγαπητέ Κύριε |
| **Request** | Μου δίνεις…; | Θα σας παρακαλούσα να… |
| **Because** | γιατί | λόγω, εξαιτίας, δεδομένου ότι |
| **So** | λοιπόν, άρα | επομένως, συνεπώς |
| **Agent** | named: *ο υπουργός ανακοίνωσε* | hidden: **ανακοινώθηκε** |
| **Verb or noun** | *αποφάσισαν να…* | **η απόφαση για…** |
| **Clauses** | *όταν έφτασε* | **φτάνοντας, κατά την άφιξή του** |
| **Vocabulary** | λέω, κάνω, παίρνω | δηλώνω, πραγματοποιώ, λαμβάνω |
| **Close** | Φιλιά, Τα λέμε | Με εκτίμηση, Μετά τιμής |

**That last row of verbs is worth learning as a set.** Formal Greek replaces the four workhorse verbs with Latinate-feeling heavy equivalents, exactly as formal English swaps *get* for *obtain*:

| Plain | Formal |
| --- | --- |
| λέω | δηλώνω, αναφέρω |
| κάνω | πραγματοποιώ, διενεργώ |
| παίρνω | λαμβάνω, παραλαμβάνω |
| δίνω | παρέχω, χορηγώ |
| βάζω | τοποθετώ |
| βλέπω | παρατηρώ, διαπιστώνω |
| θέλω | επιθυμώ |
| στέλνω | αποστέλλω |

**The error to avoid, and it is the commonest learner error in writing**: mixing levels in one text. A formal letter that opens **Αξιότιμε Κύριε** and then says **λοιπόν** reads as unintentionally comic. **Pick a level before the first word and hold it to the end.**

**And the error in the other direction**: over-formality. A learner who has read official Greek writes a friendly email in level 3 and sounds cold. **Neutral is the default**, and most of what you write should be level 2.

**Practice.** Take one sentence — say, *I would like to ask about Sunday's service* — and write it four times, once at each level. Then look at the last thing you wrote in Greek and name its level. Then check whether it holds it throughout.
The passive and the impersonal in writin:
Stage 6 taught the passive's forms. This lesson is about what written Greek uses it *for*, because it is far commoner in writing than in speech and it is one of the markers of a formal text.

**The three jobs the written passive does:**

**1. Hiding the agent**, which is the main one. Official and journalistic Greek avoids naming who did a thing:

> **Ανακοινώθηκε ότι τα σχολεία θα κλείσουν.** — *It was announced that…*
> **Αποφασίστηκε η αναστολή της λειτουργίας.** — *The suspension was decided.*
> **Η αίτηση απορρίφθηκε.** — *The application was rejected.*

**Nobody is responsible in any of those sentences**, and that is the point. Learning to read it is learning to notice the omission.

**2. Putting the important thing first.** Greek word order is flexible, but the passive makes the affected thing the subject:

> **Ο ναός χτίστηκε το 1890.** — the church is the subject, which is what the sentence is about.

**3. Impersonal statement**, where the subject is nobody in particular:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **θεωρείται ότι** | it is considered that |
| **πιστεύεται ότι** | it is believed that |
| **υποστηρίζεται ότι** | it is maintained that |
| **λέγεται ότι** | it is said that |
| **αναμένεται να** | it is expected to |
| **προβλέπεται ότι** | it is foreseen that |
| **απαγορεύεται να** | it is forbidden to |
| **επιτρέπεται να** | it is permitted to |
| **συνιστάται να** | it is recommended to |
| **παρατηρείται ότι** | it is observed that |

**Those ten are the written register's spine** and they are worth knowing cold, because they open paragraphs.

**The true impersonals**, which are not passives at all but do the same job:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **πρέπει να** | it is necessary to, one must |
| **μπορεί να** | it is possible that |
| **είναι απαραίτητο να** | it is essential to |
| **είναι προφανές ότι** | it is obvious that |
| **είναι γνωστό ότι** | it is well known that |
| **αξίζει να** | it is worth |
| **χρειάζεται να** | it is needed to |
| **συμβαίνει να** | it happens that |

**And the deponents**, which look passive and are not — from stage 6, and they matter here because they are common in written Greek:

**έρχομαι, κάθομαι, σκέφτομαι, αισθάνομαι, φοβάμαι, θυμάμαι, χρειάζομαι, εργάζομαι, ασχολούμαι, χειρίζομαι, αποτελούμαι**

**The register warning, which is the point of the lesson.** The passive makes a text formal, distant and institutional. **That is right for a notice and wrong for a letter to a person.** Learner writing often ends up accidentally bureaucratic because the passive is what the learner has read.

**The test**: if the sentence has a human doing something to another human, use the active. **Σας ευχαριστώ** — not **Ευχαριστίες εκφράζονται**.

**And one grammatical note for writing.** Greek has two past passive forms and the register differs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γράφτηκε** | the ordinary modern aorist passive |
| **εγράφη** | the learned form — found in headlines, notices and church texts |

**Read both. Write the first.** The second belongs to the later curriculum, with the exception of the fixed phrases — **εκοιμήθη, ανέστη, ετελέσθη** — which are the Church's own and are quoted whole.

**Practice.** Take a news item and underline every passive. Then rewrite three of its sentences in the active, naming an agent, and notice how the tone changes. Then write a notice of your own, three sentences, using three of the ten impersonals.
Nominalisation:
Turning verbs into nouns, which is the single most characteristic move of formal written Greek — and the one that will most change how your writing reads.

**What it is.** A clause becomes a noun phrase:

| Clause | Nominalised |
| --- | --- |
| **αποφάσισαν να κλείσουν τα σχολεία** | **η απόφαση για το κλείσιμο των σχολείων** |
| **ανακοίνωσε ότι θα παραιτηθεί** | **η ανακοίνωση της παραίτησής του** |
| **οι τιμές αυξήθηκαν** | **η αύξηση των τιμών** |
| **έφτασε** | **η άφιξή του** |
| **ο ναός χτίστηκε** | **η ανέγερση του ναού** |

**Why Greek does it so readily.** Greek nouns decline, so a noun phrase can be slotted into any case and carry any role — subject, object, after a preposition — without rewriting the sentence. English has to use *the* plus *-ing* or a subordinate clause, which is clumsier, so English prose resists it.

**The suffixes that make nouns from verbs**, and knowing them means you can build the noun yourself:

| Suffix | From | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** | the perfective stem | γράφω → **η γραφή**; αποφασίζω → **η απόφαση**; αυξάνω → **η αύξηση**; λαμβάνω → **η λήψη** |
| **-μα** | the action or its result | γράφω → **το γράμμα**; κλείνω → **το κλείσιμο**; τρώω → **το φαγητό** |
| **-σιμο** | the act of doing it | κλείνω → **το κλείσιμο**; ανοίγω → **το άνοιγμα** |
| **-μός** | the process | αναπτύσσω → **η ανάπτυξη**; πολιτίζω → **ο πολιτισμός** |
| **-τής / -τρια** | the doer | διδάσκω → **ο διδάσκαλος**; εργάζομαι → **ο εργάτης** |
| **-τικός** | the adjective from it | **αποφασιστικός, ενημερωτικός** |

**The -ση group is the one to master**, because it is where most of the abstract vocabulary of written Greek comes from: **απόφαση, ανακοίνωση, αύξηση, μείωση, κατανόηση, παραγωγή, εξέλιξη, ανάπτυξη, πρόσκληση, συμμετοχή**.

**And the genitive is what holds it together.** A nominalised phrase needs a genitive for its subject or object, which is why formal Greek is full of genitive chains:

> **η ανακοίνωση της απόφασης της κυβέρνησης** — *the announcement of the government's decision*

**Three deep is normal. Four is bad writing even in Greek.**

**The prepositions that take nominalisations**, which is how they get into sentences:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **μετά + accusative** | after — **μετά την ανακοίνωση** |
| **πριν από** | before — **πριν από την άφιξή του** |
| **κατά + accusative** | during — **κατά τη διάρκεια της λειτουργίας** |
| **λόγω + genitive** | because of — **λόγω της αύξησης** |
| **με σκοπό + genitive** | with the aim of |
| **σχετικά με** | concerning |
| **όσον αφορά** | as regards |
| **παρά + accusative** | despite — **παρά τις δυσκολίες** |

**The caution, and it matters.** Nominalisation makes writing dense, abstract and impersonal. **Formal Greek overuses it and so will you**, if you learn it from official texts. A sentence with three nominalisations and one weak verb is bad Greek, exactly as it is bad English:

> **Η πραγματοποίηση της υλοποίησης της απόφασης έγινε.** — nonsense, and recognisably the nonsense of an official document.

**The rule: one nominalisation per sentence, and keep a real verb.**

**Practice.** Take five sentences you wrote in the active and nominalise one element in each. Then take a news paragraph, underline every nominalisation, and rewrite it with verbs instead — which is how you see what the nominalising cost in clarity.
The participles in writing:
Stage 6 taught both participles. This lesson is their job in a written text, because they are where written Greek differs most visibly from spoken Greek.

**The two forms, recalled:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The active, indeclinable: -οντας / -ώντας** | **γράφοντας, μιλώντας, φτάνοντας** — *writing, speaking, arriving* |
| **The passive, declinable: -μένος / -μένη / -μένο** | **γραμμένος, κλεισμένος, κουρασμένος** — *written, closed, tired* |

**What the active participle does in writing: it replaces a subordinate clause**, and that is its whole value — one word instead of a conjunction plus a verb.

| Clause | Participle |
| --- | --- |
| **Όταν έφτασα, είδα…** | **Φτάνοντας, είδα…** |
| **Επειδή δεν ήξερα, ρώτησα.** | **Μη γνωρίζοντας, ρώτησα.** |
| **Ενώ μιλούσε, κρατούσε σημειώσεις.** | **Μιλώντας, κρατούσε σημειώσεις.** |
| **Αν λάβουμε υπόψη…** | **Λαμβάνοντας υπόψη…** |

**The negative is μη**, not δεν: **μη γνωρίζοντας, μη έχοντας**.

**The compound participle**, which is formal and useful:

> **Έχοντας διαβάσει το βιβλίο, κατάλαβα γιατί.** — *Having read the book…*
> **Έχοντας ολοκληρώσει τις σπουδές του, επέστρεψε.** — *Having completed his studies…*

**The iron rule, and the error every learner makes**: the participle's subject must be the main clause's subject.

> **Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, η πόρτα ήταν ανοιχτή.** ✗ — the door did not arrive.
> **Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, βρήκα την πόρτα ανοιχτή.** ✓

**Check every participle you write against its main verb's subject.** It goes on the editing checklist.

**The passive participle's two jobs:**

**1. As an adjective**, and it declines:

> **ένα γραμμένο κείμενο, μια κλεισμένη πόρτα, τα κουρασμένα παιδιά**

**2. As a state, with είμαι:**

> **Η πόρτα είναι κλειστή.** — and note **κλειστή**, not **κλεισμένη**: Greek has a separate stative adjective for many of these, and **κλειστός** (closed, as a state) is commoner than **κλεισμένος** (having been closed, as an event).

**That distinction is worth the attention**: **ανοιχτός / ανοιγμένος, κλειστός / κλεισμένος, γεμάτος / γεμισμένος**. The short form is the state; the **-μένος** form implies someone did it.

**The learned participles you will read and should not write**, except as fixed phrases:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-ων / -ούσα / -ον** | the ancient active participle — **ο παρών** (the present one), **οι ενδιαφερόμενοι**, **ο υπογράφων** (the undersigned) |
| **-θείς / -θέντος** | the ancient aorist passive — **ο αποβιώσας, τα αναφερθέντα** |

**These are live in official and church Greek**, so recognise them. A few are fully naturalised nouns and you can use those: **ο ενδιαφερόμενος** (the interested party), **ο παρών** (present, on a register), **ο υπεύθυνος** (the person responsible), **τα δεδομένα** (the data), **το περιεχόμενο** (the content).

**The practical advice for your own writing.** Use the active participle, once or twice a text, for the front-loading effect; use the passive participle freely as an adjective; leave the learned ones alone. **One well-placed participle makes a paragraph read as written Greek. Three in a row make it unreadable.**

**Practice.** Take four sentences with **όταν**, **επειδή** or **ενώ** and rewrite each with a participle. Then check each one's subject against the main verb's. Then find three learned participles in an official or church text and say what each means.
The learned forms you cannot avoid:
His ruling is that the learned register is skipped and kept for the later classical curriculum. This lesson is the exception list: the katharevousa survivals that are live in ordinary modern writing, which you must read and in a few cases must write.

**Why they are there.** Katharevousa was the official written language until 1976. Everything administrative, legal, academic and ecclesiastical was written in it for a century and a half, and the forms survive in the places where that writing is still copied: signs, forms, notices, headlines, law, and the Church.

**What survives, by kind:**

**1. The dative, in fixed phrases**, which modern Greek otherwise does not have:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **εν τω μεταξύ** | meanwhile |
| **εν πάση περιπτώσει** | in any case |
| **εν τάξει → εντάξει** | all right — and nobody hears the dative in it any more |
| **εν ονόματι** | in the name of |
| **εν ζωή** | alive, living |
| **τοις εκατό (%)** | per cent |
| **δόξα τω Θεώ** | glory to God |
| **εν Κυρίω** | in the Lord |

**2. The learned relatives and demonstratives:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ο οποίος / η οποία / το οποίο** | who, which — **and this one you should write** in formal texts |
| **όστις, ήτις** | who — read only |
| **ούτος, αύτη, τούτο** | this — read only, except **τούτο** and **τούτου** in a few phrases |
| **ο εν λόγω** | the aforementioned, the said — **live in official writing** |
| **ως εκ τούτου** | hence |
| **εξ ου** | from which |

**ο οποίος is the one to actually use.** It is the formal alternative to **που**, it declines, and it resolves ambiguity: **η απόφαση του υπουργείου, η οποία ανακοινώθηκε χθες** makes clear that the decision, not the ministry, was announced.

**3. The learned participles**, from the last lesson: **ο υπογράφων, οι ενδιαφερόμενοι, τα αναφερθέντα, ο αιτών**.

**4. The learned prepositions with their old cases:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **εκ / εξ + genitive** | from — **εξ αρχής, εκ νέου, εξ ολοκλήρου** |
| **εις / εν** | in, to — only in fixed phrases now |
| **διά + genitive** | by means of — **διά ζώσης, δι' αλληλογραφίας** |
| **υπέρ / κατά + genitive** | for / against — **and both are live**: υπέρ της πρότασης |
| **πλην** | except — **and live**: πλην ενός |
| **άνευ** | without — **άνευ όρων** |
| **περί + genitive** | concerning — **περί ορθογραφίας** |

**5. The learned vocabulary**, which is simply the formal half of the lexicon: **λαμβάνω, δηλώνω, αποστέλλω, διενεργώ, παρέχω, καθίσταται, τυγχάνει, δύναται, οφείλεται, προβλέπεται**.

**The ones you should write**, and this is the operative list:

1. **ο οποίος**, in formal texts.
2. **ο εν λόγω**, in official writing.
3. **The fixed dative phrases** — **εν τω μεταξύ, εν πάση περιπτώσει, εντάξει, δόξα τω Θεώ**.
4. **εκ / εξ in its set expressions** — **εξ αρχής, εκ νέου**.
5. **υπέρ and κατά + genitive**, in an argument.
6. **The formal verb set**, in a letter or a notice.
7. **The forms of address for clergy**, which have their own lesson.

**Everything else: read it and move on.** Writing **όστις** or **ετελέσθη** yourself would be affectation, and that is the reason for his ruling rather than mere convenience — producing a register you do not fully control makes you sound confused, not learned.

**The honest note about where this goes.** The later curriculum takes all of it properly: katharevousa as a system, the Koine verb, the ancient participles and cases in full, and the hymnography that uses them. **This lesson is a reading key, not a grammar.**

**Practice.** Find an official document — a bank form, a council notice, a church encyclical — and list every learned form in it. Mark which of the seven above you could use. Then write one formal sentence using **ο οποίος** and one using **υπέρ** with the genitive.
Messages, and the internet's Greek:
The register you will write most, which no textbook teaches and which has its own conventions, abbreviations and script.

**Greeklish, first, because you will meet it.** Greek written in Latin letters — **kalimera, ti kaneis, pame avrio** — a hangover from phones that had no Greek keyboard. It survives among older users and in some casual messaging.

**His position should be: read it, do not write it.** You learned the script from lesson one for a reason, and writing Greeklish undoes that. Greeks under forty mostly write in Greek letters now.

**The genuine conventions of Greek messaging:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Accents dropped** | very common, and not an error in this register: **καλημερα τι κανεις** |
| **Lower case throughout** | normal |
| **Punctuation minimal**, but the **;** kept for questions | because without it a question is not a question |
| **Repeated letters for emphasis** | **καλααα, ωραιαααα** |
| **Ellipsis everywhere** | **...** — Greeks use it far more than English does, for softening and for trailing off |
| **No full stop at the end** | a full stop in a short message reads as curt, as in English |

**The abbreviations:**

| Greek | Full | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **τσκ** | τίποτα | nothing / nothing much |
| **τλκ** | τελικά | in the end, so |
| **δλδ** | δηλαδή | i.e., I mean |
| **κτλ / κλπ** | και τα λοιπά / και λοιπά | etc. |
| **π.χ.** | παραδείγματος χάριν | e.g. |
| **μλκ** | μαλάκα | mate — vulgar, and recognition only |
| **ευχ** | ευχαριστώ | thanks |
| **καλ** | καληνύχτα | night |
| **σγν** | συγγνώμη | sorry |
| **ΟΚ / οκ** | — | and Greeks write **εντάξει** too |

**The openers and closers of a message:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Γεια σου / Γεια σας** | hi |
| **Τι κάνεις; / Τι γίνεται;** | how are you / what's happening |
| **Είσαι εκεί;** | are you there |
| **Πες μου** | let me know |
| **Τα λέμε** | talk later |
| **Φιλιά** | kisses — ordinary between friends and family, including men and women |
| **Καληνύχτα, καλό βράδυ** | night, have a good evening |
| **Φιλάκια** | little kisses — warmer, lighter |
| **Να 'σαι καλά** | be well — warm and very common |

**The parish group chat**, which is the one you will actually be in: a mix of level 2 and level 1, announcements in near-formal Greek, replies in short informal Greek, and a great deal of **Χρόνια πολλά**, **Καλή Σαρακοστή**, **Καλή Ανάσταση** and **Αμήν** according to the season.

**What to write in it, safely:**

> **Καλημέρα σε όλους. Θα είμαι εκεί στις 9.**
> **Χρόνια πολλά στον εορτάζοντα!**
> **Ευχαριστώ πολύ, τα λέμε την Κυριακή.**
> **Να 'στε καλά.**

**A comment under a post**, which is the one piece of public writing worth practising:

> **Πολύ ωραία φωτογραφία, ευχαριστούμε για την ενημέρωση.**
> **Συμφωνώ απόλυτα.**
> **Χρόνια πολλά και καλή δύναμη.**

**The emoji question**: Greeks use them heavily, in every register short of formal, and across generations. There is nothing to learn beyond that.

**One warning.** Informal written Greek drops accents, and your spelling study depends on them. **So keep the accents in your own messages**, even though natives drop them. Writing accent-free is a habit you cannot afford while you are still learning where they go.

**Practice.** Write four messages: one to a friend, one to the parish group, one comment under a post, and one reply declining an invitation politely. Keep the accents. Then read a Greek comment thread and count the abbreviations you recognise.
An email:
The text you will write most often that actually has rules — and the register judgement is most of the work.

**Three kinds of email, three registers:**

**1. To a friend or someone you know well** — level 2, barely a letter:

> **Γεια σου Γιάννη,**
>
> **Ήθελα να σου πω για την Κυριακή. Η λειτουργία αρχίζει στις 9 και μετά θα μείνουμε για καφέ. Θα έρθεις;**
>
> **Τα λέμε,**
> **[name]**

**2. To someone you do not know, informally** — a shop, a parish office, a question:

> **Καλημέρα σας,**
>
> **Θα ήθελα να ρωτήσω αν η εκκλησία είναι ανοιχτή το Σάββατο το πρωί.**
>
> **Σας ευχαριστώ εκ των προτέρων.**
>
> **Με εκτίμηση,**
> **[name]**

**3. Formal, institutional** — an office, an application, a complaint:

> **Αξιότιμε Κύριε / Αξιότιμη Κυρία,**
>
> **Σας αποστέλλω το παρόν σχετικά με την αίτησή μου της 3ης Μαρτίου.**
>
> **Θα σας παρακαλούσα να με ενημερώσετε για την πορεία της διαδικασίας. Παραμένω στη διάθεσή σας για οποιαδήποτε περαιτέρω πληροφορία.**
>
> **Με εκτίμηση,**
> **[full name]**

**The openings, which are the register's first signal:**

| Greek | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **Γεια σου / Γεια σας** | informal |
| **Καλημέρα σας** | neutral, safe, very common |
| **Αγαπητέ Κύριε / Αγαπητή Κυρία** | *Dear Sir / Madam* — semi-formal |
| **Αγαπητέ κύριε Παπαδόπουλε** | with a name — **and note the vocative ending** |
| **Αξιότιμε Κύριε / Αξιότιμη Κυρία** | formal, institutional |
| **Προς [the office]** | *To:* — on a letter or a formal notice |

**The vocative trap, which is the error to avoid.** When you address someone by name, Greek uses the vocative:

| Nominative | Vocative |
| --- | --- |
| ο Κύριος | **Κύριε** |
| ο Γιάννης | **Γιάννη** |
| ο Παπαδόπουλος | **Παπαδόπουλε** |
| ο Νίκος | **Νίκο** |
| η Μαρία | **Μαρία** — feminines do not change |
| ο Πέτρος | **Πέτρο** |

**Writing Αγαπητέ κύριε Παπαδόπουλος is a visible error.** Masculine **-ος** becomes **-ε**; **-ης** becomes **-η**.

**The closings:**

| Greek | Register |
| --- | --- |
| **Φιλικά / Τα λέμε / Φιλιά** | informal |
| **Με φιλικούς χαιρετισμούς** | warm, neutral |
| **Σας ευχαριστώ** | neutral and safe |
| **Με εκτίμηση** | *Yours sincerely* — the formal default |
| **Μετά τιμής** | *Respectfully* — very formal |
| **Παραμένω στη διάθεσή σας** | *I remain at your disposal* — formal, and expected in business |

**The useful middles:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Σας γράφω σχετικά με…** | I am writing concerning… |
| **Θα ήθελα να ρωτήσω / να ενημερωθώ για…** | I would like to ask / to be informed about… |
| **Σε συνέχεια της επικοινωνίας μας…** | following our communication… |
| **Σας επισυνάπτω…** | I attach… |
| **Όπως σας ανέφερα…** | as I mentioned… |
| **Θα σας παρακαλούσα να…** | I would ask you to… — the polite conditional |
| **Σας ευχαριστώ εκ των προτέρων** | thank you in advance |
| **Αναμένω την απάντησή σας** | I await your reply |
| **Συγγνώμη για την καθυστέρηση** | apologies for the delay |

**The subject line (θέμα)**: a noun phrase, not a sentence. **Αίτηση για βεβαίωση. Ερώτηση σχετικά με το ωράριο. Ευχαριστήρια επιστολή.**

**The rule that saves you.** Pick level 2 unless there is a specific reason for level 3. **Καλημέρα σας … Σας ευχαριστώ … Με εκτίμηση** is appropriate for nine emails in ten, and it cannot cause offence in either direction.

**Practice.** Write three emails: one to a friend about Sunday, one to a parish office asking a question, and one formal one following up an application. Then check every vocative and every **εσείς**.
A formal letter:
The full apparatus, because a letter on paper still exists where it matters most — officialdom, the Church, and anything that has to be kept on file.

**The layout, which is conventional and expected:**

> **[Your name]**
> **[Your address]**
> **[Telephone, email]**
>
> **[Place], [date]**
>
> **Προς**
> **[The recipient's title]**
> **[The organisation]**
> **[Address]**
>
> **Θέμα: [a noun phrase]**
>
> **Αξιότιμε Κύριε / Αξιότιμη Κυρία,**
>
> [the body]
>
> **Με εκτίμηση,**
>
> **[signature]**
> **[name in full]**

**The date**, which has its own convention:

> **Υόρκη, 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026**

**The place first, then the date**, and the month in the **genitive**: **Ιανουαρίου, Φεβρουαρίου, Μαρτίου, Απριλίου, Μαΐου, Ιουνίου, Ιουλίου, Αυγούστου, Σεπτεμβρίου, Οκτωβρίου, Νοεμβρίου, Δεκεμβρίου**. The day is a plain number; ordinals appear as **1η** for the first.

**The body, in three parts:**

**1. Why you are writing**, in one sentence:

> **Με την παρούσα επιστολή σας ενημερώνω ότι…**
> **Σας απευθύνομαι σχετικά με…**
> **Με αφορμή…, θα ήθελα να…**

**2. The substance**, in one or two paragraphs — facts, dates, references, in order. Formal Greek expects completeness here, so include the file number, the date of the previous letter, the names.

**3. What you want**, stated plainly:

> **Για τους λόγους αυτούς, σας παρακαλώ να…**
> **Παρακαλώ για τις δικές σας ενέργειες.** — *I ask you to take the appropriate action.* A standard and very useful formula.
> **Αναμένω την απάντησή σας εντός…**

**The formulas that make a letter read as a Greek letter:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Με την παρούσα** | by the present (letter) |
| **Σε απάντηση της επιστολής σας της…** | in reply to your letter of… |
| **Σε συνέχεια του υπ' αριθμ. … εγγράφου** | following document number… |
| **Σας επισυνάπτω τα κάτωθι δικαιολογητικά** | I attach the following supporting documents |
| **Παρακαλώ για τις δικές σας ενέργειες** | please take the necessary action |
| **Παραμένω στη διάθεσή σας** | I remain at your disposal |
| **Είμαι στη διάθεσή σας για κάθε διευκρίνιση** | available for any clarification |
| **Σας ευχαριστώ για την κατανόηση** | thank you for your understanding |
| **Μετά τιμής** | respectfully — the most formal close |

**The words a formal letter needs:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η επιστολή** | the letter (formal; **το γράμμα** is a letter to a friend) |
| **η αίτηση** | the application |
| **η βεβαίωση** | the certificate, the confirmation |
| **το δικαιολογητικό** | a supporting document |
| **η υπεύθυνη δήλωση** | a sworn declaration — a Greek institution |
| **το έγγραφο** | the document |
| **ο αριθμός πρωτοκόλλου** | the reference number |
| **η υπογραφή** | the signature |
| **η σφραγίδα** | the stamp, the seal |
| **αρμόδιος** | competent, responsible (the right office) |
| **εντός** | within (a period) |

**The letter of complaint**, which has a tone to hit — firm, impersonal, factual:
