> **Με την παρούσα θα ήθελα να εκφράσω τη δυσαρέσκειά μου για… Παρά τις επανειλημμένες οχλήσεις μου, το ζήτημα δεν έχει επιλυθεί. Παρακαλώ για τις δικές σας ενέργειες εντός δεκαπέντε ημερών.**

**Do not write an angry letter in Greek.** The formal register is the whole weapon; adding heat weakens it, and a foreigner writing angry Greek is simply hard to read.

**The letter of thanks**, which is the one you will most want:

> **Αξιότιμε Πάτερ,**
>
> **Θα ήθελα να σας ευχαριστήσω θερμά για… Η φιλοξενία σας και η καλοσύνη όλων στην ενορία ήταν κάτι που δεν θα ξεχάσω.**
>
> **Με βαθύ σεβασμό,**

**That one gets its own lesson later**, because addressing clergy has fixed forms you should get right.

**Practice.** Write one formal letter in the full layout — an application for a certificate, a thanks, or a question to an office. Date it the Greek way. Then check: the vocative, the **εσείς** throughout, one level only, and no **λοιπόν**.
Forms, applications and officialdom:
The least glamorous writing in the language and the most likely to be needed — and Greek bureaucracy has a vocabulary that is worth learning once.

**What a form asks for**, in the order it usually asks:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Επώνυμο** | surname |
| **Όνομα** | first name |
| **Πατρώνυμο** | father's name — **required on almost every Greek form** |
| **Μητρώνυμο** | mother's name |
| **Ημερομηνία γεννήσεως** | date of birth — note the learned genitive |
| **Τόπος γεννήσεως** | place of birth |
| **Υπηκοότητα / Ιθαγένεια** | nationality / citizenship |
| **Διεύθυνση κατοικίας** | home address |
| **Οδός, Αριθμός, Τ.Κ.** | street, number, postcode |
| **Τηλέφωνο, Κινητό** | telephone, mobile |
| **Ηλεκτρονική διεύθυνση** | email |
| **Α.Δ.Τ.** (Αριθμός Δελτίου Ταυτότητας) | ID card number |
| **Α.Φ.Μ.** | tax number |
| **Α.Μ.Κ.Α.** | social insurance number |
| **Οικογενειακή κατάσταση** | marital status |
| **Επάγγελμα** | occupation |
| **Υπογραφή** | signature |
| **Ημερομηνία** | date |

**The πατρώνυμο is the one that surprises foreigners.** Greek identity documents carry the father's first name, and forms ask for it as a matter of course.

**The instruction language**, which you must be able to read:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Συμπληρώστε** | fill in |
| **Συμπληρώνεται από την υπηρεσία** | to be completed by the office |
| **Υποβάλλεται εις διπλούν** | to be submitted in duplicate |
| **Επιλέξτε** | select |
| **Διαγράψτε ό,τι δεν ισχύει** | delete what does not apply |
| **Με κεφαλαία** | in capitals |
| **Θεωρημένο αντίγραφο** | certified copy |
| **Επικυρωμένο** | authenticated |
| **Συνημμένα** | attachments |
| **Απαιτούμενα δικαιολογητικά** | required documents |
| **Ισχύει έως** | valid until |
| **Άνευ αντικειμένου** | not applicable |
| **Κατά περίπτωση** | as applicable |

**Note the learned forms throughout**: **γεννήσεως** (genitive), **εις διπλούν** (dative-flavoured), **άνευ** (ancient preposition), **κάτωθι** and **ανωτέρω** (below, above). **Official Greek is where katharevousa is most alive**, which is why the last lesson taught the reading key.

**The υπεύθυνη δήλωση**, which deserves its own paragraph because it is a fixture of Greek life: a sworn declaration, on a standard form, in which you state something and accept the legal consequences of lying. Its opening formula is fixed:

> **Με ατομική μου ευθύνη και γνωρίζοντας τις κυρώσεις που προβλέπονται από τις διατάξεις της παρ. 6 του άρθρου 22 του Ν. 1599/1986, δηλώνω ότι:**

**You do not need to produce that**, and you do need to recognise it, because it is the sentence at the top of the form.

**The offices and their names:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **το Δημαρχείο** | the town hall |
| **η Δημοτική Υπηρεσία** | the municipal service |
| **η Εφορία / Δ.Ο.Υ.** | the tax office |
| **το ΚΕΠ** | the citizens' service centre — the one-stop shop |
| **το Ληξιαρχείο** | the registry office |
| **το Προξενείο / η Πρεσβεία** | the consulate / the embassy |
| **η Μητρόπολη** | the diocesan office |
| **το Γραφείο της ενορίας** | the parish office |

**The ones you will actually use** are the consulate and the Μητρόπολη — a baptismal certificate, a marriage certificate, a letter from a parish. Those are all **βεβαιώσεις** and they are all requested with a short **αίτηση**.

**The application, in four lines**, which is all one needs:

> **ΑΙΤΗΣΗ**
>
> **Προς: [the office]**
>
> **Παρακαλώ να μου χορηγήσετε βεβαίωση [of what], για [the purpose].**
>
> **Συνημμένα υποβάλλω: [the documents].**
>
> **[Place, date] — [signature, name]**

**χορηγήσετε** is the word: *to grant, to issue*. **Παρακαλώ να μου χορηγηθεί βεβαίωση…** is the passive version, and both are standard.

**Practice.** Fill in a Greek form — any one you can find online — with your own details, including the πατρώνυμο. Then write a four-line αίτηση requesting a certificate. Then find a υπεύθυνη δήλωση and read its opening formula until you recognise it on sight.
A notice, a programme, an announcement:
Short public texts, which are the most useful writing you can do for a parish — and the register is distinctive: terse, nominal, and almost verbless.

**What a notice is, grammatically.** Headline grammar from stage 8, extended: articles present but verbs often absent, everything carried by noun phrases and dates.

> **ΙΕΡΟΣ ΝΑΟΣ ΑΓΙΟΥ ΝΙΚΟΛΑΟΥ**
>
> **ΠΡΟΓΡΑΜΜΑ ΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΙΩΝ**
>
> **Σάββατο 18 Οκτωβρίου**
> **Εσπερινός, 6.00 μ.μ.**
>
> **Κυριακή 19 Οκτωβρίου**
> **Όρθρος, 8.30 π.μ. — Θεία Λειτουργία, 9.30 π.μ.**
>
> **Μετά τη Λειτουργία θα ακολουθήσει καφές στην αίθουσα.**

**Note the features**: all capitals in the heading, hence no accents; the genitive in the title (**Αγίου Νικολάου, Ακολουθιών**); the date with no year; **π.μ.** and **μ.μ.** for a.m. and p.m.; and one real verb, in the future, at the end.

**The time conventions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **π.μ. / μ.μ.** | προ μεσημβρίας / μετά μεσημβρίας — a.m. / p.m. |
| **6.00 or 6:00** | both used; the full stop is commoner in print |
| **στις 9** | *at 9* — the preposition in running text |
| **9.30 π.μ.** | and in speech **εννιά και μισή** |

**The announcement, which has a verb and a short body:**

> **ΑΝΑΚΟΙΝΩΣΗ**
>
> **Ενημερώνουμε τα μέλη της ενορίας ότι η συνάντηση της Τετάρτης αναβάλλεται λόγω της εορτής. Νέα ημερομηνία θα ανακοινωθεί.**
>
> **Ευχαριστούμε για την κατανόηση.**
>
> **Το Εκκλησιαστικό Συμβούλιο**

**The formulas for an announcement:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Ενημερώνουμε ότι…** | we inform you that… |
| **Σας γνωρίζουμε ότι…** | we advise you that… |
| **Ανακοινώνεται ότι…** | it is announced that… — the impersonal version |
| **Θα πραγματοποιηθεί…** | will take place |
| **αναβάλλεται / ματαιώνεται** | is postponed / is cancelled |
| **Η συμμετοχή είναι ελεύθερη** | participation is free / open |
| **Δηλώσεις συμμετοχής έως…** | registrations by… |
| **Πληροφορίες στο τηλέφωνο…** | information on… |
| **Ευχαριστούμε για την κατανόηση** | thank you for your understanding |
| **Ευχαριστούμε εκ των προτέρων** | thank you in advance |

**The invitation**, which is the warmest of these texts:

> **ΠΡΟΣΚΛΗΣΗ**
>
> **Με χαρά σας προσκαλούμε στην εορτή του πολιούχου μας, την Κυριακή 26 Οκτωβρίου. Μετά τη Θεία Λειτουργία θα ακολουθήσει δεξίωση στην αίθουσα της ενορίας.**
>
> **Η παρουσία σας θα μας τιμήσει.**

**Η παρουσία σας θα μας τιμήσει** — *your presence will honour us* — is the standard closing of a Greek invitation and worth having whole.

**The church-notice vocabulary, which is the set you will use:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ο Εσπερινός** | Vespers |
| **ο Όρθρος** | Matins |
| **η Θεία Λειτουργία** | the Divine Liturgy |
| **η Παράκληση** | the Paraklesis / supplicatory canon |
| **η αγρυπνία** | the vigil |
| **το μνημόσυνο** | the memorial service |
| **η αρτοκλασία** | the blessing of the loaves |
| **ο πολιούχος** | the patron saint of a place |
| **η πανήγυρις / το πανηγύρι** | the patronal feast |
| **η δεξίωση** | the reception |
| **η αίθουσα** | the hall |
| **το Εκκλησιαστικό Συμβούλιο** | the parish council |
| **το κατηχητικό** | the Sunday school |
| **ο δίσκος** | the collection |
| **ο έρανος** | the appeal |

**The thing to notice about the register.** A notice uses level 3 — **εσείς**, formal vocabulary, the impersonal — even for an informal event. **Public writing is formal in Greek** more consistently than in English, where a parish newsletter might be chatty. A chatty Greek notice would read as odd.

**Practice.** Write a programme for next weekend's services, in the layout above, with capitals and genitives. Then write an announcement postponing something, and an invitation to a feast. Keep all three to level 3.
The CV and the covering letter:
A practical text with fixed conventions, and the Greek ones differ from the British enough to matter.

**The Greek CV — το βιογραφικό σημείωμα**, usually shortened to **το βιογραφικό**.

**The structure:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ΠΡΟΣΩΠΙΚΑ ΣΤΟΙΧΕΙΑ** | personal details |
| **ΣΠΟΥΔΕΣ / ΕΚΠΑΙΔΕΥΣΗ** | studies / education |
| **ΕΠΑΓΓΕΛΜΑΤΙΚΗ ΕΜΠΕΙΡΙΑ** | professional experience |
| **ΞΕΝΕΣ ΓΛΩΣΣΕΣ** | foreign languages |
| **ΓΝΩΣΕΙΣ Η/Υ** | computer skills (Η/Υ = ηλεκτρονικός υπολογιστής) |
| **ΣΕΜΙΝΑΡΙΑ / ΕΠΙΜΟΡΦΩΣΗ** | courses / further training |
| **ΔΗΜΟΣΙΕΥΣΕΙΣ** | publications |
| **ΑΛΛΕΣ ΔΡΑΣΤΗΡΙΟΤΗΤΕΣ / ΕΝΔΙΑΦΕΡΟΝΤΑ** | other activities / interests |
| **ΣΥΣΤΑΣΕΙΣ** | references |

**The Greek conventions that differ:**

1. **More personal detail is normal** — date of birth, marital status, and military service (**στρατιωτικές υποχρεώσεις: εκπληρωμένες**) for men. A British CV omits all of that; a Greek one includes it without comment.
2. **Language levels are stated by certificate**, not by self-assessment: **Αγγλικά: άριστη γνώση (C2, Proficiency)**. The scale is **άριστη / πολύ καλή / καλή / βασική γνώση** — excellent, very good, good, basic.
3. **Reverse chronological order**, as in Britain.
4. **A photograph** is still common and is not required.

**The language levels table, which is the part you will actually fill in:**

| Greek | Level |
| --- | --- |
| **άριστη γνώση** | C2 |
| **πολύ καλή γνώση** | C1 |
| **καλή γνώση** | B2 |
| **μέτρια / βασική γνώση** | B1 and below |

**And the honest entry for you, in due course**: **Ελληνικά: καλή γνώση** at the end of this stage, and **πολύ καλή** after some years of stage 8. No certificate, since no exam is taken — and **χωρίς πιστοποίηση** is a perfectly ordinary thing to write.

**The covering letter — η συνοδευτική επιστολή**, level 3 throughout, three paragraphs:

> **Αξιότιμε Κύριε / Αξιότιμη Κυρία,**
>
> **Με ιδιαίτερο ενδιαφέρον διάβασα την αγγελία σας για τη θέση του [post], και σας αποστέλλω το βιογραφικό μου σημείωμα.**
>
> **Διαθέτω [n] χρόνια εμπειρίας στον τομέα του [field], και κατά τη διάρκεια αυτή ανέπτυξα [the skills]. Θεωρώ ότι τα χαρακτηριστικά αυτά ανταποκρίνονται στις απαιτήσεις της θέσης.**
>
> **Θα χαρώ πολύ να συζητήσουμε την υποψηφιότητά μου σε μια προσωπική συνάντηση. Παραμένω στη διάθεσή σας για οποιαδήποτε περαιτέρω πληροφορία.**
>
> **Με εκτίμηση,**

**The formulas worth keeping:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Με ιδιαίτερο ενδιαφέρον διάβασα την αγγελία σας** | I read your advertisement with particular interest |
| **υποβάλλω την υποψηφιότητά μου** | I submit my candidacy |
| **Διαθέτω εμπειρία στον τομέα…** | I have experience in the field of… |
| **ανταποκρίνομαι στις απαιτήσεις** | I meet the requirements |
| **κατά τη διάρκεια της θητείας μου** | during my time there |
| **ανέλαβα / ήμουν υπεύθυνος για** | I took on / I was responsible for |
| **Θα χαρώ να συζητήσουμε** | I would be glad to discuss |
| **Παραμένω στη διάθεσή σας** | I remain at your disposal |

**The vocabulary of work**, which is also conversation vocabulary:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η θέση εργασίας** | the job, the post |
| **η αγγελία** | the advertisement |
| **η συνέντευξη** | the interview |
| **ο εργοδότης / ο εργαζόμενος** | the employer / the employee |
| **ο μισθός, τα αποδοχές** | the salary, the pay |
| **πλήρης / μερική απασχόληση** | full-time / part-time |
| **η σύμβαση** | the contract |
| **η προϋπηρεσία** | previous experience |
| **η άδεια** | leave; a licence |
| **η προαγωγή** | promotion |
| **αυτοαπασχολούμενος / ελεύθερος επαγγελματίας** | self-employed / freelance |

**The practical note.** You are unlikely to apply for work in Greek — but writing your own CV in Greek is the best single self-description exercise there is, because it forces you to name what you do, what you know and what you have done, which is the content of every conversation about yourself. **Write it even if you never send it.**

**Practice.** Write your own βιογραφικό in Greek, with all the headings. Then write a covering letter for any job you can imagine wanting. Then say out loud, from the CV, what you do and what you have done.
Describing:
The first of the four modes: making someone see something they have not seen. The grammar is adjectives and the **imperfect**, and the skill is order.

**Describing a place**, which has a conventional order in Greek as in English: general to particular, outside to inside, whole to detail.

> **Η εκκλησία βρίσκεται στην άκρη του χωριού, πάνω σε έναν λόφο. Είναι μικρή, πέτρινη, με έναν ψηλό καμπαναριό στα δεξιά. Μπαίνοντας, το πρώτο που βλέπεις είναι το τέμπλο — σκούρο ξύλο, γεμάτο εικόνες, με τη λάμπα να καίει μπροστά στην Παναγία. Μυρίζει θυμίαμα και κερί. Είναι σκοτεινά, και το φως μπαίνει από ψηλά.**

**The devices in that paragraph:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **βρίσκεται** | *is situated* — the standard verb for placing something |
| **Prepositions of place** | στην άκρη, πάνω σε, στα δεξιά, μπροστά, από ψηλά |
| **A participle to move the viewpoint** | **μπαίνοντας** — *on entering* |
| **The senses** | smell and light, not only shape |
| **Impersonal verbs of state** | **είναι σκοτεινά, μυρίζει** |

**The prepositions of place, as a set:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **πάνω σε / από** | on / above |
| **κάτω από** | under |
| **μέσα σε** | inside |
| **έξω από** | outside |
| **μπροστά από** | in front of |
| **πίσω από** | behind |
| **δίπλα σε / στο** | next to |
| **ανάμεσα σε** | between |
| **απέναντι από** | opposite |
| **γύρω από** | around |
| **κοντά σε / μακριά από** | near / far from |
| **στα δεξιά / στα αριστερά** | on the right / left |
| **στην άκρη / στη μέση** | at the edge / in the middle |
| **στη γωνία** | on the corner |

**Describing a person**, which Greek does in a fixed order too: build, then face, then manner, then character.

> **Είναι ψηλός, αδύνατος, γύρω στα εβδομήντα. Έχει λευκά μαλλιά και μια φωνή πολύ βαθιά. Μιλάει αργά, σαν να ζυγίζει κάθε λέξη. Είναι από τους ανθρώπους που ακούν περισσότερο απ' ό,τι μιλούν.**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ψηλός / κοντός** | tall / short |
| **αδύνατος / παχύς / γεροδεμένος** | thin / heavy / solidly built |
| **γύρω στα…** | around (an age) |
| **μελαχρινός / ξανθός / καστανός** | dark-haired / fair / brown-haired |
| **γενειοφόρος** | bearded — and **με γένια** more plainly |
| **ευγενικός, καλόκαρδος, σοβαρός, γλυκός, αυστηρός** | polite, kind-hearted, serious, sweet, stern |
| **Είναι από τους ανθρώπους που…** | he is one of those people who… — a very Greek frame |

**The tense question, which is the grammatical point of the lesson.** Description in the past uses the **imperfect**, not the aorist:

> **Ήταν ψηλός. Φορούσε πάντα το ίδιο παλτό. Μιλούσε σιγά.** — states and habits, so imperfect.
> **Μπήκε, κάθισε και άρχισε να μιλάει.** — events, so aorist.

**A description in the aorist reads as a sequence of events**, which is the next lesson's job. Mixing them wrongly is the commonest error in a learner's narrative, and the editing checklist asks about it.

**The comparison devices**, which lift a description out of a list:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **σαν** | like — **σαν παιδί** |
| **σαν να** + subjunctive | as if — **σαν να ήξερε κάτι** |
| **μοιάζει με** | resembles |
| **θυμίζει** | is reminiscent of |
| **περισσότερο… από ό,τι…** | more… than… |
| **τόσο… που…** | so… that… |

**Practice.** Write a paragraph describing your parish church, inside and out, in the present. Then write a paragraph describing one person there, in the past, using the imperfect throughout. Then check that no aorist slipped in.
Narrating:
Telling what happened: the mode that uses everything stage 4 taught about aspect, and the one where that teaching is tested.

**The two tenses and the division of labour**, which is the whole of narrative grammar:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Aorist** | the events. What happened, one thing after another. |
| **Imperfect** | the background. What was going on, what used to happen, what the weather was like, what people were wearing. |

> **Ήταν Κυριακή πρωί και έβρεχε.** — background, imperfect.
> **Μπήκα στην εκκλησία, άφησα το παλτό μου και κάθισα πίσω.** — events, aorist.
> **Ο ψάλτης διάβαζε.** — background again, imperfect.
> **Σε κάποια στιγμή γύρισε και με κοίταξε.** — event, aorist.

**That alternation is what a Greek narrative is made of**, and getting it right is worth more than any amount of vocabulary.

**The pluperfect, for what happened before the story:**

> **Είχα φτάσει αργά, γιατί είχε χαλάσει το αυτοκίνητο.** — *I had arrived late, because the car had broken down.*

**The time words that structure a narrative:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Μια μέρα / Ένα βράδυ** | one day / one evening — the standard opening |
| **Πριν από λίγο καιρό** | a little while ago |
| **Στην αρχή** | at first |
| **Μετά, έπειτα, ύστερα** | then, afterwards |
| **Αμέσως** | immediately |
| **Ξαφνικά** | suddenly |
| **Σε κάποια στιγμή** | at some point |
| **Την ίδια στιγμή** | at that same moment |
| **Λίγο αργότερα** | a little later |
| **Τελικά, στο τέλος** | finally, in the end |
| **Από τότε** | ever since |

**The historic present**, which Greek uses heavily and which English uses only in anecdote: a story told in the present tense for immediacy.

> **Μπαίνω μέσα, και τι να δω; Είναι γεμάτη.** — *So I go in, and what do I see? It's full.*

**That is extremely common in spoken Greek narrative** — the kind of story told after the service — and worth being able to do, because it is how people actually tell things. **Τι να δω;** is a fixed move for the surprise.

**Reported speech in a narrative.** From stage 6, and the rule is simpler than English: **no tense shift.**

> **Μου είπε ότι θα έρθει.** — *He told me he would come.* The verb stays as he said it.
> **Με ρώτησε αν ήμουν καλά.**
> **Μου είπε να μην ανησυχώ.**

**Quoting directly**, with the guillemets and the dash from the punctuation lesson:

> **Γύρισε και μου είπε: «Μην ανησυχείς».**

**The structure of a told story, which is conventional:**

1. **Setting** — when, where, who. Imperfect.
2. **The ordinary state of things.** Imperfect.
3. **The event that breaks it.** Aorist, usually with **ξαφνικά** or **σε κάποια στιγμή**.
4. **What followed.** Aorist, in order.
5. **The outcome and what it meant.** Aorist, then present or imperfect for the reflection.

**And the ending, which Greek expects**: a told story usually closes with a judgement rather than just stopping — **Από τότε δεν ξαναπήγα. · Και κατάλαβα ότι… · Έτσι είναι.**

**The practice that matters most here.** Narrating is the one mode you will use in speech constantly, so write it and then **tell** it. Writing it out makes the aspect decisions deliberate; telling it afterwards makes them automatic.

**Practice.** Write the story of one thing that happened to you at church, in about two hundred words: background in the imperfect, events in the aorist, one pluperfect for what came before, and a closing judgement. Then tell the same story out loud without the text.
Explaining:
The expository mode: making something clear to someone who does not know it. The grammar is the present tense, impersonals and the passive, and the skill is order.

**What explanation needs that description does not**: a structure the reader can follow without you. Description can wander; an explanation cannot.

**The four shapes of an explanation**, and most texts are one of them:

**1. Process — how something is done**, in steps:

> **Η προετοιμασία του αντίδωρου γίνεται ως εξής. Πρώτα ζυμώνεται το πρόσφορο, με αλεύρι, νερό, αλάτι και προζύμι. Στη συνέχεια σφραγίζεται με τη σφραγίδα, που φέρει τα αρχικά. Έπειτα ψήνεται και μεταφέρεται στον ναό. Τέλος, κατά τη Λειτουργία, αφαιρείται ο Αμνός και το υπόλοιπο κόβεται σε κομμάτια και μοιράζεται.**

**Note the apparatus**: the impersonal passive throughout (**ζυμώνεται, σφραγίζεται, ψήνεται, μοιράζεται**), because the agent does not matter, and the sequencers **πρώτα, στη συνέχεια, έπειτα, τέλος**.

**2. Classification — what kinds there are:**

> **Υπάρχουν τρεις βασικές κατηγορίες… Η πρώτη… Η δεύτερη… Η τρίτη…**

**3. Cause and effect:**

> **Αυτό συμβαίνει επειδή… Ως αποτέλεσμα… Συνέπεια αυτού είναι…**

**4. Definition and distinction**, which is the hardest and most useful:

> **Η νηστεία δεν είναι δίαιτα. Η δίαιτα αφορά το σώμα· η νηστεία αφορά τη σχέση. Η διαφορά βρίσκεται στον σκοπό, όχι στο περιεχόμενο του πιάτου.**

**The formulas, by job:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **γίνεται ως εξής** | is done as follows |
| **με άλλα λόγια** | in other words |
| **δηλαδή** | that is |
| **πρόκειται για…** | it is a matter of…, this is a… |
| **ονομάζεται / λέγεται** | is called |
| **αποτελείται από** | consists of |
| **χωρίζεται σε** | is divided into |
| **διαφέρει από… ως προς…** | differs from… in respect of… |
| **σε αντίθεση με** | in contrast to |
| **αντίστοιχα** | correspondingly |
| **Αξίζει να σημειωθεί ότι** | it is worth noting that |
| **Για να γίνει πιο κατανοητό…** | to make it clearer… |
| **Ας πάρουμε ένα παράδειγμα** | let us take an example |
| **Συνοψίζοντας** | summing up |

**The tense: the gnomic present**, for things that are generally true:

> **Η Σαρακοστή αρχίζει την Καθαρά Δευτέρα και διαρκεί σαράντα ημέρες.**

**Not the future, not the past.** An explanation of how something works sits in the present even when the thing happens annually.

**The device that makes an explanation readable: the known-to-new order.** Each sentence starts from something the previous sentence established and adds one new thing.

> **Η Λειτουργία έχει δύο μέρη. Το πρώτο μέρος ονομάζεται Λειτουργία του Λόγου. Σε αυτό διαβάζονται ο Απόστολος και το Ευαγγέλιο. Μετά τα αναγνώσματα ακολουθεί το κήρυγμα…**

**Each sentence's subject is the previous sentence's new information.** That is the single most useful compositional habit in expository writing, in any language.

**And the nominalisation chain from the earlier lesson is how Greek does it**: *they read the Gospel* → **τα αναγνώσματα** → the subject of the next sentence.

**The two errors to avoid:**

1. **Explaining in the order you learned it** rather than the order a reader needs. Write the structure first, in four lines, then fill it.
2. **Using the second person.** **Παίρνεις το αλεύρι και…** is a recipe register, which is fine for a recipe and wrong for an explanation. **Use the impersonal passive.**

**Practice.** Explain, in about two hundred words, something you know and a Greek reader might not — how an Orthodox fast works, how your work works, how a thing is made. Use the impersonal passive, the four sequencers, and the known-to-new order. Then write the four-line structure you should have written first, and check whether your text matches it.
Arguing: building a position:
The B2 mode, and the one the Ellinomatheia writing paper is built around: stating a position and supporting it.

**The structure Greek writing expects**, from the paragraph lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πρόλογος** | the subject, why it matters, and the question |
| **Κύριο μέρος** | two to four paragraphs, one argument each |
| **Επίλογος** | the position stated and a closing thought |

**The introduction, with the formulas that are expected:**

> **Τα τελευταία χρόνια γίνεται πολλή συζήτηση για το αν… Το ζήτημα είναι σύνθετο, καθώς αφορά τόσο… όσο και… Στο κείμενο που ακολουθεί θα υποστηρίξω ότι…**

**And the last of those sentences is the thesis**, which Greek essayistic convention places at the end of the introduction, as English does.

**Each body paragraph, in four moves:**

1. **The claim.** **Κατά πρώτον, …**
2. **The reason.** **Αυτό συμβαίνει επειδή…**
3. **The evidence or example.** **Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα είναι…**
4. **The link back to the thesis.** **Συνεπώς, …**

**A worked paragraph:**

> **Κατά πρώτον, η γλώσσα μαθαίνεται μέσα από τη χρήση και όχι μέσα από τους κανόνες. Αυτό συμβαίνει επειδή η κατανόηση προηγείται της παραγωγής: κανείς δεν μίλησε ποτέ μια γλώσσα που δεν είχε πρώτα ακούσει. Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα είναι τα παιδιά, που μαθαίνουν τη μητρική τους χωρίς καμία διδασκαλία γραμματικής. Συνεπώς, η μελέτη των κανόνων είναι χρήσιμη μόνο εφόσον συνοδεύεται από άφθονη επαφή με τη γλώσσα.**

**The vocabulary of argument:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **υποστηρίζω ότι** | I maintain that |
| **θεωρώ ότι / πιστεύω ότι** | I consider / believe that |
| **το επιχείρημα** | the argument |
| **το γεγονός ότι** | the fact that |
| **η άποψη** | the view |
| **η θέση** | the position |
| **αποδεικνύει / δείχνει ότι** | proves / shows that |
| **οδηγεί στο συμπέρασμα ότι** | leads to the conclusion that |
| **έχει ως αποτέλεσμα** | has as its result |
| **το πλεονέκτημα / το μειονέκτημα** | the advantage / the disadvantage |
| **ο λόγος για τον οποίο** | the reason for which |
| **Κατά πρώτον / δεύτερον** | firstly / secondly |
| **Επιπροσθέτως** | moreover — formal |
| **Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα είναι** | a characteristic example is |

**The hedges, which are what make an argument credible rather than shrill:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **κατά τη γνώμη μου** | in my opinion |
| **σε μεγάλο βαθμό** | to a large extent |
| **μέχρι ενός σημείου** | up to a point |
| **σε γενικές γραμμές** | broadly speaking |
| **φαίνεται ότι** | it seems that |
| **ενδέχεται να** | it may be that |
| **υπό ορισμένες προϋποθέσεις** | under certain conditions |
| **δεν είναι βέβαιο ότι** | it is not certain that |

**A B2 text is marked up for hedging and down for flat assertion**, and the same is true of how it reads to a person.

**The conclusion, which must state a position:**

> **Συμπερασματικά, θεωρώ ότι… Αυτό δεν σημαίνει ότι…, αλλά ότι… Και αν κάτι αξίζει να κρατήσουμε, είναι ότι…**

**The three failures to avoid:**

1. **No thesis.** A text that discusses without concluding. Greek convention is harder on this than English.
2. **Assertion without reason.** Each claim needs its **επειδή**.
3. **Register drift.** An argument is level 3, so no **λοιπόν**, no **ρε**, and **εσείς** if you address the reader at all.

**Practice.** Write a three-hundred-word argument, in the full πρόλογος–κύριο μέρος–επίλογος shape, on something you actually hold a view about. Two body paragraphs, each in the four moves, with at least three hedges. Then check: is there a thesis sentence, and does the conclusion state a position?
Arguing: conceding and refuting:
The second half of argument, and what separates a B2 text from a B1 one: handling the other side.

**Why it matters.** A text that only argues its own case reads as naive. Acknowledging the opposing view and then answering it is what makes an argument persuasive, and Greek has a specific apparatus for it.

**The concession-and-counter move**, which is the single most useful structure in argumentative writing:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Είναι αλήθεια ότι…, όμως…** | it is true that…, however… |
| **Αναμφίβολα…, παρ' όλα αυτά…** | undoubtedly…, nevertheless… |
| **Δεν μπορεί να αμφισβητηθεί ότι…, από την άλλη…** | it cannot be disputed that…, on the other hand… |
| **Αν και…, εντούτοις…** | although…, nevertheless… |
| **Παρά το γεγονός ότι…** | despite the fact that… |
| **Ορισμένοι υποστηρίζουν ότι…** | some maintain that… |
| **Θα μπορούσε να αντιτείνει κανείς ότι…** | one might object that… |
| **Σε αυτό θα απαντούσα ότι…** | to that I would answer that… |

**A worked concession:**

> **Είναι αλήθεια ότι η μελέτη της γραμματικής απαιτεί χρόνο που θα μπορούσε να αφιερωθεί στην ανάγνωση. Αναμφίβολα, μάλιστα, υπάρχουν μαθητές που έμαθαν μια γλώσσα χωρίς ποτέ να ανοίξουν γραμματική. Παρ' όλα αυτά, η εμπειρία δείχνει ότι οι περισσότεροι ενήλικες προχωρούν γρηγορότερα όταν καταλαβαίνουν τι ακούν. Η γραμματική, δηλαδή, δεν αντικαθιστά την επαφή με τη γλώσσα — την κάνει αποδοτικότερη.**

**The shape: concede fully, then turn.** A half-hearted concession is worse than none, because the reader sees it.

**The ways to refute**, in increasing strength:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Αυτό ισχύει μόνο εν μέρει.** | that is only partly true |
| **Το επιχείρημα αυτό παραβλέπει ότι…** | this argument overlooks that… |
| **Η άποψη αυτή συγχέει… με…** | this view confuses… with… |
| **Δεν προκύπτει ότι…** | it does not follow that… |
| **Το αντίθετο μάλιστα συμβαίνει.** | the opposite is in fact the case |
| **Η θέση αυτή δεν τεκμηριώνεται.** | this position is not substantiated |
| **Θα ήταν υπερβολή να πούμε ότι…** | it would be an exaggeration to say that… |

**Το επιχείρημα αυτό παραβλέπει ότι…** is the workhorse and worth memorising whole.

**Qualifying your own claim**, which is the other half of the skill:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **εφόσον / υπό την προϋπόθεση ότι** | provided that |
| **εκτός αν** | unless |
| **σε ορισμένες περιπτώσεις** | in certain cases |
| **όχι πάντα, αλλά συχνά** | not always, but often |
| **κυρίως / ιδίως** | mainly / particularly |
| **τουλάχιστον όσον αφορά…** | at least as regards… |

**The connective that carries the turn: όμως, and where it sits.** Unlike *however*, it commonly comes second or third in its clause:

> **Αυτό όμως δεν σημαίνει τίποτα.** — and that is the natural Greek placement.
> **Όμως αυτό δεν σημαίνει τίποτα.** — also correct, and slightly more emphatic.

**The tone note**, which is a real difference from English. Greek argumentative writing is **more direct** than British English: **Αυτό είναι λάθος** is normal where a British writer would say *this is perhaps not quite right*. Over-hedging in Greek reads as evasive rather than polite.

**So the balance is**: hedge your own claims, and refute the other side plainly.

**The debate register, spoken**, which is worth knowing because conversation after the service turns into it:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Συμφωνώ, αλλά…** | I agree, but… |
| **Δεν συμφωνώ καθόλου.** | I don't agree at all |
| **Έχεις δίκιο σε αυτό.** | you're right about that |
| **Ναι, αλλά σκέψου και…** | yes, but consider also… |
| **Δεν είναι έτσι ακριβώς.** | it's not quite like that |
| **Με την ίδια λογική…** | by the same logic… |
| **Ας συμφωνήσουμε ότι διαφωνούμε.** | let's agree to disagree |

**Practice.** Take the argument you wrote last lesson and add a concession paragraph: state the strongest objection fully, then turn it. Then take someone else's view you disagree with and refute it in three sentences, using **παραβλέπει**, **εν μέρει** and **δεν προκύπτει ότι**.
Summarising:
Saying in five sentences what someone else said in a thousand, which is the hardest short task in a second language and the best single exercise in it.

**Why it is hard, and why it is worth it.** A summary requires full comprehension, the judgement to decide what matters, and the ability to say it in your own words rather than the author's. **You cannot fake any of the three.** It is also the exercise that most directly converts reading into writing.

**The method:**

1. **Read the whole thing** without notes.
2. **Say what it was about in one sentence**, out loud, without looking.
3. **Reread, and mark the main claim of each paragraph.** One phrase each.
4. **Write the summary from your marks, not from the text.** Looking back at the original makes you copy its sentences.
5. **Check**: have you kept the author's emphasis, or imposed your own?
6. **Cut by a third.**

**Step four is the discipline that makes it work.** Writing with the text open produces paraphrase; writing from marks produces summary.

**The length conventions:** a summary is usually a quarter to a tenth of the original. The Ellinomatheia paper specifies a word count, and hitting it is part of the task.

**The reporting verbs, which are what a summary is built from** — and choosing well tells the reader the author's stance:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **αναφέρει ότι** | states that — neutral |
| **υποστηρίζει ότι** | maintains, argues that |
| **τονίζει ότι** | stresses that |
| **επισημαίνει ότι** | points out that |
| **διαπιστώνει ότι** | finds, observes that |
| **καταλήγει στο συμπέρασμα ότι** | concludes that |
| **αμφισβητεί** | questions, disputes |
| **παραδέχεται ότι** | concedes that |
| **προτείνει να** | proposes that |
| **διερωτάται αν** | asks whether |
| **αντιτίθεται σε** | opposes |
| **συνδέει… με…** | links… with… |

**The frame of a summary:**

> **Στο άρθρο αυτό ο συγγραφέας υποστηρίζει ότι… Για να στηρίξει τη θέση του, αναφέρεται σε… Επισημαίνει, επιπλέον, ότι… Παραδέχεται ότι…, αλλά τονίζει ότι… Καταλήγει στο συμπέρασμα ότι…**

**That frame fits almost any argumentative text** and is worth having by heart.

**The three rules:**

1. **No new information.** A summary adds nothing.
2. **No opinion.** Your view goes in a separate paragraph, clearly marked: **Προσωπικά, θεωρώ ότι…**
3. **No copied sentences.** If a phrase is unavoidable, quote it: **όπως γράφει, «…»**.

**The two things to keep that learners drop**: the author's **main claim**, stated as a claim rather than as a topic, and the **structure** of the argument — that there were three reasons, that the second was conceded.

**And the thing to drop that learners keep**: examples. An example illustrates a point; the summary keeps the point. **Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα…** has no place in a summary unless the example is the argument.

**The spoken version, which is the retelling habit from stage 8**, and the two reinforce each other: the thirty-second out-loud retelling is a summary under time pressure, and writing summaries makes the retellings better.

**Practice.** Take one essay from your reading and summarise it in five sentences, using the frame and at least four different reporting verbs. Write it from your marks with the original closed. Then compare it to the original and ask whether you kept its emphasis.
A review, and an opinion piece:
Two real forms you can write and publish — a comment, a review, a post — which makes them the first writing in this stage with an audience.

**The review — η κριτική**, of a book, a film, a restaurant, a place.

**Its four parts:**

1. **What it is**, in one sentence — the facts.
2. **What it does**, without spoiling it.
3. **What is good and what is not.**
4. **The verdict**, with a recommendation.

**A worked short review:**

> **Το «Καπλάνι της βιτρίνας» της Άλκης Ζέη είναι ένα μυθιστόρημα για παιδιά που διαβάζεται και από ενήλικες.**
>
> **Η ιστορία τοποθετείται σε ένα ελληνικό νησί τη δεκαετία του '30 και παρακολουθεί δύο αδελφές στα χρόνια της δικτατορίας του Μεταξά. Τα γεγονότα δίνονται μέσα από τα μάτια ενός παιδιού, κάτι που κάνει τη βία της εποχής ακόμη πιο αισθητή.**
>
> **Το μεγαλύτερο πλεονέκτημα του βιβλίου είναι η γλώσσα του: απλή, καθαρή, χωρίς διάθεση να εντυπωσιάσει. Από την άλλη, ο αναγνώστης που δεν γνωρίζει την ελληνική ιστορία μπορεί να χάσει μέρος του υπονοούμενου.**
>
> **Το συνιστώ ανεπιφύλακτα, και ιδιαίτερα σε όποιον μαθαίνει ελληνικά.**

**The review vocabulary:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **το βιβλίο / η ταινία / η παράσταση** | the book / film / performance |
| **ο συγγραφέας / ο σκηνοθέτης / ο ηθοποιός** | author / director / actor |
| **η πλοκή** | the plot |
| **ο ήρωας, ο πρωταγωνιστής** | the hero, the protagonist |
| **διαδραματίζεται / τοποθετείται** | is set |
| **πραγματεύεται** | deals with |
| **αξίζει τον κόπο** | is worth the trouble |
| **με συγκίνησε** | it moved me |
| **με απογοήτευσε** | it disappointed me |
| **υπερτιμημένο** | overrated |
| **το συνιστώ ανεπιφύλακτα** | I recommend it unreservedly |
| **δεν με έπεισε** | it didn't convince me |

**The opinion piece — το άρθρο γνώμης**, which is the argument lesson applied to a current subject and written for a real reader.

**What makes it different from an essay**: it has an occasion. Greek opinion writing almost always opens with the news hook:

> **Με αφορμή τη συζήτηση που άνοιξε τις τελευταίες μέρες για…**
> **Η πρόσφατη απόφαση για… φέρνει ξανά στο προσκήνιο ένα παλιό ζήτημα.**

**Με αφορμή…** — *prompted by…* — is the standard opening of Greek opinion writing and worth having.

**And it closes with a turn, not a summary:**

> **Το ερώτημα, τελικά, δεν είναι αν… αλλά αν…**
> **Και αυτό, νομίζω, είναι το ουσιαστικό.**

**The restaurant or place review**, which is the easiest to write and the most likely to be read:

> **Μικρό μαγαζί, στην άκρη της αγοράς, χωρίς τραπέζια έξω. Παραγγείλαμε…, και ήταν από τα καλύτερα που έχω φάει. Η τιμή λογική, η εξυπηρέτηση ζεστή. Το μόνο μειονέκτημα είναι ο χώρος: γεμίζει γρήγορα, και δεν δέχονται κρατήσεις. Θα ξαναπάω.**

**The social-media opinion**, which is three sentences and has its own rules: a claim, a reason, and no hedging — the format rewards directness and punishes length.

**The honest caution about publishing.** Posting Greek in public means being corrected in public, sometimes bluntly. **That is a feature**, not a hazard: a corrected sentence is worth ten uncorrected ones, and Greeks correcting a foreigner's Greek are almost always pleased rather than scornful. The next lesson is about what to do with it.

**And the register check**: a review is level 2, an opinion piece level 2 or 3, a social-media comment level 1 or 2. **Match the place.**

**Practice.** Write three things and post at least one: a short review of the last Greek book or film you finished, a three-sentence opinion on something current, and a review of a place you know. Then read the replies.
Writing to the Church:
The forms of address for clergy and monastics, which are fixed, which matter, and which are the one place where this curriculum asks you to produce the learned register.

**Why it is an exception to his ruling.** Everywhere else the learned forms are read and not written. Here they are not optional: a letter to a bishop that opens **Γεια σας** is not informal, it is wrong, and the correct forms are formulae rather than a register you have to control. **Learn the formulas whole.**

**The address for a priest — ο ιερέας, ο πρεσβύτερος:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spoken** | **Πάτερ** — the vocative of πατήρ, and the universal address |
| **With a name** | **Πάτερ Νικόλαε** — the name in the vocative too |
| **Letter opening** | **Αιδεσιμότατε Πάτερ,** or more simply **Σεβαστέ Πάτερ,** |
| **Of a married priest's wife** | **η πρεσβυτέρα** — and addressed as **Πρεσβυτέρα** |
| **Referring to him** | **ο πατήρ Νικόλαος**, or **ο π. Νικόλαος** in writing |
| **Close** | **Με βαθύ σεβασμό,** or **Ασπάζομαι τη δεξιά σας,** |

**Ασπάζομαι τη δεξιά σας** — *I kiss your right hand* — is the traditional close of a letter to a priest or bishop, and it is entirely ordinary in Greek church correspondence.

**For an archimandrite or a senior priest:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spoken** | **Πάτερ**, or **Γέροντα** if he is one's spiritual father |
| **Letter** | **Πανοσιολογιώτατε,** |

**For a bishop — ο επίσκοπος:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spoken** | **Σεβασμιώτατε** — for a metropolitan; **Θεοφιλέστατε** for an auxiliary bishop |
| **Letter opening** | **Σεβασμιώτατε Πάτερ και Δέσποτα,** |
| **Referring to him** | **ο Σεβασμιώτατος Μητροπολίτης [of the see]** |
| **Close** | **Ασπαζόμενος τη δεξιάν σας, διατελώ ελάχιστος εν Χριστώ,** |

**For an archbishop or patriarch:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Archbishop** | **Μακαριώτατε** |
| **Patriarch** | **Παναγιώτατε** — for the Ecumenical Patriarch |
| **Referring** | **ο Μακαριώτατος Αρχιεπίσκοπος**, **η Υμετέρα Παναγιότης** |

**For monastics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A monk** | **Πάτερ**, or **Γέροντα** for an elder |
| **An abbot** | **Πανοσιολογιώτατε**, or **Γέροντα** |
| **A nun** | **Αδελφή**, or **Γερόντισσα** for an abbess |
| **An abbess, in writing** | **Οσιωτάτη Γερόντισσα,** |
| **A deacon** | **Διάκονε**, in writing **Ιερολογιώτατε** |

**The superlative -τατος ending is the pattern**, and it is the ancient superlative: **Σεβασμιώτατος** (most reverend), **Παναγιώτατος** (all-holy), **Μακαριώτατος** (most blessed), **Πανοσιολογιώτατος**, **Αιδεσιμότατος**, **Οσιωτάτη**. **They are all vocatives in -ε or -η when you address someone**, which is why they look unfamiliar.

**A worked letter to a priest:**

> **Σεβαστέ Πάτερ Νικόλαε,**
>
> **Ευλογείτε.**
>
> **Θα ήθελα να σας ευχαριστήσω για τη θερμή υποδοχή της περασμένης Κυριακής, και για τον χρόνο που μου αφιερώσατε. Η συζήτησή μας με βοήθησε περισσότερο απ' όσο μπορώ να γράψω.**
>
> **Θα ήθελα, αν είναι δυνατόν, να σας ζητήσω… [the request]**
>
> **Σας ευχαριστώ εκ βάθους καρδίας και ζητώ τις ευχές σας.**
>
> **Με βαθύ σεβασμό,**
> **[name]**

**Two things in that letter are worth naming.**

**Ευλογείτε** — *bless* — is what you say to a priest on meeting him, in person and at the head of a letter, and the reply is **Ο Κύριος**. It functions as the greeting, in place of **Καλημέρα**. **It is the single most useful word in this lesson.**

**Ζητώ τις ευχές σας** — *I ask your prayers* — is the standard closing request, and it is expected rather than presumptuous.

**The other fixed phrases of church correspondence:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Ευλογείτε. — Ο Κύριος.** | Bless. — The Lord (blesses). |
| **Δι' ευχών σας** | through your prayers |
| **Ζητώ τις ευχές σας** | I ask your prayers |
| **Εύχομαι καλή δύναμη** | I wish you strength — for someone working or in a hard time |
| **Καλή Σαρακοστή** | a good Lent |
| **Καλή Ανάσταση** | a good Resurrection — before Pascha |
| **Χριστός Ανέστη! — Αληθώς Ανέστη!** | Christ is risen! — Truly He is risen! |
| **Χρόνια πολλά** | many years — for a feast, a name day, a birthday |
| **Αιωνία η μνήμη** | eternal be his memory — for the dead |
| **Ο Θεός να τον αναπαύσει** | may God give him rest |
| **Με αγάπη Χριστού** | with the love of Christ — a warm close |
| **Αμήν** | and it ends things in a group chat too |

**The honest note about the register.** Several of those are Koine or Byzantine rather than modern Greek — **Ανέστη, Αληθώς, Αιωνία, Δι' ευχών** — and that is exactly the point made in stage 7: they survive as whole formulas because they belong to the Church. **You use them without analysing them**, and the later curriculum is where they get taken apart.

**Practice.** Write two letters: one to a priest thanking him for something real, and one to a monastery asking a question. Use the correct opening and close for each. Then learn **Ευλογείτε / Ο Κύριος** well enough to say it without thinking, because you will need it this Sunday.
Editing your own Greek:
The checklist, in order, which is the most valuable single page of this stage — because a text edited against it is worth three texts written and abandoned.

**The rule that makes editing possible: leave it a day.** You cannot see your own sentences an hour after writing them. Write today, edit tomorrow. If there is no tomorrow, read it aloud, which is the next best thing.

**The checklist, in the order that catches most for least effort:**

**1. Read it aloud.** First, before anything else. Half your errors are audible: a wrong ending, a missing article, a clause with no verb, a sentence that will not end.

**2. One main verb per sentence, and it is present.** Find it. Front-loaded Greek sentences lose their verb.

**3. Agreement.** Every article, adjective and noun in the same gender, number and case. Check the chains especially — **η απόφαση της κυβέρνησης** — where a genitive run invites a slip.

**4. Case after prepositions.** **σε, από, με, για, προς** take the accusative. **λόγω, εξαιτίας, κατά** (in the sense of *according to*) take the genitive. **μετά** takes the accusative for *after*.

**5. Aspect in every past verb.** Event or background? Aorist or imperfect? A narrative with the wrong choice is comprehensible and wrong.

**6. The participles' subjects.** Every **-οντας** participle's subject must be the main clause's subject.

**7. The accents.** One per polysyllabic word. Count them.

**8. The *i* spellings.** For every *i*, ask whether it is an ending. If it is, the grammar decides.

**9. Final -ν** on **τον, την, δεν, μην, έναν**.

**10. Register.** One level, held from the first word to the last. Look for the stray **λοιπόν** in a formal text and the stray **επομένως** in a message.

**11. Connectives.** Is each one doing the job you think? Replace every lazy **και** and **γιατί**.

**12. Length.** Cut by a tenth. There is always a tenth.

**The errors specific to an English speaker writing Greek**, which are not on the general list and are worth a second pass:

| Error | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| **Missing article** | Greek uses the article where English does not: **η Ελλάδα, ο Γιάννης, η ζωή** |
| **A possessive adjective** | Greek has none: **το σπίτι μου**, not *το μου σπίτι* |
| **An infinitive** | there is none: **θέλω να πάω**, not *θέλω πάω* |
| **Pronoun order** | **μου το έδωσε**, indirect before direct, and both before the verb |
| **A subject pronoun in every sentence** | drop **εγώ** unless it is emphatic |
| **English word order for emphasis** | Greek moves the word instead |
| **για να for every purpose** | and **να** alone after verbs of wanting |
| **English punctuation** | **?** instead of **;** |
| **Calquing an idiom** | translating an English expression word for word. If you have not read it in Greek, do not write it. |

**The last row is the editing rule of this whole stage**: **delete any sentence whose shape you have not seen in Greek.** Replace it with two simpler ones you know are right.

**The two-pass method**, which is faster than one careful pass:

**Pass one, for sense**: read aloud, fix the sentences that do not work, cut what is not needed. Ignore spelling entirely.

**Pass two, for form**: items 3 to 9 above, mechanically, one at a time. Do not reread for sense — you will start rewriting.

**And keep the file.** Every text you write in this stage goes in one place, dated. The file is the stage's deliverable and the measure of the year.

**Practice.** Take the two hundred words you wrote in the first lesson of this stage. Run the twelve-item checklist on it, then the English-speaker list. Count what you found by category. Then do the same to something you wrote last week, and see whether the categories have changed.
Getting corrected:
How to get your Greek corrected, which is the scarcest resource in self-teaching — and what to do with a correction once you have one.

**The problem, stated plainly.** You cannot correct what you cannot see. Everything in the last lesson catches errors you know how to look for; the errors that matter most are the ones you do not know are errors, and only a Greek speaker will find those.

**Where corrections come from, free:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One person at church** | the best source, and the ask from stage 8: **Διόρθωσέ με, σε παρακαλώ.** |
| **A language exchange** | Tandem, HelloTalk — correction is the explicit deal |
| **Journaly, LangCorrect, and the writing-exchange sites** | you write a paragraph, natives correct it, you correct their English |
| **r/greek and the learner forums** | post a sentence, get three answers and an argument |
| **Comment threads** | post in Greek in public and you will be corrected, invited or not |
| **A corpus search** | not a person, and the next best thing: search the exact phrase in quotes and see whether Greeks write it |

**LangCorrect and Journaly deserve the recommendation**: they are built for exactly this, they are free, and the reciprocity makes it fair — you correct someone's English, which costs you nothing, and a native rewrites your paragraph.

**How to ask so that you get a useful answer:**

1. **Short.** A paragraph, not a page. Nobody corrects a page for free.
2. **Say what you were trying to say**, in English, so the corrector can tell you what you actually wrote.
3. **Ask for the natural version, not the correct one.** *Is this right?* gets you *yes, fine*. **Πώς θα το έλεγες εσύ;** — *how would you say it?* — gets you the real answer.
4. **Ask about one thing** if you want detail.
5. **Thank them, and correct something of theirs.**

**Point three is the important one.** Learners get told their Greek is correct when it is correct and foreign, which is the hardest problem to fix because nothing is wrong. **Ask for the native version and compare.**

**What to do with a correction, which is where most of the value is lost:**

1. **Write down both versions**, yours and theirs, side by side.
2. **Work out what kind of error it was.** Grammar? Vocabulary? Register? Idiom? Or simply not what a Greek would say?
3. **If it is a pattern, make a card** — a sentence card with the corrected version.
4. **If it is a one-off, note it and let it go.**
5. **Reuse the corrected sentence** within a week, deliberately, in speech or writing. **A correction you do not reuse is forgotten within a fortnight.**

**Step five is the one that converts a correction into Greek you own.**

**The error categories worth tracking**, because the pattern tells you what to study:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Form errors** | endings, agreement, aspect. Study the Forms track. |
| **Spelling errors** | the Spelling track. |
| **Word-choice errors** | you used a real word wrongly. More reading. |
| **Collocation errors** | the words do not go together in Greek. Reverso Context. |
| **Register errors** | right words, wrong level. This stage. |
| **Calques** | an English idiom in Greek words. **Stop composing and start imitating.** |

**If most of your corrections are the last two, you are writing English in Greek**, and the fix is reading rather than study.

**The thing to brace for, honestly.** Greek correction is blunt. **Δεν λέμε έτσι** — *we don't say it like that* — with no cushioning, is not rudeness; it is the normal register of help. And it is far more useful than the British habit of saying *that's lovely* and letting the error stand.

**And the thing in your favour, from stage 8**: a foreigner writing Greek is a rarity, and the pleasure people take in it means you will get more help than you ask for. Use it.

**Practice.** Write one paragraph and get it corrected — post it on LangCorrect, send it to an exchange partner, or hand it to someone at church. Write both versions side by side. Then classify the errors by the six categories above, and use one corrected sentence this week.
Where you should be at the end of stage:
The honest checkpoint: what you can do, what you still cannot, and whether it is time to move.

**What you should be able to write**, without help and in about half an hour each:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A message or a comment** | in the right informal register, with the abbreviations understood |
| **An email** | to a friend, a stranger, or an office, with the register chosen deliberately |
| **A formal letter** | with the layout, the date, the vocative and the correct close |
| **A letter to a priest or a monastery** | with the forms of address right |
| **An application** | four lines, requesting a certificate |
| **A notice or a programme** | in the terse public register |
| **A description** | of a place or a person, in the right tense |
| **A narrative** | two hundred words, aspect under control |
| **An explanation** | with the impersonal passive and a structure |
| **An argument** | three hundred words, with a thesis, reasons, a concession and a conclusion |
| **A summary** | five sentences of someone else's thousand |
| **A review** | and you should have posted one |

**What you should be able to do mechanically:**

- Write by hand at speed, with the accents placed.
- Type Greek without thinking about the layout.
- Punctuate properly — **;** and **« »** and the apostrophes.
- Edit yourself against the twelve-item checklist.
- Name the register of any Greek text you read.
- Read the learned forms in an official or church document without stalling.

**What you still cannot do, and should not expect to:**

- **Write literary Greek.** That is not a stage, it is a life's work, and the same is true in English.
- **Produce the learned register.** By ruling, and it belongs to the classical curriculum.
- **Write without errors.** Nobody does. The goal was to know your own error list.
- **Write fast.** Fluency in writing comes from volume, and this stage gave you method rather than volume.

**The honest state of the four skills now:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reading** | B2, going to C1 with time — stage 8's work, continuing |
| **Listening** | B2 — same |
| **Writing** | B2 — this stage |
| **Speaking** | depends entirely on whether the ten minutes a week happened |

**That last row is the one to look at.** Writing and reading can be done alone; speaking cannot, and a learner at this point is often B2 in three skills and B1 in the fourth. If that is you, the fix is not another stage — it is the parish, weekly, in Greek.

**The checkpoint questions:**

1. **Is there a file of what you wrote in this stage**, and does it have a dozen texts in it?
2. **Has anything you wrote been corrected by a Greek?**
3. **Can you write a letter to a priest without looking up the forms?**
4. **Did you write the argument, with a concession in it?**
5. **Can you name the register of a text at a glance?**
6. **Are the Spelling and Forms tracks finished?**

**If the answer to the second is no, that is the gap.** Everything else in this stage you can do alone; correction you cannot, and writing without it fossilises.

**What comes next.** Two stages remain: **Cyprus**, which is twenty lessons on the dialect he asked for by name, and **Literature and ad astra**, which is open-ended and has no end. Neither is a prerequisite for the other, and neither is a prerequisite for continuing stage 8's reading, which should by now simply be what you do.

**And the other thing that comes next**: the classical curriculum, whenever you want it. Nothing is gating it. **Everything from here is addition rather than progression.**

**Practice.** Answer the six questions honestly, in the journal. Then read the two hundred words you wrote in the first lesson of this stage, and mark every error you can now see. That count is the stage's real result.
Review: stage 9:
Thirty lessons on producing Greek, and the stage most self-taught learners skip.

**The mechanics**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Handwriting at speed** | the joins, the accent as one movement at the end of a word, and dictation as the best combined drill in the curriculum |
| **Spelling under pressure** | six error types, and the endings are grammar rather than memory |
| **Punctuation** | **;** for a question, **·** for a semicolon, **« »** for quotes, the apostrophe for elision, a comma around every vocative |

**The sentence and the text**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Five ways to extend a sentence** | coordination, subordination, relatives, participles, nominalisation |
| **Front-loading** | the most characteristic move of written Greek |
| **The connective inventory** | by job: adding, contrasting, causing, concluding, exemplifying, sequencing, qualifying |
| **The paragraph** | four to eight sentences, one idea; πρόλογος, κύριο μέρος, επίλογος |
| **Known-to-new order** | each sentence starting from the last one's new information |

**Register**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Four levels** | intimate, neutral, formal, learned |
| **Hold one level** | the commonest learner error in writing is mixing them |
| **Neutral is the default** | most of what you write is level 2 |
| **The written apparatus** | the passive to hide the agent, ten impersonals, nominalisation in **-ση**, the participle replacing a clause |
| **The learned exception list** | **ο οποίος**, **ο εν λόγω**, the fixed datives, **εκ/εξ**, **υπέρ/κατά**, the formal verbs, and the clergy's forms of address |

**The practical texts**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A message** | accents kept, though natives drop them |
| **An email** | three registers, and the vocative in **-ε** |
| **A formal letter** | place and date, **Θέμα:**, **Με εκτίμηση**, **Παρακαλώ για τις δικές σας ενέργειες** |
| **A form** | πατρώνυμο, Α.Φ.Μ., υπεύθυνη δήλωση, and **χορηγήσετε** |
| **A notice** | verbless, capitals, genitives, **π.μ./μ.μ.** |
| **A CV** | and writing it is the best self-description exercise there is |
| **To the Church** | **Ευλογείτε. — Ο Κύριος.** and **Ζητώ τις ευχές σας** |

**The four modes**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Describing** | adjectives, prepositions of place, and the **imperfect** |
| **Narrating** | aorist for events, imperfect for background, the historic present for a told story |
| **Explaining** | the impersonal passive, the four sequencers, known-to-new |
| **Arguing** | thesis, four moves per paragraph, hedges, and the concession-and-turn |
| **Summarising** | written from marks with the original closed, and the reporting verbs |

**The discipline**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Leave it a day** | you cannot see your own sentences an hour later |
| **The twelve-item checklist** | read aloud first; then verb, agreement, case, aspect, participles, accents, *i*, final -ν, register, connectives, and cut a tenth |
| **The English-speaker list** | the missing article, the possessive, the infinitive that does not exist, and the calque |
| **The rule of the stage** | **write what you can say; delete any sentence whose shape you have not seen in Greek** |
| **Get corrected** | ask **Πώς θα το έλεγες εσύ;**, write both versions, and reuse the corrected one within a week |

**Where you are.** B2 across all four skills, if the speaking happened. You can write any practical text you need, argue a position, adapt the register, and edit yourself. **The file of what you wrote in this stage is the proof**, and rereading its first page is the most convincing thing in the curriculum.

**What remains.** Two stages, neither gating the other: **Cyprus**, twenty lessons, because he asked for standard **and** Cypriot; and **Literature, and ad astra**, which is open and does not finish. And underneath both, stage 8's reading, which should by now be a habit rather than a stage.

**And then the second curriculum** — classical Greek into theological and liturgical Greek, which is what all of this was for. There is no gate on it and no requirement to wait.

**Practice.** Read the first thing you wrote in this stage and the last. Then write one page, in Greek, about what you can now do in Greek that you could not a year ago — and put it at the front of the file.
What stage 10 is, and why Cyprus:
His answer to the dialect question was **standard and Cypriot**, so Cyprus gets a stage rather than a footnote. Twenty lessons on the largest divergence in the Greek-speaking world.

**What Cypriot Greek is.** The variety of Greek spoken by about a million people in Cyprus and by the Cypriot diaspora — which in Britain is the larger part of the Greek-speaking population. It is Greek, descended from the same Koine as the standard, and it is divergent enough that a Greek from Athens sometimes does not follow a Cypriot speaking freely.

**How divergent, honestly.** Not a separate language, and not a light accent either. It differs in:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sounds** | double consonants pronounced long, a **sh** sound the standard has not got, **κ** becoming **τζ** before front vowels |
| **Grammar** | the pronoun after the verb, a different future particle, **εν** for both *is* and *not*, ancient survivals the standard lost |
| **Vocabulary** | several hundred everyday words, plus layers from French, Italian, Turkish and English |
| **Register** | a genuine diglossia: the dialect at home, standard Greek in writing and in public |

**Why it matters to you specifically.** The Greek community in Britain is substantially Cypriot. **The Greeks at your church are statistically more likely to be Cypriot or of Cypriot descent than from Greece**, and the Greek you hear in the parish hall may be Cypriot rather than standard. That is the whole argument for this stage.

**What this stage is for, and what it is not.**

**It is for understanding.** By the end you should follow Cypriot speech, read Cypriot writing where you find it, and know what is dialect and what is standard — which is the main confusion for a learner, who otherwise thinks a Cypriot form is a mistake.

**It is not for producing.** A foreigner speaking Cypriot can come off as mockery, and the diglossia means a Cypriot will address you in standard Greek anyway. **Learn to understand it; keep speaking the standard** — and let the handful of words that are simply useful (**ίντα**, **λαλώ**, **κόρη**) enter your speech naturally if they do.

**The diglossia, which is the key to the whole stage.** Cypriots switch:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The dialect** | home, friends, the village, jokes, anger, affection, most speech |
| **Standard Greek** | school, writing, news, church, public speaking, talking to Greeks |
| **A mix** | most ordinary situations, sliding between them sentence by sentence |

**So every Cypriot can speak standard Greek**, and you are never dependent on the dialect. You are dependent on it to understand what is said when they are not speaking to you.

**What the stage covers**: the sounds, the writing problem, the grammar, the vocabulary and its four foreign layers, the food, the manner, the Church of Cyprus, the history and what not to say about it, the music, and where to find material.

**The resource that runs under all of it**: **Kypros.org**, which has been in this curriculum's resource list from stage 1 — 105 free audio lessons, Cyprus-based, in Cypriot-inflected Greek.

**Practice.** Listen to ten minutes of Cypriot speech — a clip from ΡΙΚ, a Cypriot sitcom, a street interview — and write down what percentage you follow. That is the number this stage moves.
The sounds of Cypriot:
The five phonological differences, which account for most of the difficulty — and once you can hear them, half the dialect becomes transparent.

**1. The double consonants are real.** Standard Greek writes **άλλος, θάλασσα, γράμμα** with double letters and pronounces one consonant. **Cypriot pronounces them long**, as Ancient Greek did:

> **άλλος** — *al-los*, the λ held
> **θάλασσα** — the σ held
> **γράμμα** — the μ held

**And Cypriot has far more of them**, including in words the standard spells single: **ούλλος** (όλος), **σ̌ύλλος** (σκύλος), **έννα** (θα).

**This is the single most audible feature of the dialect** and it is a retention rather than an innovation.

**2. The double voiceless stops are aspirated.** **ππ, ττ, κκ** come out with a puff of air, roughly as in English *pot, top, cat*:

> **παππούς** — the ππ aspirated, close to *pap-phous*
> **κόττα** (κότα, hen) — the ττ aspirated

**To an English ear this sounds more familiar than standard Greek**, whose stops are unaspirated.

**3. κ before ε and ι becomes τσ.** The commonest single feature:

| Standard | Cypriot |
| --- | --- |
| **και** | **τζαι** (also written τσαι, τζιαι) |
| **καιρός** | **τζαιρός** |
| **κερί** | **τζερί** |
| **εκείνος** | **ετσείνος** |
| **κυρία** | **τζυρά** |

**4. χ before ε and ι becomes sh.** A sound standard Greek does not have, written **σ̌** in linguistic work and **σι** or **sh** in ordinary writing:

| Standard | Cypriot |
| --- | --- |
| **χέρι** | **σ̌έρι** |
| **χίλια** | **σ̌ίλια** |
| **όχι** | **όσ̌ι** |
| **παιδί** (σκ-) | and **σκύλος** → **σ̌ύλλος** |

**That sh is the second most audible feature**, and it is the one that makes Cypriot recognisable in three words.

**5. Final -ν survives.** Standard Greek dropped it; Cypriot kept it:

| Standard | Cypriot |
| --- | --- |
| **καλό** | **καλόν** |
| **ποταμό** | **ποταμόν** |
| **είδαν / είδα** | **είδαν** |
| **το παιδί** | **το παιδίν** |

**And that too is a retention**, from the same ancient state the Spelling track's final-**ν** rule descends from.

**Two further features worth knowing:**

**Voicing after a nasal.** **έν πόλλα** → the π voiced; the dialect voices stops in places the standard does not.

**The intonation**, which no description captures: Cypriot has a distinctive contour, often described as flatter and more clipped than mainland Greek, with a rise at the end of statements.

**What this means for listening.** Run the five rules in reverse and most unfamiliar words resolve:

> **Ίντα τζαιρόν κάμνει;** → **κ** for **τζ**, final **-ν** off → *τι καιρό κάνει;* — *What's the weather doing?*
> **Εν θωρώ τίποτε.** → *δεν βλέπω τίποτα* — *I can't see anything.*

**Practice.** Take twenty Cypriot words from a clip or a song and run them back through the five rules to their standard forms. Then listen for the **sh** and the long consonants specifically, and count how often each occurs in a minute.
Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp:
A practical problem rather than a grammatical one: the dialect is written and has no agreed orthography, so the same word appears four ways.

**Why there is none.** Cypriot has never been an official written language. Standard Greek is what is taught, written, printed and used in church and government in Cyprus. The dialect is written anyway — in texts, in comments, in song lyrics, in comic strips, in dialect poetry — by people improvising a spelling.

**The result, for one word:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **και** → | **τζαι, τζιαι, τσαι, τσιαι, τζ̌αι** |
| **χέρι** → | **σ̌έρι, σιέρι, shέρι, σέρι** |
| **έννα** → | **έννα, εννά, έναν να, να** |

**So you must be able to read all of them**, and you should not try to settle which is right. There is no right.

**The three systems you will meet:**

**1. Ordinary improvised spelling**, which is what most people use: **τζαι, σιέρι, κόρη**. Approximate, readable, inconsistent.

**2. The linguists' system**, with carons, used in dictionaries and academic work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **σ̌** | the *sh* sound |
| **ζ̌** | its voiced partner |
| **τσ̌, τζ̌** | the affricates |
| **Doubled letters** | for the long consonants |

**3. Greeklish**, in messaging — and Cypriot Greeklish has its own conventions, with **sh** and **j** doing work no Greek letter does.

**What this means for you, practically:**

- **Read loosely.** Sound the word out and match it to a standard word.
- **Do not card Cypriot spellings** as spellings. Card the word and the meaning.
- **Expect the same text to be inconsistent** with itself.

**Where the dialect genuinely is written**, and these are worth knowing because they are the material:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Dialect poetry** | **Βασίλης Μιχαηλίδης** and **Δημήτρης Λιπέρτης** — the Cypriot canon, and in the dialect by choice |
| **Τσιαττιστά** | the improvised rhyming couplets, written down |
| **Song lyrics** | the folk revival, and rap |
| **Comics and cartoons** | where dialect is the joke |
| **Social media** | by far the largest body of written Cypriot |
| **Subtitles for comedy** | Cypriot sitcoms subtitled for Greek broadcast |

**The dictionaries, which solve most problems:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γιαγκουλλής, Λεξικό της Κυπριακής Διαλέκτου** | the standard reference, by the main Cypriot lexicographer |
| **The Academy of Athens' Ιστορικό Λεξικό** | historical, exhaustive, and for the serious question |
| **The Centre for Scientific Research of Cyprus** | publications and glossaries, much of it online |
| **Online dialect glossaries** | and the crowd-sourced ones, which are uneven and useful |

**The learner's shortcut when you meet an unknown Cypriot word**: apply the five sound rules in reverse first. If that yields a standard word, you are done. If not, it is one of the few hundred genuinely distinct items, or a loanword, and both are coming in later lessons.

**Practice.** Find one Cypriot text — a comment thread, a song's lyrics, a dialect poem — and read a paragraph. For each unfamiliar word, try the sound rules first. List the ones that do not resolve: those are the real vocabulary, and the next lessons cover most of them.
The grammar: pronouns and negation:
The grammatical differences you must know to parse a Cypriot sentence at all. There are not many, and three of them do most of the work.

**1. The weak pronoun follows the verb.** This is the big one. Standard Greek puts it before the verb in a statement; Cypriot puts it after:

| Standard | Cypriot |
| --- | --- |
| **σου λέω** | **λαλώ σου** |
| **σε βλέπω** | **θωρώ σε** |
| **μου είπε** | **είπεν μου** |
| **το ξέρω** | **ξέρω το** |
| **μας έδωσε** | **έδωκεν μας** |

**Why it matters.** This is the **older** Greek order — the standard's pre-verbal placement is the innovation. And it means a Cypriot sentence looks inside out to someone who learned the standard, which is the single commonest source of a learner's bafflement.

**And the standard's own exception is the key to remembering it**: standard Greek also puts the pronoun after the verb in the imperative — **πες μου, δώσ' μου, κοίτα με**. **Cypriot does that everywhere.**

**2. εν does two jobs.**

**εν = είναι:**

> **Εν καλόν.** — *It's good.*
> **Εν εδώ.** — *He's here.*
> **Ίντα εν τούτον;** — *What's this?*

**εν = δεν:**

> **Εν ξέρω.** — *I don't know.*
> **Εν θωρώ τίποτε.** — *I don't see anything.*
> **Εν εν καλόν.** — *It isn't good.* — and yes, both at once.

**Context distinguishes them**, and in practice a following verb means *not* while a following adjective, noun or adverb means *is*.

**3. The future is εννά, not θα.**

> **Εννά πάω.** — *I'll go.*
> **Εννά σου πω.** — *I'll tell you.*

Written **εννά, έννα, να**, and derived historically from **θέλω να**, as the standard's **θα** is. **Standard θα is also used in Cyprus**, especially in the more standard registers, so you will hear both.

**4. μεν for μην:**

> **Μεν πάεις.** — *Don't go.*

**5. The ancient interrogatives survive**, and this is the most charming part of the dialect:

| Cypriot | Standard | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ίντα** | τι | what |
| **ίνταλως / ίντα λοής** | πώς | how |
| **πόθεν** | από πού | from where — **the ancient word** |
| **πκοιος** | ποιος | who |
| **πόσον** | πόσο | how much |
| **ίντα μπου…** | τι είναι που… | what is it that… |

**πόθεν is Ancient Greek, unchanged**, and it is ordinary speech in Cyprus.

**6. Verb endings differ in places:**

| Standard | Cypriot |
| --- | --- |
| **είπε** | **είπεν** |
| **έδωσε** | **έδωκεν** |
| **κάνω** | **κάμνω** |
| **βλέπω** | **θωρώ** |
| **λέω** | **λαλώ** |
| **πηγαίνεις** | **πάεις** |
| **είμαστε** | **είμαστεν** |

**κάμνω, θωρώ and λαλώ are the three verbs to know**, because they are among the commonest verbs in the language and they are unrecognisable if you have only the standard.

**7. The ancient -ούμαι and -ώ verbs** are better preserved, and Cypriot keeps some old aorists: **είδα / είδεν**, **έφαα** (έφαγα), **ήρτα** (ήρθα).

**Putting it together:**

> **Ίντα λαλείς, κόρη; Εν σε θωρώ. Εννά έρτω αύριον.**
>
> *Τι λες, κορίτσι μου; Δεν σε βλέπω. Θα έρθω αύριο.*

**Practice.** Translate ten standard Greek sentences into Cypriot using the three main rules — pronoun after the verb, **εν** for **δεν**, **εννά** for **θα** — and then translate ten Cypriot sentences back. The point is parsing, not production.
The vocabulary that is genuinely differe:
The few hundred words that do not resolve by sound rules — the real learning of this stage, and the ones you will hear daily if the parish is Cypriot.

**The everyday core**, which is where to start:

| Cypriot | Standard | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ίντα** | τι | what |
| **λαλώ** | λέω | I say |
| **θωρώ** | βλέπω | I see |
| **κάμνω** | κάνω | I do, I make |
| **ούλλος, ούλλοι** | όλος, όλοι | all |
| **τούτος, τούτον** | αυτός, αυτό | this |
| **ετσείνος** | εκείνος | that |
| **μανιχός μου** | μόνος μου | by myself |
| **πελλός** | τρελός | mad, crazy |
| **μιτσής** | μικρός | small, young |
| **πόθεν** | από πού | from where |
| **εννά** | θα | will |
| **εν** | είναι / δεν | is / not |
| **μεν** | μην | don't |
| **τίποτε** | τίποτα | nothing |
| **πολλά** | πολύ | very — **and this one causes real confusion** |
| **ίσια** | ευθεία | straight ahead |
| **συντυχάννω** | μιλώ, συνομιλώ | I talk, I converse |
| **θέλω να** | and **θέλω** also means *I need* | |

**πολλά is worth its own note.** In Cypriot it means *very*, where standard Greek uses **πολύ** and reserves **πολλά** for *many things*. **Εν πολλά καλόν** is *it's very good*, not *it's many good*.

**People and family:**

| Cypriot | Standard | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **το κοπέλι** | το αγόρι, το παιδί | the boy, the child |
| **το κοπελλούι** | το παιδάκι | the little one |
| **η κοπέλα** | and in Cyprus it means a girl of any age | |
| **κόρη** | κορίτσι μου | **girl — and used as an address to any woman**, affectionately, including by women |
| **ρε κουμπάρε** | and **κουμπάρε** is the universal address between men | |
| **ο μάστρος** | ο μάστορας | the craftsman, and an address |
| **η γιαγιά, ο παππούς** | the same, with the long consonants | |
| **τζυρά, τζύρης** | κυρία, κύριος / πατέρας | madam, sir — and **τζύρης** can mean *father* |

**κόρη is the one to recognise first.** Hearing a man in his sixties call a woman of the same age **κόρη** is ordinary Cypriot affection, not condescension, and it has no standard-Greek equivalent.

**Things around the house and the day:**

| Cypriot | Standard | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **η τσαέρα** | η καρέκλα | the chair |
| **το ποτήριν** | το ποτήρι | the glass |
| **η πόρτα** | the same, with the long consonant | |
| **το τσακκούδι** | το μαχαιράκι | the little knife |
| **η λαμπρή** | το Πάσχα | **Easter** — *the bright one* |
| **η αυλή** | the same, and central to Cypriot domestic life | |
| **το σπίτιν** | το σπίτι | the house |
| **η στράτα** | ο δρόμος | the road |
| **το ποτάμιν** | το ποτάμι | the river |

**η Λαμπρή** is worth knowing: the Cypriot word for Pascha, from **λαμπρός**, *bright* — and it is the ordinary word, not a poeticism.

**Verbs you will hear:**

| Cypriot | Standard | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **πιάννω** | πιάνω, παίρνω | I take, I catch |
| **θέλω** | and in Cyprus also *I need* | |
| **αρκεύκω** | αργώ | I'm late |
| **φκάλλω** | βγάζω | I take out |
| **μπαίννω / βκαίννω** | μπαίνω / βγαίνω | I go in / out |
| **έρκουμαι** | έρχομαι | I come |
| **ποζέρνω / ποσπάζω** | — | dialect verbs with no neat standard equivalent |
| **χάννω** | χάνω | I lose |

**The method for learning these.** Do not try to learn them as a list. **Listen to Cypriot material, and when a word does not resolve by the sound rules, look it up and card it.** Thirty or forty of them cover most ordinary speech, and they will be the thirty or forty that your parish actually uses.

**Practice.** Watch or listen to twenty minutes of Cypriot and write down every word that does not resolve by the sound rules. Look them up. Card the ones that recurred — and expect **ίντα, λαλώ, θωρώ, κάμνω, ούλλοι, εν, εννά, πολλά** to be among them.
The four foreign layers:
Cyprus was ruled by Franks, Venetians, Ottomans and the British in succession, and each left words. Knowing which layer a word comes from makes it memorable and explains the island's history in vocabulary.

**The layers, in order:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Old French** | 1192–1489, the Lusignan kingdom |
| **Venetian Italian** | 1489–1571 |
| **Ottoman Turkish** | 1571–1878 |
| **English** | 1878–1960, and still |

**And underneath all four, the oldest layer**: Cypriot's own Ancient Greek retentions, which are not foreign at all — **πόθεν**, the long consonants, the final **-ν**, the post-verbal pronoun.

**The French and Italian layer**, from the three centuries of Latin rule:

| Cypriot | Origin | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **η τσαέρα** | French *chaise* / Italian | the chair |
| **κουμαντάρω** | Italian *comandare* | I manage, I command |
| **η κουμανταρία** | the Commandaria of the Knights | **the sweet wine**, named for the Grand Commandery — and reputedly the oldest named wine still made |
| **το μιτσέλλι** | Italian | — one of many building and household terms |
| **ο πιάτος, τα πιάτα** | Italian *piatto* | and in standard Greek too |

**The Commandaria is worth the detail**: the wine takes its name from the Grand Commandery, the Knights Hospitaller's estate around Kolossi, and it is one of the few things in modern Cypriot life whose name is directly Frankish.

**The Turkish layer**, the largest of the four, from three centuries of Ottoman rule — and found in food, administration, trade and daily objects:

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ο μουχτάρης** | the village headman |
| **το κιόσκι** | the kiosk, the pavilion |
| **ο τεντζερές** | the cooking pot |
| **ο μπακάλης** | the grocer |
| **το τζαμί** | the mosque |
| **ο χαλλούμης** | and the cheese's own name is debated between Greek and Semitic origins |
| **μπάφος, τσαττιστά, γιαλλούρι** | and a great many more |

**A caution worth stating.** Standard Greek also has hundreds of Turkish loanwords — **καφές, γιαούρτι, κέφι, μεζές, ντουβάρι** — so a Turkish origin does not mark a word as Cypriot. Cypriot simply has more of them, and keeps some that mainland Greek has replaced.

**And a sensitivity worth knowing.** Pointing out Turkish loanwords in Cypriot can land badly, given 1974. **Do not make a thing of it.** Linguists discuss it freely; it is not small talk.

**The English layer**, which is live and growing, from the colonial period and from the Cypriot diaspora in Britain:

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **το σάντουιτς, το μπρέκι** | sandwich, brake |
| **το κάρο** | the car — and standard Greek uses **αυτοκίνητο** |
| **μάρκετ, σουπερμάρκετ** | and these are everywhere |
| **πάρκιν, σέντερ, οφφις** | parking, centre, office |
| **φούλ** | full — and used as an intensifier, *completely* |

**The diaspora dimension matters to you.** Cypriot Greek as spoken in London, Birmingham and Nottingham has a further English layer again — words, whole phrases, and a code-switching habit mid-sentence. **That is the Greek you are most likely to hear in Britain**, and it is nobody's error: it is what a community language does in its third generation.

**Why this lesson is useful rather than ornamental.** Half the Cypriot words that do not resolve by sound rules are loanwords, and recognising the layer tells you where to look. A food word is probably Turkish; a household or legal word, Italian or French; anything to do with cars, shops or offices, English.

**Practice.** Take the list of unresolved words from the last lesson's practice and try to assign each to a layer. Then ask someone at church what they call a chair, a pot and the grocer — and listen for which layer answers.
Food and the table in Cyprus:
A vocabulary you will meet in the parish hall and at every Cypriot table — and the one part of this stage you can use immediately without sounding as though you are imitating anyone.

**The cheeses and dairy:**

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **το χαλλούμι** | halloumi — grilled, fried or raw, and the national food |
| **η αναρή** | anari, the fresh whey cheese — like ricotta |
