| **ο τραχανάς** | trachanas, cracked wheat soured with yoghurt, dried and made into soup |
| **το γιαούρτι** | yoghurt, and eaten with everything |

**Halloumi's two facts worth knowing**: it squeaks because it is heated during making, which is why it holds its shape on a grill; and it is traditionally made with sheep's and goat's milk, with mint between the folds.

**The dishes:**

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **τα κουπέπια** | stuffed vine leaves — mainland Greek calls them **ντολμαδάκια** |
| **το κολοκάσι** | taro root, braised with pork or chicken — a Cypriot staple with no mainland equivalent |
| **η σούβλα** | large pieces of meat on a long skewer over coals — **not souvlaki**, which is the small version |
| **τα σουβλάκια / το σεφταλιά** | and **σεφταλιά** is the Cypriot sausage in caul fat |
| **τα αφέλια** | pork in red wine and coriander seed |
| **οι κολοκοτές** | pumpkin and cracked wheat pasties |
| **το ρέσι** | the wheat-and-meat dish served at weddings |
| **το μακαρόνι του φούρνου** | the baked pasta — Cyprus's version of pastitsio |
| **τα λουβιά** | black-eyed beans, boiled and dressed with lemon and oil |
| **οι φλαούνες** | **the Easter cheese pastries** — made in Holy Week, eaten after the Resurrection |
| **τα δάκτυλα κυρίας** | *lady's fingers* — the almond pastries |
| **ο παλουζές, ο σουτζούκκος** | grape-must puddings, made at the vintage |
| **τα γλυκά του κουτάλιού** | spoon sweets — fruit in syrup, offered to a guest |

**οι φλαούνες deserve their place**, because they are a church food: made during the last week of the fast, filled with cheese, eggs, mint and raisins, and eaten the moment the fast breaks. **If the parish is Cypriot, they will appear at Pascha**, and knowing the word is worth a great deal socially.

**The drink:**

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η ζιβανία** | zivania, the grape spirit — strong, clear, and offered |
| **η κουμανταρία** | Commandaria, the sweet wine of the Knights' estates |
| **ο κυπριακός καφές** | and ordered the same way: **γλυκύς, μέτριος, σκέτος** |
| **το φραπέ** | and in Cyprus the iced coffee culture is as strong as in Greece |

**The table vocabulary:**

| Cypriot | English |
| --- | --- |
| **ο μεζές / οι μεζέδες** | the small dishes — and in Cyprus a **μεζέ** can be a whole twenty-course meal |
| **η ταβέρνα** | the taverna |
| **το καφενείο** | the village coffee shop — the social institution |
| **Καλή όρεξη!** | enjoy your meal |
| **Στην υγειά μας!** | to our health — and **Γεια μας!** |
| **Φάε!** | eat! — an instruction you will receive |
| **Εν πολλά νόστιμον!** | it's very tasty — **and with the Cypriot πολλά** |

**The Cypriot μεζέ is worth explaining** because you may be subjected to one: a sequence of twenty or thirty small dishes brought over two or three hours, ending with the grilled meat. Refusing food is difficult; **pacing yourself early is the only strategy.**

**The hospitality rules, from stage 7, intensified.** Cypriot hospitality is more insistent than mainland Greek, which is already insistent. You will be fed, you will be given more than you asked for, and the attempt to pay will be refused. **The correct response is to accept graciously and reciprocate later** — and **Να 'στε καλά** covers most of it.

**Practice.** Learn ten of these words — the ones most likely to appear at your parish. Then ask someone Cypriot what **φλαούνες** are and whether they make them, and let them talk.
Greetings and the Cypriot manner:
The social surface: how Cypriots greet, address and talk to each other, which differs from mainland Greek in ways worth knowing before you are in the hall.

**The greetings, which are mostly the standard ones with Cypriot sounds:**

| Cypriot | Standard | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Καλημέρα / Καλησπέρα** | the same | universal |
| **Είντα κάμνεις;** | τι κάνεις; | **the Cypriot *how are you***, and the one to recognise first |
| **Είντα νέα;** | τι νέα; | what's new |
| **Ίντα γίνεται;** | τι γίνεται; | what's happening |
| **Καλώς τον! / Καλώς τους!** | the same | *welcome* — said to the arriving person about them, in the third person |
| **Έλα!** | the same | and in Cyprus it also answers the telephone |
| **Γεια σου / Γεια σας** | the same | |
| **Τα λέμε** | the same | see you |
| **Να 'σαι καλά / Να 'στε καλά** | the same | **the universal Cypriot thanks and blessing** |

**Καλώς τον is worth the explanation**, because it is odd to an English ear: the host says **Καλώς τον!** — *welcome him* — rather than *welcome you*, in the third person, and the arriving guest replies **Καλώς σας βρήκα** — *I find you well*.

**The addresses, which are the distinctive part:**

| Cypriot | To whom |
| --- | --- |
| **κόρη** | **to any woman**, of any age, affectionately — and used by both men and women |
| **ρε κουμπάρε / κουμπάρε** | **to any man** — literally *godfather of my child*, in practice *mate* |
| **ρε / βρε** | as in standard Greek, and more freely |
| **μάστρε** | to a craftsman, and to any man whose name you don't know |
| **τζύρη / τζυρά** | father / madam |
| **παιδί μου, κοπέλι μου** | to someone younger |
| **αρφή μου** | *my brother* — αδελφή/αδελφός, contracted |

**κουμπάρε is the one you will hear constantly.** The kinship system makes the godfather of your child a lifelong relation, and the word has broadened until it means roughly *friend*. Being called **κουμπάρε** is a small welcome.

**The manner, honestly described:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Louder and more direct** | than mainland Greek, which is already both |
| **More physical** | the hand on the arm, the shoulder, the embrace |
| **Insistently hospitable** | past the point where a British person would stop |
| **Teasing as affection** | the πείραγμα, which is constant and is not hostility |
| **Slower to formality** | **εσύ** arrives faster than in Athens |
| **Village-rooted** | *where are you from?* means which village, and the answer matters |

**The πείραγμα deserves a note.** Cypriot sociability runs heavily on teasing — about your accent, your age, your football team, your appetite. **Being teased is being included**, and the correct response is to tease back or laugh, never to take offence or explain yourself.

**The question you will be asked:**

> **Πόθεν είσαι;** — *Where are you from?*

**And for a Cypriot the honest answer is a village**, even for someone born in London — **ο παππούς μου ήταν από…** Having a village is how a Cypriot is placed. You do not have one, and saying where you are from plainly, and then asking theirs, is the right move: **Εσείς πόθεν είστε;** will produce a long and happy answer.

**What Cypriots in Britain will do with your Greek.** They will be surprised, pleased, and they will probably switch to English to help you — the same reflex as mainland Greeks and the same answer: ask in Greek and keep going. **And several of them will tell you that what they speak "isn't proper Greek"**, which is the diglossia talking. It is proper Greek, and saying so is a kindness.

**Practice.** Learn **Είντα κάμνεις;**, **κόρη**, **κουμπάρε** and **Πόθεν είσαι;** well enough to recognise them instantly. Then ask one Cypriot person at church which village their family is from, and let the conversation go where it goes.
The Church of Cyprus:
The oldest autocephalous Church after the ancient patriarchates, with its own saints, its own privileges and its own place in Cypriot identity — and the part of this stage closest to the reason for the curriculum.

**The facts worth knowing:**

**Autocephaly since 431.** The Church of Cyprus was recognised as self-governing by the Council of Ephesus, making it one of the oldest autocephalous Churches in Orthodoxy — older than most of the national Churches by a millennium and a half.

**The three privileges of the Archbishop.** By tradition, granted by the Emperor Zeno after the discovery of the Apostle Barnabas's relics: the Archbishop of Cyprus signs in **cinnabar — red ink**, carries an **imperial sceptre** instead of a pastoral staff, and wears a **purple mantle**. Those privileges are still exercised, and they are a visible link to the Byzantine court.

**The founding apostles.** **Saint Barnabas**, a Cypriot Jew from Salamis, and **Saint Paul** preached on the island — Acts 13 — and Barnabas is the island's apostle and founder of its Church. His tomb near Salamis, with a copy of Matthew's Gospel on his chest, is the basis of the autocephaly claim.

**The saints of Cyprus**, which is a long list for a small island:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Άγιος Βαρνάβας** | the Apostle Barnabas, the founder |
| **Άγιος Λάζαρος** | **Lazarus**, raised by Christ, who by tradition came to Cyprus and was bishop of Kition — and his church stands in Larnaca |
| **Άγιος Επιφάνιος** | Epiphanius of Salamis, the fourth-century bishop and writer |
| **Άγιος Σπυρίδων** | a Cypriot bishop, whose relics went to Corfu |
| **Άγιος Νεόφυτος ο Έγκλειστος** | the twelfth-century hermit, whose cave-monastery is near Paphos |
| **Άγιος Μάμας** | the shepherd saint, with the lion — hugely popular, and many churches |
| **Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Λαμπαδιστής** | and his monastery in the Troodos |
| **Οι Τριακόσιοι Αλαμάνοι** | the three hundred Alaman saints, who came after the fall of the Holy Land |

**The monasteries, which are the island's landmarks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Παναγία του Κύκκου** | **Kykkos** — the greatest of them, with an icon of the Mother of God attributed by tradition to Saint Luke, kept veiled |
| **Σταυροβούνι** | Stavrovouni, founded by tradition by Saint Helen with a relic of the Cross |
| **Μαχαιράς** | Machairas, in the Troodos |
| **Απόστολος Ανδρέας** | Apostolos Andreas, on the tip of the Karpas peninsula — **in the occupied north**, and a pilgrimage that was interrupted for decades |
| **Άγιος Νεόφυτος** | near Paphos, with the hermit's own carved cave |

**The painted churches of the Troodos**, which are a set of ten small mountain churches with Byzantine and post-Byzantine frescoes, on the UNESCO list — and the finest surviving body of Byzantine wall painting in a small area anywhere.

**Why the Church matters more in Cyprus than in Greece.** Under Ottoman rule the Archbishop was the **Ethnarch** — the civil head of the Greek Orthodox population, responsible to the Sultan for them. **The Church was the nation's administration for three centuries**, and Archbishop Makarios III was the first President of the Republic from 1960, which is the logical conclusion of that history. The result is a Church far more entangled with national identity than the Church of Greece.

**What this means for your Greek.** The vocabulary of church life from stage 6 is the same, with Cypriot sounds. The things that are different are the names — of the saints, the monasteries and the feasts — and knowing a dozen of them is worth a great deal in a Cypriot parish.

**The feasts with particular Cypriot weight:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Η Λαμπρή** | Pascha, with the **φλαούνες** and the **λαμπρατζιά**, the Holy Saturday bonfire |
| **Του Αγίου Λαζάρου** | Lazarus Saturday, kept with particular force in Larnaca |
| **Κατακλυσμός** | the Pentecost Monday festival by the sea — flowers, water, and an old pre-Christian layer |
| **Του Αγίου Μάμα** | and the local panayiri of every village's own saint |

**Practice.** Learn the names of five Cypriot saints and three monasteries. Then read today's saint on saint.gr and notice when a Cypriot one comes up. Then ask at church which saint their village's church is dedicated to.
Cypriot history, in brief:
What a conversation assumes, in the same spirit as stage 7's ten dates — and the essential background for the next lesson, which is about what not to say.

**The dates:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **c. 1200 BC** | Mycenaean Greek settlement. **Cyprus has been Greek-speaking for over three thousand years** — the longest continuous Greek presence anywhere outside Greece. |
| **45 AD** | Paul and Barnabas preach; the proconsul Sergius Paulus converts — the first Roman governor to become Christian |
| **431** | autocephaly at Ephesus |
| **649–965** | the Arab raids, and three centuries of condominium between Byzantium and the Caliphate |
| **1191** | **Richard I takes the island** on the Third Crusade and sells it; the **Lusignan** kingdom follows |
| **1489** | Venice |
| **1571** | **the Ottoman conquest** — the siege of Famagusta, and Bragadin's death |
| **1821** | Archbishop Kyprianos and the bishops are executed in the Greek Revolution's reprisals |
| **1878** | **British administration** — leased from the Ottomans, annexed in 1914, a Crown Colony in 1925 |
| **1931, 1950** | the enosis movement; the 1950 plebiscite in which 96 per cent voted for union with Greece |
| **1955–59** | **the EOKA struggle** against British rule |
| **1960** | **independence** — the Republic of Cyprus, with Makarios III as President, and Britain keeping two Sovereign Base Areas |
| **1963–64** | intercommunal violence; the Green Line drawn through Nicosia |
| **1974** | **the Greek junta's coup against Makarios, and the Turkish invasion.** The island is divided. |
| **1983** | the unilateral declaration of the "TRNC", recognised only by Turkey |
| **2004** | the Annan Plan referendum — rejected by Greek Cypriots, accepted by Turkish Cypriots; **Cyprus joins the EU** |
| **2008** | the euro; the Ledra Street crossing opens in Nicosia |
| **2013** | the banking crisis and the bail-in |

**The five things that recur in conversation:**

**1. Three thousand years of Greek.** Cypriots are conscious of a continuity longer than the Greek state's, and of being Greek without ever having been in Greece. **It is a point of some sensitivity**: Cyprus was not part of the Greek kingdom, and the mainland has not always treated the island as fully Greek.

**2. Enosis, and its failure.** The movement for union with Greece ran from the nineteenth century through 1950's plebiscite and the EOKA struggle, and it ended in independence rather than union — then in the junta's coup, which destroyed the thing it claimed to want. **The subject is painful and complicated.**

**3. 1974.** The next lesson.

**4. Makarios.** Archbishop and President, Ethnarch and politician, the dominant figure of twentieth-century Cyprus, and **genuinely divisive** — revered by most, blamed by some for the path to 1974. Do not have a view.

**5. The British.** Colonial rule, the EOKA struggle against it, the Sovereign Base Areas which remain British territory today, and the enormous Cypriot migration to Britain in the 1950s and 60s. **The relationship is ambivalent and mostly warm** — and relevant to you, since it is why there are Cypriots in York at all.

**The migration, which is the fact closest to you.** Large-scale Cypriot migration to Britain began in the 1930s, accelerated in the 1950s, and surged after 1974 with refugees from the north. **The British Cypriot community is around 300,000 people** and is the reason the Greek Orthodox parishes of Britain exist in the form they do. Many were founded by Cypriots, and many are still majority Cypriot.

**So the history in this lesson is not background to a holiday.** It is the history of the congregation.

**Practice.** Read the Greek Wikipedia article on **Ιστορία της Κύπρου** — which is far fuller than the English — and note the ten dates you did not know. Then ask one person at church when their family came to Britain, and why.
1974, and what not to say:
The one subject in this curriculum that requires explicit care, because it is living grief rather than history and because a foreigner can cause real pain carelessly.

**What happened, plainly.** In July 1974 the Greek military junta backed a coup in Nicosia against President Makarios, aiming at union with Greece. Five days later Turkey invaded, citing its treaty rights as a guarantor power. In two phases that summer Turkish forces took **about 37 per cent of the island**. Roughly **160,000 Greek Cypriots** fled or were expelled from the north and **about 50,000 Turkish Cypriots** moved north from the south. **Around 1,500 Greek Cypriots and 500 Turkish Cypriots went missing**, many of them identified only in recent decades as graves are excavated. The island has been divided ever since.

**Why it is not history.** The people who fled are alive. The missing are still being identified. The houses are still standing, occupied by others. **Many of the Cypriots in Britain are the refugees or their children**, and a significant number came to Britain because of 1974.

**The words Greek Cypriots use**, and using them correctly signals that you understand:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **τα κατεχόμενα** | **the occupied territories** — the standard Greek Cypriot term for the north |
| **η εισβολή** | the invasion |
| **η κατοχή** | the occupation |
| **οι πρόσφυγες** | the refugees |
| **οι αγνοούμενοι** | **the missing** |
| **η Πράσινη Γραμμή** | the Green Line |
| **το Κυπριακό** | **the Cyprus problem** — the standard shorthand for the whole question |
| **ο εγκλωβισμένος** | the enclaved — those who stayed in the north |
| **το ψευδοκράτος** | *the pseudo-state* — the usual Greek Cypriot term for the "TRNC" |
| **Δεν ξεχνώ** | **"I do not forget"** — the slogan taught to schoolchildren since 1974, and the most loaded three words in Cypriot Greek |

**Δεν ξεχνώ is worth understanding.** It accompanies images of the occupied towns — Famagusta, Kyrenia, Morphou — and it has been part of Greek Cypriot schooling for fifty years. It is not a political slogan in the ordinary sense; it is closer to a vow.

**What not to say, specifically:**

1. **Do not call it anything a Turkish official would call it.** *Northern Cyprus* as a country, *the TRNC* without qualification, *the peace operation*. Even said innocently, it reads as a position.
2. **Do not offer a solution.** Everyone has heard every plan. A foreigner proposing federation or partition over coffee is at best tedious.
3. **Do not apportion blame.** The junta, Makarios, Britain as guarantor, Turkey, the Cypriot leaderships — every attribution is contested and each has adherents in any room.
4. **Do not say it was a long time ago.** It is not over.
5. **Do not ask whether they have been back.** Many have, through the crossings; many will not; for some it is unbearable. **Let them raise it.**
6. **Do not generalise about Turks.** Turkish Cypriots and mainland Turkey are distinct in Cypriot thinking, and the distinction is often carefully kept.

**What to say, if it comes up:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Ξέρω λίγα, πείτε μου.** | I know little; tell me. |
| **Λυπάμαι πολύ.** | I am very sorry. |
| **Δεν μπορώ να το φανταστώ.** | I can't imagine it. |
| **Από πού ήταν η οικογένειά σας;** | Where was your family from? — **the right question, if it has already been raised** |
| **Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.** | May God put His hand to it. — a pious wish, entirely appropriate, and it commits to nothing |

**The last one is genuinely useful.** It expresses sympathy, hope and helplessness together, in a register the Church shares, without taking a political position.

**And the general rule, which is the lesson**: listen. This is not a subject on which a newcomer has anything to contribute, and that is fine. **Being the person who listened well is worth more than any opinion.**

**One further thing worth knowing.** Many Greek Cypriots have warm memories of Turkish Cypriot neighbours and say so; bicommunal friendships and projects exist; and some of the most careful voices about 1974 are the refugees themselves. **Do not assume the hardest line in the room is the common one.**

**Practice.** Learn **τα κατεχόμενα**, **οι αγνοούμενοι**, **το Κυπριακό** and **Δεν ξεχνώ**. Then, if the subject arises, say nothing except a question, and listen to the whole answer.
The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain:
The variety you are most likely to hear, and the one no course anywhere teaches: Greek as spoken by British Cypriots, which is its own thing and is not anybody's broken Greek.

**The community.** Cypriot migration to Britain began in the 1930s, grew through the 1950s and 60s as the empire wound down, and surged after 1974. **Around 300,000 people in Britain are of Cypriot descent**, concentrated in north London — Haringey, Enfield, Palmers Green — with communities in Birmingham, Manchester, Nottingham and most sizeable cities.

**And the Greek Orthodox parishes of Britain were largely built by them.** The Archdiocese of Thyateira and Great Britain, its parishes, its church schools and its community halls are a Cypriot achievement in the main, with mainland Greeks, Pontians, Antiochians and converts alongside.

**What the language looks like in the third generation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **First generation** | Cypriot dialect as the mother tongue, English learned later, and often imperfectly |
| **Second generation** | Cypriot at home, English everywhere else; fluent in both, literate mainly in English |
| **Third generation** | **English dominant**, Greek understood more than spoken, often with a stock of phrases, food words and the church vocabulary |
| **Fourth generation** | often no Greek, and a strong Cypriot identity regardless |

**What that means for you, concretely.** The people at church range from fluent dialect speakers to people with ten words, **and your Greek may well be better than that of someone whose grandparents were born in Cyprus.** That is a delicate thing. Do not display it, and never correct anyone.

**The features of British Cypriot Greek:**

1. **Code-switching mid-sentence**, which is the most noticeable: **Θα πάω στο shop τζαι εννά πιάσω milk.** This is normal bilingual behaviour, not decay.
2. **English loanwords naturalised with Greek endings** — **παρκάρω, σοπάρω, ντραϊβάρω, μπουκάρω** (to park, shop, drive, book).
3. **A frozen vocabulary** — the Greek of a 1960s village, preserved while mainland and Cypriot Greek moved on. Some older speakers use words that are archaic in Cyprus now.
4. **English intonation on Greek words**, in the younger generations.
5. **No literacy in Greek**, commonly — which means people may speak well and not read at all, and some will ask you what a sign says.

**The last point is worth holding onto**, because it inverts the usual relationship: **you can read better than many fluent speakers**, and they can speak better than you will for years. Both facts are ordinary.

**The institutions you will meet:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The parish and its hall** | the centre of community life |
| **The Greek school** | Saturday or weekday-evening classes for children, usually attached to the parish |
| **The associations** | village and regional associations — people from the same village in Cyprus, organised in London |
| **The coffee shop** | where it exists, the first generation's institution |
| **The Archdiocese of Thyateira** | the canonical structure, under the Ecumenical Patriarchate |

**The Greek school deserves a note.** Most parishes run one, they are chronically short of help, and they teach standard Greek rather than the dialect — which means **helping at one is both useful and the best Greek practice available to you locally**, and it is a thing you can offer.

**A thing worth being prepared for.** Some British Cypriots will say they speak "village Greek" or "not real Greek" and apologise for it. **It is real Greek**, it is older than the standard in several features, and the apology comes from a century of being told otherwise by Athens. Saying so plainly — **Είναι κανονικά ελληνικά, και πιο παλιά από τα αθηναϊκά** — is a genuine kindness, and it is true.

**Practice.** Listen for one of the five features in the parish this Sunday. Then ask about the Greek school: whether there is one, when it meets, and whether they need help. Then ask one older person what their village was called and what it was like.
Cypriot music:
A living tradition that is distinct from mainland Greek music, and the one part of the dialect you can learn by enjoying it.

**The genres:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τα τσιαττιστά** | **the improvised rhyming couplet duels** — two singers trading fifteen-syllable verses, each capping the last, to a fixed tune. UNESCO lists it as intangible heritage. |
| **Η φωνή** | the traditional Cypriot melodic patterns — **η φωνή της Μεσαρκάς, η φωνή της Πάφου** — on which singers improvise words |
| **Τα δημοτικά** | the folk repertoire: wedding songs, harvest songs, laments |
| **Το ρεμπέτικο and το λαϊκό** | shared with Greece |
| **Το έντεχνο κυπριακό** | the art-song tradition, often in standard Greek |
| **Η παραδοσιακή αναβίωση** | the folk revival — new recordings of the old repertoire |
| **Το κυπριακό ραπ και χιπ-χοπ** | **and this is where the dialect is most alive in new writing** |

**Τα τσιαττιστά is the one to know about.** Two singers, a violin and a lute, and a contest of improvised couplets — praise, insult, courtship, politics — in the dialect, each verse answering the last and using the same rhyme. It is a competitive art with named masters, it happens at village festivals, and the verses are often very funny and occasionally brutal. **There is nothing comparable in mainland Greek music.**

**The instruments:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το βιολί** | the violin, which leads |
| **το λαούτο** | the lute |
| **ο πιθκιαύλι** | the Cypriot flute, a shepherd's instrument |
| **το ταμπουτσιά** | the frame drum |

**The names worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μιχάλης Τερλικκάς** | the leading figure in the traditional repertoire's preservation and performance |
| **Αλκίνοος Ιωαννίδης** | the best-known Cypriot singer-songwriter — mostly standard Greek, and widely loved in Greece too |
| **Μόνσιερ Ντουμανί** | *Monsieur Doumani* — the contemporary group reworking the Cypriot folk repertoire |
| **Ανδρέας Παπαδόπουλος, Χριστίνα Πλεύρη** | and the generation of traditional singers recorded in the twentieth century |

**Alkinoos Ioannides is the practical recommendation** for a learner: clear diction, mostly standard Greek, serious lyrics, and widely enough known that mentioning him works as conversation.

**The religious music of Cyprus**, which belongs with the Church lesson: Byzantine chant as everywhere in Orthodoxy, with local traditions of psalmody and a strong Cypriot school of chanters. **The texts are Koine and Byzantine Greek** — the later curriculum.

**What song gives you here, specifically.** The dialect in its most memorable form, with the words available in writing. **stixoi.info** carries Cypriot lyrics alongside the mainland repertoire, and the comments often explain the dialect words — which makes a Cypriot song a complete lesson: text, audio, a gloss and a reason to care.

**The method, from stage 8's song lesson, unchanged**: listen cold, read the lyrics, look up ten words, listen reading along, sing along, sing without the text.

**One honest caution about the dialect in song.** Folk lyrics use the oldest, densest layer of Cypriot — village vocabulary, agricultural terms, and words that are archaic even in Cyprus. **Expect to understand less of a traditional song than of ordinary speech**, and treat the obscure words as scenery rather than homework.

**Practice.** Listen to one τσιαττιστά duel — there is plenty of it recorded — and follow the rhyme even where you lose the words. Then take one Alkinoos Ioannides song and do the six steps on it. Then ask at church whether anyone sings, or knows who does.
Dialect poetry: Michaelides and Lipertis:
The Cypriot literary canon, which is written in the dialect by deliberate choice — and the one body of writing where Cypriot is used for serious literary purposes.

**Why it matters.** Everywhere else the dialect is spoken and the standard is written. **Cypriot poetry is the exception**: two poets of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries made the dialect a literary language, and what they wrote is learned in Cypriot schools and quoted by Cypriots.

**Βασίλης Μιχαηλίδης (1849–1917)** — the national poet of Cyprus.

**His great poem is *Η 9η Ιουλίου 1821 εν Λευκωσία Κύπρου*** — *The 9th of July 1821 in Nicosia, Cyprus* — on the execution of **Archbishop Kyprianos** and the bishops by the Ottoman governor in the reprisals of the Greek Revolution. It is in the Cypriot dialect, in the fifteen-syllable folk metre, and it is the central text of Cypriot literature.

**Its most quoted passage** is Kyprianos's answer to the governor Küçük Mehmed, where the Archbishop refuses to save himself by flight. The lines about the Greek nation — **η Ρωμιοσύνη έν' φυλή συντúχαννε τζιαι κάμνει** — are known by heart across the island.

**And it is a church text as much as a national one**: the martyrdom of a bishop who would not abandon his people, written in the people's own dialect.

**His other famous poem**, **Η Χιώτισσα**, on the massacre of Chios.

**Δημήτρης Λιπέρτης (1866–1937)** — the other pillar, and the gentler one.

His four volumes of **Κυπριακά Τραγούδια** are lyric poems in the dialect: village life, love, exile, the land. Many were set to music and are sung rather than read. **Where Michaelides is monumental, Lipertis is domestic**, and his poems are the easier way into dialect verse.

**The others worth the names:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Παύλος Λιασίδης** | the twentieth-century dialect poet, and a τσιαττιστής |
| **Κώστας Μόντης** | a major modern Cypriot poet, in standard Greek and in the dialect both — short, epigrammatic, and very good |
| **Θεοδόσης Πιερίδης** | political poetry of the mid-century |
| **Κυριάκος Χαραλαμπίδης** | the leading contemporary Cypriot poet, in standard Greek, much of it about 1974 and about Cypriot antiquity |

**Κώστας Μόντης is the recommendation for a learner**: very short poems, ordinary vocabulary, and a dry wit that survives translation badly and reads beautifully in Greek. His **Στιγμές** are two or three lines each.

**And Χαραλαμπίδης is the one to come back to later**, because his subject is exactly the one the history lessons covered, written by someone for whom it is not history.

**How to read dialect verse as a learner:**

1. **Read it aloud**, which the metre requires — fifteen syllables, a break after the eighth.
2. **Do not look up the obscure words first.** Get the shape and the rhyme.
3. **Then one pass with a dialect glossary**, which for Michaelides exists in every school edition.
4. **Then read it aloud again** and notice how much more there is.

**Where to find them.** The school editions of Michaelides are standard in Cyprus and available online; **snhell.gr** holds some of the Cypriot poets with recordings; and Cypriot cultural sites carry the texts with glossaries. **Hearing *Η 9η Ιουλίου* recited** — and there are recordings — is the right first encounter, because it was written to be heard.

**The honest expectation.** This is the hardest Greek in the curriculum: dialect, nineteenth-century, metrical, and full of village and ecclesiastical vocabulary. **Read it for the sound and the moment rather than for comprehension**, and come back to it in the literature stage.

**Practice.** Find a recording of *Η 9η Ιουλίου 1821* and listen to ten minutes of it with the text. Then read three of Kostas Montis's *Στιγμές*, which you will understand completely. Then ask a Cypriot at church whether they know the Kyprianos poem — many will.
Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms:
The best listening material for this stage, because comedy is where the dialect lives at full strength — and because the jokes tell you what Cypriots think about themselves.

**Why comedy is the right material.** A sitcom gives you the dialect at natural speed, in short exchanges, with the situation visible, and often subtitled in standard Greek for broadcast in Greece — **which makes it a dialect-to-standard parallel text with audio.** There is nothing better available.

**The series worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αίγια Φούξια** | the long-running Cypriot village sitcom — the dialect at its broadest, and a national institution |
| **Οι Τάκκοι** | the sketch series, satirical and very fast |
| **Το Κυπριακό Παραμύθι, and the ΡΙΚ archive** | decades of Cypriot television, much of it online |
| **Μες στην Καλή Χαρά** | not Cypriot, but useful as a comparison of mainland television |
| **Cypriot YouTube sketch channels** | current, short, and the dialect of people under thirty |

**Αίγια Φούξια is the recommendation.** A fictional village, broad characters, and dialect so thick that mainland Greeks need subtitles — which means you get the subtitles too. **Watch it with the Greek subtitles on** and you have the five sound rules demonstrated line by line.

**What Cypriot humour is about**, which is its own cultural lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The village against the town** | the villager's cunning, the townsman's pretension |
| **The dialect itself** | and the embarrassment about it — a standing joke |
| **Bureaucracy and officialdom** | which in Cyprus is a national comic subject |
| **Family obligation** | the mother, the dowry, the matchmaking, the in-laws |
| **Hospitality as warfare** | the insistence on feeding you |
| **The diaspora returning** | the *Εγγλέζος* cousin with bad Greek and opinions — **and that one may be about you** |
| **Mainland Greeks** | their accent, their self-importance, their inability to understand Cypriot |

**The last two deserve the warning.** The returning diaspora Cypriot with mangled Greek is a stock comic figure, and so is the foreigner trying to speak dialect. **If you are teased on either count, the joke is affectionate** and the response is to laugh. Being in on it is better than being spared it.

**The comic registers of the dialect** worth recognising:

- **Βαρετά κυπριακά** — the thickest village dialect, used for comic effect even by Cypriots who do not speak it that way.
- **Κυπραίικα με αθηναϊκή προφορά** — a Cypriot putting on an Athenian accent, which is a joke in itself.
- **Code-switching for effect** — dropping into English mid-sentence as a punchline.

**And the self-deprecation**, which is constant: Cypriots joke about Cypriot more than anyone. **Do not join in on that one.** Jokes about a dialect are for its speakers to make.

**What to do with the material:**

1. **Watch an episode** with Greek subtitles, extensively.
2. **Take one exchange** and compare the dialect you hear with the standard in the subtitle. **Write both out.** That is the clearest dialect lesson you can give yourself.
3. **Learn five lines.** Comedy lines are the most quotable Greek there is, and quoting one correctly is a social event.

**Where to find it**: ΡΙΚ — the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation — has an online archive, and much of the material is on YouTube, legally uploaded. **ΡΙΚ's news is in standard Greek** and its drama and comedy in dialect, which makes the one channel useful for both.

**Practice.** Watch one episode of a Cypriot sitcom with Greek subtitles. Take one thirty-second exchange and write out both the dialect you heard and the standard subtitle, side by side. Then count how many of the five sound rules you can see operating.
Where to find Cypriot:
The resource list for this stage, because Cypriot material is less abundant than standard Greek material and knowing where it is saves a great deal of searching.

**Audio and video:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ΡΙΚ (CyBC)** | the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation — news in standard Greek, drama and comedy in dialect, radio, and a large online archive |
| **Cypriot sitcoms** | *Αίγια Φούξια*, *Οι Τάκκοι*, and the ΡΙΚ back catalogue, much of it on YouTube |
| **Cypriot YouTube** | sketch channels, vloggers, cooking channels — the dialect of people under thirty |
| **Cypriot radio stations** | and the local ones, which are the broadest dialect on air |
| **Cypriot podcasts** | fewer than Greek ones, and growing |
| **Church of Cyprus media** | sermons and services, mostly in standard Greek with Cypriot accent |
| **Τσιαττιστά recordings** | the couplet duels, widely uploaded |

**Courses and learning material:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Kypros.org** | **105 free audio lessons**, Cyprus-based, in the curriculum's resource list since stage 1. Standard Greek with Cypriot pronunciation and some dialect. |
| **University of Cyprus material** | linguistics departments publish on the dialect, some of it freely |
| **The Centre for Scientific Research of Cyprus** | glossaries and publications on dialect, folklore and history |

**Dictionaries and reference:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γιαγκουλλής, Λεξικό της Κυπριακής Διαλέκτου** | the standard dialect dictionary |
| **The Academy of Athens' Ιστορικό Λεξικό** | historical and exhaustive |
| **Online crowd-sourced glossaries** | uneven and genuinely useful for current slang |
| **Greek Wikipedia's Κυπριακή διάλεκτος article** | a good technical overview, in Greek |

**Written Cypriot:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Dialect poetry** | Michaelides, Lipertis, Liasidis — school editions with glossaries |
| **Social media** | by far the largest body of written Cypriot |
| **Cypriot news sites** | in standard Greek, with Cypriot subject matter: philenews, Politis, Sigmalive |
| **Comics and cartoons** | where dialect is the joke |
| **Subtitles** | the dialect-to-standard parallel text from the last lesson |

**And the resource that is not on any list.** The Cypriots at your church. **They are the material**, they are free, they are here, and nothing online will teach you the particular Greek of the particular village your parish came from.

**The honest note about scarcity.** Cypriot has far less learner material than standard Greek — no graded readers, no comprehensible-input channel, no courses that teach the dialect as a target. **This stage is therefore a listening-and-reading stage with the method of stage 8 applied to scarcer material**, and the sound rules plus the vocabulary lessons substitute for a course that does not exist.

**The one priority, if you only do one thing**: watch a Cypriot sitcom with Greek subtitles, regularly. It is the only resource that gives dialect, standard, audio and context simultaneously.

**Practice.** Find and bookmark five of these: ΡΙΚ's archive, one sitcom, one Cypriot YouTube channel, one dialect glossary, and the Kypros.org lessons. Then use one of them for twenty minutes today.
The island itself: places and names:
The geography and the names, because a Cypriot conversation is full of them and because the place names carry the island's whole history.

**The cities:**

| Greek | English | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **η Λευκωσία** | Nicosia | the capital, **and the last divided capital in Europe** |
| **η Λεμεσός** | Limassol | the biggest port, and the commercial centre |
| **η Λάρνακα** | Larnaca | the main airport, and **Saint Lazarus's city** |
| **η Πάφος** | Paphos | the west; Aphrodite's birthplace, and Saint Paul's landing |
| **η Αμμόχωστος** | Famagusta | **in the occupied area** — and **Βαρώσι** is the sealed quarter |
| **η Κερύνεια** | Kyrenia | **occupied** — the north coast and the castle |
| **η Μόρφου** | Morphou | **occupied** — and its feast of Saint Mamas is a byword |
| **το Παραλίμνι, η Αγία Νάπα** | Paralimni, Ayia Napa | the south-east |

**The three names to be careful with** — Famagusta, Kyrenia, Morphou — because they are in the occupied north and they are the names on the posters that say **Δεν ξεχνώ**. Using the Greek names is correct and expected.

**The regions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η Μεσαορία / Μεσαρκά** | the central plain — the island's granary, and now largely occupied |
| **ο Τρόοδος** | the mountain range: the painted churches, the villages, the snow |
| **ο Όλυμπος** | and the highest peak, at nearly 2,000 metres, is Cyprus's own Olympus |
| **ο Πενταδάκτυλος** | the Kyrenia range — *the five fingers*, and occupied |
| **η Καρπασία** | the long north-eastern peninsula, with Apostolos Andreas at its tip |
| **η Ακάμας** | the wild north-western peninsula |
| **τα κατεχόμενα** | and the term for all of the north |

**The village**, which is the unit of Cypriot identity:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το χωριό / το χωρκό** | the village, in standard and in dialect |
| **η κοινότητα** | the community, as an administrative unit |
| **ο μουχτάρης** | the village headman — the Turkish-derived title, still in use |
| **η πλατεία, το καφενείο, η εκκλησία** | the three things a village has |
| **η γειτονιά** | the neighbourhood |

**Village name endings, which are a history lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-ού, -ιού** | ancient and Byzantine: **Λεμεσός, Μόρφου** |
| **-ια, -ιά** | **Κερύνεια, Λάρνακα** |
| **Frankish and Venetian names** | **Λυσί, Κοντέα, Αγκαστίνα** |
| **Turkish-derived names** | widespread, and **renamed in the north since 1974** |
| **Saints' names** | **Άγιος Δομέτιος, Αγία Νάπα, Άγιος Θεόδωρος** — and there are dozens |

**That the northern villages were renamed after 1974** is itself a subject: the Greek names persist in Greek Cypriot usage and on maps published in the Republic, and the Turkish names on maps published in the north. **Use the Greek ones**, as the previous lesson said.

**The practical geography worth knowing** for conversation: the island is about 240 km long, it is the third largest in the Mediterranean, it is hot and dry in summer and green in spring, it has water shortages, and the Troodos gets snow. Those four facts carry a surprising amount of small talk.

**The other thing worth knowing**: Cyprus is closer to Syria and Lebanon than to Greece, which has shaped everything — its food, its loanwords, its history, and its politics.

**And the question again, from the manner lesson**: **Πόθεν είσαι;** The answer is a village, and now you know the shape of the answers.

**Practice.** Learn the six cities and which three are occupied. Then look at a map of Cyprus with the Greek names. Then ask someone at church which village their family came from, find it on the map, and ask what was near it.
Speaking with Cypriots:
The practical conclusion of the stage: how to use all of this in the parish hall without getting it wrong.

**The core advice, in one line: understand the dialect, speak the standard.**

**Why not speak the dialect.** Three reasons, and all of them real:

1. **A foreigner speaking dialect reads as imitation**, and imitation of a dialect its own speakers have been mocked for is worse than clumsy.
2. **You will get it wrong** in ways that are funny rather than endearing, because dialect competence is the one thing no amount of study gives you.
3. **You do not need to.** Every Cypriot speaks standard Greek, and that is the register they will use with you anyway.

**What does enter your speech naturally, and should.** A handful of words that are simply what people around you say, and using them is participation rather than imitation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **κουμπάρε** | to a man, once you are on those terms |
| **Να 'στε καλά** | the universal thanks, and it is Cypriot-flavoured in Britain |
| **Ίντα κάμνεις;** | if it is what is said to you, answering in kind is fine |
| **The food words** | φλαούνες, χαλλούμι, κουπέπια — **there are no standard alternatives** |
| **Η Λαμπρή** | if that is what the parish calls Pascha |
| **The place and saint names** | which are facts, not dialect |

**The rule**: adopt what you hear said to you repeatedly; do not import anything you have only read.

**How to handle the diglossia in conversation.** They will speak dialect to each other and standard to you, sometimes switching mid-sentence. **Do not ask them to speak standard** — it implies their Greek is a problem. Instead:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη, πιο αργά;** | sorry, more slowly? |
| **Πώς το λένε αυτό στα κανονικά;** | and **avoid this phrasing** — *proper Greek* is the loaded term |
| **Πώς θα το έλεγε ένας Ελλαδίτης;** | **how would someone from Greece say it?** — the right way to ask, because it treats both as equal |
| **Τι σημαίνει αυτό;** | what does that mean? |
| **Αυτό είναι κυπριακό;** | is that Cypriot? — a perfectly good question, and people enjoy answering it |

**Πώς θα το έλεγε ένας Ελλαδίτης;** is the phrasing of this lesson. It gets you the standard equivalent without implying that the dialect is deficient.

**The four things not to do:**

1. **Do not correct anyone's Greek.** Ever. Not the dialect, not the code-switching, not the English loanwords.
2. **Do not call it *τα χωριάτικα*** or anything like it, even if they do.
3. **Do not perform the dialect.** Saying **ίντα κάμνεις** as a joke is a different act from saying it because it is what you heard.
4. **Do not treat Cypriot as a lesser Greek.** It is older than the standard in several features, and the lesson on the diaspora said the useful thing: **Είναι κανονικά ελληνικά, και πιο παλιά από τα αθηναϊκά.**

**The two things to do:**

1. **Ask about the village.** It is the best question available and it never fails.
2. **Learn the parish's own words.** Every community has a few — the name it uses for a feast, a food, a service, a person's role. **Those are the words that matter most and no book contains them.**

**And the thing that will actually happen.** You will be fed, teased, encouraged well beyond your merits, asked why on earth you are learning Greek, and told that your Greek is excellent when it is not. **The correct response to all of it is to keep turning up.**

**Practice.** This week, at church: ask one person about their village, ask one dialect word's standard equivalent using **Πώς θα το έλεγε ένας Ελλαδίτης;**, and write down three words the parish uses that you have not met in any book.
Where you should be at the end of stage:
The checkpoint for a stage whose goal is comprehension rather than production.

**What you should be able to do:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hear the five sound differences** | the long consonants, the aspirated doubles, **κ→τζ**, **χ→sh**, final **-ν** |
| **Run them in reverse** | so an unfamiliar word resolves to a standard one |
| **Parse the grammar** | pronoun after the verb, **εν** for both *is* and *not*, **εννά** for **θα**, **μεν** for **μην** |
| **Recognise the core vocabulary** | **ίντα, λαλώ, θωρώ, κάμνω, ούλλοι, πολλά, κόρη, κουμπάρε, μανιχός, πελλός** |
| **Read Cypriot writing** | across its inconsistent spellings |
| **Follow a Cypriot sitcom** | with the Greek subtitles on |
| **Name the four loanword layers** | and guess which one a word comes from |
| **Order and discuss Cypriot food** | and know what φλαούνες are |
| **Know the Church of Cyprus** | its autocephaly, its saints, its monasteries, and the Ethnarch's role |
| **Hold the history** | the dates, the migration to Britain, and **what not to say about 1974** |
| **Place the island** | the six cities, which three are occupied, and the Troodos |

**What you should not be able to do, and should not try:**

- **Speak the dialect.** By design.
- **Read dialect poetry fluently.** It is the hardest Greek in the curriculum, and the literature stage returns to it.
- **Follow two Cypriots talking fast to each other.** That takes years of exposure, and many mainland Greeks cannot do it either.

**The checkpoint questions:**

1. **Can you convert ten Cypriot words to their standard forms** by the sound rules alone?
2. **Do you recognise εν, εννά and the post-verbal pronoun** without stopping?
3. **Have you watched a Cypriot sitcom** with the subtitles, and written out one exchange both ways?
4. **Do you know the four words of 1974** — **τα κατεχόμενα, οι αγνοούμενοι, το Κυπριακό, Δεν ξεχνώ** — and what not to say?
5. **Have you asked someone at church about their village?**
6. **Do you know three words your own parish uses** that no book has?

**The fifth and sixth are the ones that matter**, because this stage was never about the dialect in the abstract. It was about the people in the hall.

**What the stage changes about your Greek**, concretely: the percentage of parish-hall conversation you follow. Measure it the way stage 8's first lesson said — a clip, a percentage — and compare it to the number you wrote at the start of this stage.

**And what remains.** One stage: **Literature, and ad astra**, which is open-ended and does not finish. Underneath it, stage 8's reading, which should by now be a habit. And whenever you want it, the classical curriculum — which the Cypriot material has, incidentally, prepared you for better than the standard did, because Cypriot kept the ancient forms the standard dropped.

**That last point is worth stating.** The long consonants, the final **-ν**, the post-verbal pronoun, **πόθεν** — all four are Ancient Greek, preserved in Cyprus and lost in Athens. **Learning to hear them is learning to hear older Greek**, and the classical curriculum begins there.

**Practice.** Answer the six questions in the journal. Then listen to the same kind of Cypriot clip you used at the start of this stage and write down the percentage you now follow.
Review: stage 10:
Twenty lessons on the largest divergence in Greek, at his word: **standard and Cypriot.**

**The sounds**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Long consonants** | **άλλος, ούλλος, έννα** — pronounced long, as in Ancient Greek |
| **Aspirated doubles** | **ππ, ττ, κκ** with a puff of air |
| **κ → τζ** before ε and ι | **και → τζαι, καιρός → τζαιρός** |
| **χ → sh** before ε and ι | **χέρι → σ̌έρι, όχι → όσ̌ι** |
| **Final -ν kept** | **καλόν, ποταμόν, παιδίν** |
| **Run them in reverse** | and most unfamiliar words resolve to standard ones |

**The writing**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No standard orthography** | **τζαι, τζιαι, τσαι, τσιαι** are all the same word |
| **Three systems** | improvised, the linguists' carons, and Cypriot Greeklish |
| **Read loosely** | and card the word, not the spelling |

**The grammar**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The pronoun follows the verb** | **λαλώ σου, θωρώ σε, είπεν μου** — the older order, and the standard keeps it in the imperative |
| **εν** | *is* and *not*, both |
| **εννά** | for **θα** |
| **μεν** | for **μην** |
| **The ancient interrogatives** | **ίντα, ίνταλως, πόθεν, πκοιος** |
| **The three verbs** | **λαλώ** (λέω), **θωρώ** (βλέπω), **κάμνω** (κάνω) |

**The vocabulary**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The core** | ούλλοι, πολλά (*very*), μανιχός, πελλός, μιτσής, συντυχάννω, τσαέρα, η Λαμπρή |
| **The addresses** | **κόρη** to any woman, **κουμπάρε** to any man |
| **Four loanword layers** | Old French, Venetian Italian, Ottoman Turkish, English — and the Ancient Greek retentions underneath |
| **The food** | χαλλούμι, αναρή, κουπέπια, κολοκάσι, σούβλα, **φλαούνες**, ζιβανία, κουμανταρία |

**The place**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Church of Cyprus** | autocephalous since 431; the Archbishop's red ink, sceptre and purple; Barnabas, Lazarus, Mamas, Neophytos; Kykkos, Stavrovouni, Machairas, Apostolos Andreas; the painted churches; and the Ethnarch's role |
| **The history** | three thousand years of Greek, 1191, 1571, 1878, the EOKA struggle, 1960, **1974**, 2004 |
| **1974** | **τα κατεχόμενα, η εισβολή, οι αγνοούμενοι, το Κυπριακό, Δεν ξεχνώ** — and listen rather than speak |
| **The diaspora** | 300,000 British Cypriots, who built the parishes; code-switching; and **never correct anyone's Greek** |
| **The culture** | τσιαττιστά, Michaelides's *Η 9η Ιουλίου 1821*, Lipertis, Montis, the sitcoms, the villages |

**The rule of the stage**

**Understand the dialect; speak the standard.** Adopt what is said to you repeatedly; import nothing you have only read. **Πώς θα το έλεγε ένας Ελλαδίτης;** is how you ask for the standard without implying the dialect is deficient.

**And the point of it.** The Greeks at your church are more likely to be Cypriot than Greek, and the Greek in the hall may be Cypriot rather than standard. **This stage was never about a dialect. It was about following the conversation.**

**What remains.** One stage — **Literature, and ad astra** — which is open and does not finish. And the classical curriculum, whenever you want it, for which this stage has been unexpectedly good preparation: the long consonants, the final **-ν**, the post-verbal pronoun and **πόθεν** are all Ancient Greek, kept in Cyprus and lost in Athens.

**Practice.** Compare the percentage of Cypriot speech you followed at the start of this stage with the percentage now. Then write, in Greek, three sentences about one person at church and where their family is from.
What stage 11 is: no more course:
The last stage, and the one with no end. *Ad astra* was his word from the first question, and this is where the curriculum stops teaching and starts pointing.

**What is left to learn.** Nothing systematic. The grammar is finished, the registers are learned, the dialect is understood, the reading habit is running. **What remains is the literature** — which is not a skill to acquire but a body of work to spend a life on.

**Why literature is the end of the route and not the middle.** Three reasons:

1. **It is the hardest Greek.** Literary language uses the full historical depth of the language — the learned register, the dialects, the ancient forms, the invented words — and it does so deliberately.
2. **It requires the rest first.** You cannot read Papadiamantis without the katharevousa reading key, or Kazantzakis without the Cretan vocabulary, or Cavafy without hearing the register shifts that are his whole technique.
3. **It is the point.** A language's literature is what the language was for. Everything else in this curriculum was infrastructure.

**And the honest caveat**: much of what follows you will read slowly, with help, and incompletely, for years. **That is what reading literature in a second language is**, and it is also what reading literature in a first language is, if the literature is any good.

**What this stage contains:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How to read a poem** | because Greek poetry is read differently from English poetry |
| **The poets** | Solomos, Palamas, Cavafy, Seferis, Elytis, Ritsos — and the songs they became |
| **The folk tradition** | the fifteen-syllable line, the demotic song, and Crete |
| **The prose** | Papadiamantis, Kazantzakis, the Generation of the Thirties, Asia Minor, the civil war, the contemporary |
| **The religious writers** | Kontoglou, the Elders, and modern Greek theology — **which is where this curriculum and the next one meet** |
| **The essayists** | and Lorentzatos's argument about what Greek literature lost |
| **Ad astra** | what to actually do, for the rest of your life |

**The shape of the stage, which is different from the others.** Each lesson introduces a body of work rather than teaching a point: what it is, why it matters, how hard it is, where to find it free, and which single piece to start with. **The lessons are maps, and the reading is yours.**

**Where it is free.** **snhell.gr** — the Centre for Neo-Hellenic Studies' anthology — holds much of the canon **with recordings of the poets reading their own work**: Seferis, Elytis and Ritsos in their own voices. There is no equivalent resource for most languages, and it is the single best thing in this stage.

**And the honest note about where this leads.** Four of the writers in this stage — Papadiamantis, Kontoglou, the theologians, and the hymnographers behind them — write in or towards the learned register, which by his ruling this curriculum skips. **Stage 11 is therefore the threshold of the classical curriculum**: the point at which modern Greek has taken you as far as it can and the older language is what stands between you and the rest.

**Practice.** Open snhell.gr and listen to one poet reading one poem, with the text. Understand what you understand. Then read the next lesson, which is about how to do that properly.
How to read a Greek poem:
A method, because Greek poetry works differently from English poetry and reading it as though it were English loses most of it.

**The four things to listen for:**

**1. The metre, and specifically the fifteen-syllable line.** The **δεκαπεντασύλλαβος** is the Greek line — iambic, fifteen syllables, with a break after the eighth. It is the metre of the folk songs, of the *Erotokritos*, of Solomos, of Michaelides's Cypriot poem, and of a great deal of modern verse that pretends to be free.

> **Μια / να / χτα / τον / θυ / μή / θη / κα ‖ τον / πρώ / το / μου / τον / έ / ρω / τα**

**Hearing it is what makes a Greek poem sound Greek**, and reading aloud is the only way to hear it.

**2. The register shifts.** This is the central technique of Greek poetry since the nineteenth century, because the language has two registers lying on top of each other. A poet can drop a katharevousa word into demotic verse, or an ancient form, or a village word, and **the shift itself carries the meaning** — irony, distance, grandeur, bathos.

**Cavafy is the master of it**, and almost nothing of him survives translation for that reason.

**3. The weight of a single word.** Greek words carry their etymology visibly — a reader sees **ανάστασις** and hears *standing up again*. **Poets use that**, and a word's transparency is a tool English has only in Latinate vocabulary.

**4. The quotation.** Greek poetry quotes Homer, the tragedians, the Septuagint, the hymns and the folk songs constantly, and assumes you catch it. **You will not catch most of it yet.** The notes in a school edition are there for Greeks too.

**The method, for one poem:**

1. **Read it aloud, whole, without stopping.** For the sound and the shape.
2. **Read it again aloud**, feeling for the metre. Count a line.
3. **Now read it for sense**, looking up only what stops you.
4. **Mark the register shifts** — which words are learned, which are village, which are ancient.
5. **Read it aloud again.**
6. **Learn four lines by heart.**

**Step six is the one that matters most.** A poem memorised is in your Greek permanently, and the four lines will come back to you at the right moment, which is what poetry is for. **Greeks quote poetry in ordinary conversation** more than the British do, and having four lines is a form of membership.

**Where to start, and the order is deliberate:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cavafy** | the plainest vocabulary and the shortest poems |
| **Montis** | two or three lines each, and completely comprehensible |
| **Ritsos's shorter poems** | and the ones you already know as songs |
| **The folk songs** | formulaic, repetitive, and the metre at its clearest |
| **Elytis and Seferis** | later. Both are hard. |
| **Solomos and Palamas** | the nineteenth century, with its own vocabulary |
| **The dialect poets** | hardest of all |

**The resource, again: snhell.gr**, with the poets' own recordings. **Hearing Seferis read Seferis** solves the metre question instantly, because he reads it as it was written.

**And one permission.** You are allowed to read a poem and understand half of it and love it anyway. That is how most people read most poetry, in any language.

**Practice.** Take Cavafy's **Ιθάκη** and do all six steps on it, including the four lines by heart. It is the most quoted poem in modern Greek and the four lines will be useful.
Cavafy:
The way into Greek poetry, and the poet a learner can actually read: plain vocabulary, short poems, and a technique built on the register you have spent nine stages learning.

**The facts.** Κωνσταντίνος Π. Καβάφης, 1863–1933. Greek of Alexandria, from a Constantinopolitan family; worked thirty years as a clerk in the Egyptian irrigation service; published almost nothing in his lifetime, circulating poems privately on broadsheets. **The canon is 154 poems**, plus the unpublished and the repudiated.

**Why he is readable for you:**

- **Short.** Most are under twenty lines.
- **Plain vocabulary.** Almost no invented or rare words.
- **Prosaic syntax.** He writes in sentences.
- **Concrete situations** — a room, a city, a historical moment, a man at a window.

**Why he is hard, and it is a different kind of hard.** His Greek mixes demotic with katharevousa and with the Greek of Alexandria and the Phanar, and **the mixture is the poem**. A learned word in a plain line is an ironic distance; an archaism is a historical frame. You will read him correctly before you hear him correctly, and hearing him comes with time.

**The three subjects**, as he divided them himself: **the historical**, **the philosophical**, and **the erotic**.

**The poems to know, because every Greek does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ιθάκη** | *Ithaca* — the journey rather than the arrival. Quoted at graduations, retirements and funerals. **Start here.** |
| **Περιμένοντας τους Βαρβάρους** | *Waiting for the Barbarians* — a city that needs its enemy |
| **Η Πόλις** | *The City* — *you will find no new lands*. The most quoted lines in Greek about the impossibility of escape. |
| **Θερμοπύλες** | *Thermopylae* — those who hold the line knowing they will fall |
| **Απολείπειν ο Θεός Αντώνιον** | *The God Abandons Antony* — on losing with dignity |
| **Όσο Μπορείς** | *As Much As You Can* — on not cheapening your life |
| **Κεριά** | *Candles* — the years behind and ahead |
| **Μελαγχολία του Ιάσονος Κλεάνδρου** | on ageing, and on poetry as the drug for it |

**The four lines worth having by heart**, from Ιθάκη:

> **Να εύχεσαι να 'ναι μακρύς ο δρόμος.**
> **Πολλά τα καλοκαιρινά πρωιά να είναι**
> **που με τι ευχαρίστηση, με τι χαρά**
> **θα μπαίνεις σε λιμένας πρωτοειδωμένους…**

**Note λιμένας** — the learned accusative plural, where demotic would have **λιμάνια**. **That is Cavafy in one word**: the archaism lifts the harbours into myth.

**And from Η Πόλις**, which is the bleaker and more famous:

> **Δεν θα βρεις άλλη γη, δεν θα βρεις άλλη θάλασσα.**
> **Η πόλις θα σε ακολουθεί.**

**Where to read him free.** The **Cavafy Archive** (kavafis.gr / the Onassis Foundation's site) holds the complete poems with manuscripts, variants and English translations; **snhell.gr** has him with recordings. He is out of copyright and everywhere.

**The one thing to know about his reputation.** He is the most translated and most internationally known modern Greek poet, and he was almost unknown in Athens in his lifetime. **Greek literary opinion came round to him slowly**, and some of the Generation of the Thirties helped it along — Seferis wrote about him at length.

**Practice.** Read **Ιθάκη** aloud three times, learn the four lines above, and then read **Η Πόλις**, which is twelve lines and will take ten minutes. Then read **Θερμοπύλες** and notice how much of it you understand without help.
Seferis:
The first Greek Nobel, the central figure of the Generation of the Thirties, and the poet whose subject is the weight of the Greek past on the Greek present — including Cyprus.

**The facts.** Γιώργος Σεφέρης, 1900–1971, born in Smyrna and driven out of it as a boy; career diplomat, ending as ambassador in London; **Nobel Prize in Literature, 1963**, the first for a Greek. Buried in Athens after a funeral that became a silent demonstration against the junta, which he had publicly denounced in 1969.

**The subject, in one sentence**: what it is to be Greek among ruins, with three thousand years of language and an immediate past of catastrophe.

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Στροφή** (1931) | *Turning Point* — the first collection, and the formal break |
| **Μυθιστόρημα** (1935) | *Mythistorema* — **the central work**: twenty-four poems, free verse, Odysseus and the Argonauts as the century's refugees |
| **Ημερολόγιο Καταστρώματος Α´, Β´, Γ´** | *Logbook* I, II, III — the war years, the exile in Egypt and South Africa, and then **Cyprus** |
| **Κίχλη** (1947) | *Thrush* — a sunken ship, a house, and the light |
| **Δοκιμές** | the essays — on Cavafy, on Erotokritos, on the Greek language. **Readable prose, and good for a learner.** |

**Ημερολόγιο Καταστρώματος Γ´ is the Cyprus book**, and it matters for this curriculum. Seferis went to Cyprus in 1953 and found there, as he said, what he had been looking for: a Greece still whole, still village-shaped, still itself. The collection was originally titled **«Κύπρον, ου μ' εθέσπισεν…»** — *Cyprus, where it was ordained for me…*, a line from the *Helen* of Euripides. Its poems include **Ελένη**, on the war fought for a phantom, and **Σαλαμίνα της Κύπρου**.

**So the stage you just finished has a Nobel laureate's book about it**, and reading it after stage 10 is the right order.

**Why he is hard:**

- **Free verse with a submerged metre** — the fifteen-syllable line is often there, broken.
- **Dense allusion** — Homer, Aeschylus, the Septuagint, the folk songs, Dante, Eliot.
- **Abstraction.** The images are concrete and what they mean is not.
- **The syntax breaks deliberately.**

**The one to start with**, and it is genuinely approachable:

> **Ἀρνήθηκα να γνωρίσω τον εαυτό μου…**

**or better, the opening of *Μυθιστόρημα* III:**

> **Μέμνησο λουτρῶν οἷς ἐνοσφίσθης**
>
> **Ξύπνησα με το μαρμάρινο τούτο κεφάλι στα χέρια**
> **που μου εξαντλεί τους αγκώνες και δεν ξέρω πού να το ακουμπήσω.**

**A marble head, too heavy to hold and impossible to put down.** That is the whole Generation of the Thirties in two lines, and it is the most quoted image in modern Greek poetry about the classical inheritance.

**And the line everyone knows**, from *Ημερολόγιο Καταστρώματος*:

> **Όπου και να ταξιδέψω η Ελλάδα με πληγώνει.**
> *Wherever I travel, Greece wounds me.*

**Where to read him free.** **snhell.gr** holds him **with his own voice** — and hearing Seferis read is the fastest route into his rhythm. The Nobel site has the 1963 speech, which is a short and clear statement of what he thought Greek poetry was for, and worth reading in Greek.

**The essays are the recommendation for a learner.** *Δοκιμές* is prose, it is lucid, and his essay on Cavafy will teach you more about reading Cavafy than any introduction.

**Practice.** Listen to Seferis reading on snhell.gr, with the text. Then read *Μυθιστόρημα* III slowly, aloud. Then read his Nobel speech in Greek, which is expository prose and well within your range after stage 9.
Elytis:
The second Greek Nobel, the poet of light and the Aegean, and the one whose greatest work half the country knows by heart because Theodorakis set it to music.

**The facts.** Οδυσσέας Ελύτης, 1911–1996, born in Heraklion to a family from Lesvos; fought in the Albanian campaign of 1940–41; **Nobel Prize in Literature, 1979**. A real name of Αλεπουδέλης, and a chosen one assembled from **Ελλάδα, ελπίδα, ελευθερία, Ελένη** — Greece, hope, freedom, Helen.

**The subject**: the Aegean — light, sea, stone, girls, summer — raised into a metaphysics. Surrealism learned from the French and then turned into something entirely Greek.

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Προσανατολισμοί** (1940) | *Orientations* — the early, bright, surrealist poems |
| **Άσμα ηρωικό και πένθιμο για τον χαμένο ανθυπολοχαγό της Αλβανίας** (1945) | the lament for the lost lieutenant of the Albanian front — **his war poem**, and one of the great ones in Greek |
| **Το Άξιον Εστί** (1959) | **the central work**: a sequence in three parts — *Η Γένεσις*, *Τα Πάθη*, *Το Δοξαστικόν* — built deliberately on the shape of an Orthodox liturgical service |
| **Το Μονόγραμμα** (1971) | a single long love poem, and the most beautiful thing in modern Greek for many readers |
| **Ο Μικρός Ναυτίλος**, **Τα Ελεγεία της Οξώπετρας** | the late work |

**Το Άξιον Εστί needs explaining**, because it is the thing to know.

**Its title is liturgical**: *Άξιον εστί* — *it is meet and right* — is the opening of the hymn to the Mother of God in the Divine Liturgy. Elytis built the sequence as a service: a Genesis, a Passion, and a Doxology, with psalms, readings and odes alternating as in an Orthodox office.

**And in 1964 Mikis Theodorakis set part of it** for voice, chorus, bouzouki and orchestra, with Grigoris Bithikotsis singing. The result went into the national bloodstream: **Ένα το χελιδόνι**, **Της δικαιοσύνης ήλιε νοητέ**, **Τη γλώσσα μου έδωσαν ελληνική** are sung at demonstrations, memorials and school ceremonies.

**The lines every Greek knows:**

> **Τη γλώσσα μου έδωσαν ελληνική·**
> **το σπίτι φτωχικό στις αμμουδιές του Ομήρου.**
> **Μονάχη έγνοια η γλώσσα μου στις αμμουδιές του Ομήρου.**

*They gave me the Greek language; a poor house on Homer's shores. My only care my language, on Homer's shores.*

**That is the single most quoted statement in modern Greek about the Greek language**, and it is the epigraph this whole curriculum could have carried.

**And the other, from the same sequence:**

> **Ένα το χελιδόνι και η άνοιξη ακριβή,**
> **για να γυρίσει ο ήλιος θέλει δουλειά πολλή.**

*One swallow, and spring is dear; for the sun to turn takes much work.*

**Why he is hard.** Surrealist imagery, invented compound words, syntax that dissolves, and a deliberate strangeness. **And the Άξιον Εστί's liturgical shape means it is easier for you than for most readers** — you know the office it is built on.

**Where to read him free.** **snhell.gr**, with recordings; the Nobel lecture, in Greek, is a statement about poetry and the Greek language worth reading slowly. **And the songs are everywhere** — which means you can learn the poem by singing it, which is what Greeks did.

**Practice.** Listen to *Τη γλώσσα μου έδωσαν ελληνική* sung, with the text, and learn the three lines. Then read the *Άξιον Εστί*'s first ode and notice the liturgical shape. Then read *Το Μονόγραμμα*'s opening and simply enjoy the sound.
Ritsos, and the poems that became songs:
The most prolific of the great modern Greek poets, the most set to music, and the one whose words you will hear sung before you read them.

**The facts.** Γιάννης Ρίτσος, 1909–1990. A ruined landowning family, tuberculosis, and then a lifetime on the left: fought with the resistance, imprisoned and exiled on Makronisos, Ai Stratis and Leros under the post-war governments, exiled again under the junta. More than a hundred volumes. Nominated for the Nobel repeatedly and never given it, which Greeks still mention.

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Επιτάφιος** (1936) | **the one to know.** A mother's lament over her son, shot by police during the Thessaloniki tobacco workers' strike. In the fifteen-syllable folk metre, in the voice of the folk lament. The Metaxas dictatorship burned it publicly. |
| **Ρωμιοσύνη** (1945–47) | *Greekness* — on the resistance and the people. **Set by Theodorakis**, and the setting is among the best-known Greek music there is. |
| **Η Σονάτα του Σεληνόφωτος** (1956) | *The Moonlight Sonata* — a dramatic monologue, a woman in an old house. His best-known long poem. |
| **Δεκαοχτώ Λιανοτράγουδα της Πικρής Πατρίδας** (1973) | eighteen short songs of the bitter homeland — written under the junta, set by Theodorakis |
| **Τέταρτη Διάσταση** | the mythological monologues: Orestes, Helen, Ismene, Chrysothemis speaking in a modern voice |

**Επιτάφιος is where to start**, for three reasons: the metre is the folk fifteen-syllable, which you can hear; the vocabulary is the vocabulary of lament, which is concrete; and **Theodorakis set it in 1958 with Bithikotsis singing**, so you can learn it by ear.

**The lines:**

> **Γιε μου, σπλάχνο των σπλάχνων μου, καρδούλα της καρδιάς μου,**
> **πουλάκι της φτωχιάς αυλής, ανθέ της ερημιάς μου…**

*My son, flesh of my flesh, little heart of my heart, little bird of the poor yard, flower of my desolation.*

**Note what it is doing.** That is the register of the Greek funeral lament — the **θρήνος** — and of the Lamentations of Holy Friday, the **Εγκώμια**, which your church sings over the tomb. **Ritsos, an atheist and a communist, wrote a mother's lament in the Church's own form**, and every Greek hears both at once.

**That double hearing is worth understanding**, because it is characteristic of modern Greece: the Church's language is the people's language, and a poet of the left uses it without irony because there is nothing else to use.

**And from Ρωμιοσύνη:**

> **Αυτά τα δέντρα δε βολεύονται με λιγότερο ουρανό,**
> **αυτές οι πέτρες δε βολεύονται κάτου απ' τα ξένα βήματα…**

**The poems that became songs**, which is the practical point of this lesson. A great deal of the Greek poetic canon is in the national memory as **music** rather than as text:

| Poem | Composer |
| --- | --- |
| **Επιτάφιος** — Ritsos | Theodorakis, 1958 |
| **Ρωμιοσύνη** — Ritsos | Theodorakis |
| **Το Άξιον Εστί** — Elytis | Theodorakis, 1964 |
| **Μυθιστόρημα, Άρνηση** — Seferis | Theodorakis — **Στο περιγιάλι το κρυφό**, which everyone sings |
| **Λιανοτράγουδα** — Ritsos | Theodorakis |
| **Cavafy** | set by many, including Dalaras and Mikroutsikos |
| **Ο Μεγάλος Ερωτικός** — various poets | Hadjidakis, 1972 — **the best single album for a learner**, the Greek love poetry of three thousand years set to music |

**Ο Μεγάλος Ερωτικός deserves the recommendation.** Hadjidakis set Sappho, the Song of Songs, Erotokritos, Solomos, Cavafy, Elytis, Seferis and the folk songs on one record, sung by Flery Dandonaki and Dimitris Psarianos. **It is a complete anthology of Greek love poetry with audio**, and the texts are on stixoi.info.

**So the method of this lesson is stage 8's song method applied to the canon**: learn the poem by singing it, then read it, then learn four lines.

**Practice.** Listen to Theodorakis's *Επιτάφιος* with the text, and learn the first two lines. Then listen to *Στο περιγιάλι το κρυφό* and realise you are singing Seferis. Then find *Ο Μεγάλος Ερωτικός* and listen to all of it once.
Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent:
The founders — the poets who decided that modern Greek literature would be written in the people's language, and the one who wrote the national anthem.

**Διονύσιος Σολωμός, 1798–1857.** Born in Zakynthos, educated in Italy, wrote his first poetry in Italian, and then turned deliberately to Greek — to the **demotic**, at a moment when educated opinion held that serious literature required the learned language.

**His decision is the foundation of everything after him**, and he argued it in one famous sentence:

> **Μήγαρις έχω άλλο στο νου μου πάρεξ ελευθερία και γλώσσα;**
> *Have I anything else in my mind but freedom and language?*

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ύμνος εις την Ελευθερίαν** (1823) | *Hymn to Liberty* — 158 stanzas. **Its first two are the national anthem of Greece, and of Cyprus.** |
| **Ο Κρητικός** | *The Cretan* — a shipwrecked Cretan, his dying beloved, and a vision. A fragment, and his greatest. |
| **Ελεύθεροι Πολιορκημένοι** | *The Free Besieged* — on the siege of Missolonghi. Also a fragment. |
| **Η Γυναίκα της Ζάκυθος** | prose, satirical, strange |

**The thing to know about Solomos: almost everything is a fragment.** He revised obsessively and finished little. What survives is pieces of enormous poems, assembled by editors — which is itself the condition of modern Greek literature at its start.

**The anthem's first stanza**, which you should be able to recognise standing up:

> **Σε γνωρίζω από την κόψη**
> **του σπαθιού την τρομερή,**
> **σε γνωρίζω από την όψη**
> **που με βία μετράει τη γη.**

*I know you by the terrible edge of your sword; I know you by the gaze that measures the earth with violence.* — addressed to Liberty.

**And it is sung in Cyprus too**, which matters after stage 10: the Republic of Cyprus uses the same anthem.

**Ανδρέας Κάλβος, 1792–1869**, the other Zakynthian, who went the other way: twenty odes in an archaising, Pindaric Greek, austere and strange. **Hard, and admired more than read.**

**Κωστής Παλαμάς, 1859–1943.** The dominant literary figure of the generation after, the champion of the demotic in its battles, and the poet of the Greek nation's self-understanding before the catastrophe.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ο Δωδεκάλογος του Γύφτου** (1907) | *The Twelve Words of the Gypsy* — a huge philosophical poem on the fall of Byzantium and what follows |
| **Η Φλογέρα του Βασιλιά** (1910) | *The King's Flute* — Basil II and the Byzantine imperial idea |
| **Ο Τάφος** | the laments for his dead child — **and the most immediately readable thing he wrote** |
| **Ίαμβοι και Ανάπαιστοι** | the shorter lyrics |

**And the thing about Palamas that is not literary**: his funeral, in February 1943, under German occupation, became a national demonstration. Thousands followed the coffin, and Sikelianos read a poem over the grave; the crowd sang the national anthem in front of the occupying troops. **It is one of the moments of twentieth-century Greek history**, and Greeks know it.

**Why the nineteenth century is hard for a learner**: the demotic was being invented as they wrote, so the vocabulary is unstable; the Ionian poets use Italianate syntax; Kalvos and Palamas both reach for the learned register; and the subject matter assumes the national narrative of the period.

**Where to start, honestly**: the anthem's first two stanzas, Palamas's **Ο Τάφος**, and then Solomos's **Ο Κρητικός** with a school edition's notes. **Do not start here** — come to it after Cavafy and Ritsos.

**Where to read them free.** All out of copyright, all on **snhell.gr** and the Greek Wikisource, and the school editions with notes are on **ebooks.edu.gr**.

**Practice.** Learn the national anthem's first stanza, because it comes up — at church events, at national-day celebrations, at Cypriot gatherings. Then read Palamas's *Ο Τάφος* and notice how plain it is. Then read Solomos's sentence about freedom and language again.
The folk song, and Crete:
The oldest layer of modern Greek literature, which is anonymous, sung, and the source everything else draws on.

**Το δημοτικό τραγούδι** — the demotic song. Centuries of anonymous oral poetry in the fifteen-syllable line, collected from the eighteenth century onwards, and the acknowledged foundation of modern Greek literary language. **Solomos studied it, Ritsos wrote in it, and every Greek poet since has quoted it.**

**The kinds:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τα ακριτικά** | the Akritic songs — the Byzantine frontier guards, and **Διγενής Ακρίτας** wrestling with Death. The oldest layer. |
| **Οι παραλογές** | the ballads — narrative, supernatural, often terrible. **Του νεκρού αδελφού** and **Της Άρτας το γιοφύρι**. |
| **Τα κλέφτικα** | the songs of the mountain fighters under Ottoman rule |
| **Τα μοιρολόγια** | the laments — and in Mani they are a formal art with named composers |
| **Τα της ξενιτιάς** | the songs of exile and emigration — and these are the ones that reach the diaspora |
| **Τα της αγάπης, τα του γάμου, τα της δουλειάς** | love songs, wedding songs, work songs |

**The two ballads to know:**

**Του νεκρού αδελφού** — the dead brother. A mother with nine sons and one daughter; the youngest son, Constantine, swears to bring the daughter home from her distant marriage if the mother needs her. All nine die. The mother curses him; he rises from the grave and rides to fetch his sister. **The ballad exists across the whole Balkans and the Greek version is the richest**, and Lenore and the European undead-bridegroom ballads descend from the same root.

**Της Άρτας το γιοφύρι** — the bridge of Arta. Forty-five masons build a bridge all day and it falls each night; a bird tells them the bridge needs a human sacrifice, and the master builder's wife must be walled in. Her lament and her curse close the song. **Also pan-Balkan**, and the single most famous Greek folk ballad.

> **Ολημερίς το χτίζανε, το βράδυ εγκρεμιζόταν.**

**Why the folk songs matter for your Greek:**

- **The fifteen-syllable line** at its clearest — hear it here and you hear it everywhere else.
