- **A formulaic vocabulary** that recurs across hundreds of songs, so they get easier fast.
- **The register that poets borrow** — Ritsos's lament, Solomos's diction, Michaelides's Cypriot verse.
- **They are sung**, so audio is available, and the words are on stixoi.info.

**Crete, which is a literature of its own.**

The Cretan Renaissance, under Venetian rule, produced the finest Greek literature between the Byzantines and Solomos — in the Cretan dialect, in the fifteen-syllable line, and with Italian models.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ερωτόκριτος** — Βιτσέντζος Κορνάρος, c. 1600 | **10,000 lines of rhymed fifteen-syllable verse**: a romance of Erotokritos and Aretousa. Still sung in Crete, and known by heart by old Cretans. |
| **Ερωφίλη** — Γεώργιος Χορτάτσης | a tragedy, in the same tradition |
| **Η Θυσία του Αβραάμ** | the sacrifice of Abraham — a religious drama, and moving |
| **Η Βοσκοπούλα** | the shepherdess — a pastoral |

**Ο Ερωτόκριτος is the thing.** Ten thousand lines, Cretan dialect, rhyming couplets, and a living tradition: Cretan singers perform it to the lyra, and the opening lines are among the best-known in the language.

> **Του Κύκλου τα γυρίσματα, που ανεβοκατεβαίνου,**
> **και του Τροχού, που ώρες ψηλά κι ώρες στα βάθη πηαίνου…**

*The turnings of the Wheel, that rise and fall; and of the Wheel that goes now high and now into the depths…*

**It is hard** — Cretan dialect of 1600 — and it is the one work in this stage that is as much music as text. **Listen to it sung before reading it.**

**And the Cretan connection to stage 10.** Cretan and Cypriot are the two great surviving Greek dialects with literatures of their own, both preserving ancient features, both with a fifteen-syllable tradition, and both with improvised verse contests — Cretan **μαντινάδες** and Cypriot **τσιαττιστά**. **They are the same cultural form in two islands.**

**Where to find them free.** The folk songs are collected in editions long out of copyright and on the Greek Wikisource; **ebooks.edu.gr** has them in the school Ανθολόγιο with notes; the Erotokritos is online in full; and the sung versions are on YouTube and stixoi.info.

**Practice.** Read *Της Άρτας το γιοφύρι* aloud and count the syllables of three lines. Then listen to a Cretan singer performing the opening of the *Erotokritos* with the text. Then find one song of ξενιτιά and notice that it is about your own parish's grandparents.
Papadiamantis:
The great short-story writer of Greek Orthodoxy, the hardest prose in this stage, and the writer closest to the reason this curriculum exists.

**The facts.** Αλέξανδρος Παπαδιαμάντης, 1851–1911. Born on Skiathos, son of a priest; went to Athens, failed to finish a degree, lived in poverty translating and writing for newspapers; **was a chanter** — he sang in the church of Saint Elisseos in Athens for decades, in the Byzantine tradition, with his friends. Returned to Skiathos and died there.

**Two hundred short stories and three novels.** He is held, by broad Greek consensus, to be the greatest Greek prose writer.

**Why he matters to you specifically.** No writer in the language is closer to the Church. His subjects are the island parish, the feasts, the fasts, the chanting, the priest, the shepherd, the poor widow, the sea, and the saints — written from inside the liturgical year by a man who spent his nights chanting it. **Reading Papadiamantis is reading Orthodoxy as a lived thing**, and it is why his stories are reprinted in church bookshops as well as in literature series.

**Why he is hard, and this is an honest warning.** His Greek is a deliberate mixture:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Narration in katharevousa** | the learned register, with ancient datives, participles and vocabulary |
| **Dialogue in the Skiathos dialect** | demotic, island, archaic, and transcribed phonetically |
| **Liturgical and scriptural quotation** | in Koine and Byzantine Greek, unmarked, woven into sentences |
| **Long sentences** | periodic, with the verb held back |

**That mixture is the point** — the narrator's learned voice against the villagers' speech against the Church's language, all at once — and it means **he is the writer in this curriculum most dependent on the classical curriculum you have not done yet.**

**So the honest instruction is**: read the stories with a facing translation or a glossed school edition, accept that you are working, and come back to him after the classical curriculum.

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Η Φόνισσα** (1903) | *The Murderess* — an old woman on Skiathos who begins drowning infant girls, out of a terrible compassion for the dowry-burdened poor. **His masterpiece**, and about a hundred pages. |
| **Οι Χριστουγεννιάτικες ιστορίες** | the Christmas and Easter stories — written for the feast-day newspapers, and **the way into him** |
| **Όνειρο στο κύμα** | *A Dream on the Wave* — the shepherd boy, Moschoula, and the sea. The most anthologised Greek short story. |
| **Η Σταχομαζώχτρα, Ο Έρωτας στα Χιόνια, Στο Χριστό στο Κάστρο** | and twenty more that are standard |
| **Οι Έμποροι των Εθνών, Η Γυφτοπούλα** | the early novels, less read |

**Στο Χριστό στο Κάστρο** is the one to start with if you want the church: a village that walks to the old fortress church for Christmas through the snow, and keeps the feast there. **It is the Orthodox Christmas in a short story.**

**The line everyone quotes**, from his own self-description:

> **Το παν είναι να αγαπά κανείς.**

**And his best-known sentence**, which opens *Όνειρο στο κύμα* and is quoted for its rhythm:

> **Ήμουν πτωχόν παιδίον, βοσκόπουλο εις τα όρη…**

**Note πτωχόν, παιδίον, εις** — three katharevousa forms in eight words. **That is his register in one line**, and it is why he is in this stage rather than stage 8.

**Where to read him free.** Out of copyright and everywhere: the Greek Wikisource has the complete works; **ebooks.edu.gr** has the anthologised stories with school notes and glosses, which is the version to use; and audio readings exist for the famous stories.

**One more thing worth knowing.** Papadiamantis is the writer modern Greek Orthodox writers measure themselves against — Kontoglou, the Elders' biographers, and the whole twentieth-century religious revival in Greek letters look back to him. **He is the bridge between the Church and Greek literature**, and both claim him.

**Practice.** Read *Στο Χριστό στο Κάστρο* with a glossed edition — slowly, in two or three sittings. Count how many katharevousa forms you can now read without help. Then read the first page of *Η Φόνισσα* and put it on the shelf for after the classical curriculum.
Kazantzakis:
The most famous Greek writer abroad, the most argued about at home, and the one a learner is most likely to try first — with a warning about the difficulty and a note about the Church.

**The facts.** Νίκος Καζαντζάκης, 1883–1957. Cretan, born in Heraklion under Ottoman rule; studied law in Athens and philosophy in Paris under Bergson; travelled constantly; wrote in Greek, French and a great deal of journalism; translated Dante and Goethe; spent his last years in Antibes. Nominated for the Nobel repeatedly; lost to Camus in 1957 by one vote, as the story goes.

**The works:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Βίος και Πολιτεία του Αλέξη Ζορμπά** (1946) | *Zorba the Greek* — the intellectual narrator and the appetite that overwhelms him |
| **Ο Χριστός Ξανασταυρώνεται** (1948) | *Christ Recrucified* — a village passion play and the refugees who arrive during it. **His best novel, by many judgements, and the most Orthodox in material.** |
| **Ο Καπετάν Μιχάλης** (1953) | *Freedom or Death* — the Cretan risings against the Turks, and his father |
| **Ο Τελευταίος Πειρασμός** (1955) | *The Last Temptation* — the controversial one |
| **Αναφορά στον Γκρέκο** (1961) | *Report to Greco* — the autobiography, addressed to El Greco. **The most beautiful and the most readable.** |
| **Ασκητική** (1927) | *The Saviours of God* — the metaphysical credo, and the key to all the rest |
| **Οδύσσεια** (1938) | 33,333 lines of seventeen-syllable verse. Almost nobody reads it. |

**Why he is hard for a learner**, and this surprises people who have read him in English:

- **An enormous vocabulary**, much of it Cretan dialect, village words and his own coinages. He collected words deliberately.
- **Long, rolling sentences** with a rhythm borrowed from the folk song.
- **Demotic pushed to its limits** — he was a militant demoticist and used forms that are now archaic or regional.

**So the English translations read more easily than the Greek**, which is unusual, and a learner who loved *Zorba* in English can be badly discouraged by the Greek. **Start with *Αναφορά στον Γκρέκο***, whose chapters are short and whose prose is the clearest he wrote.

**The Church question, handled honestly, because it will come up.**

Kazantzakis was in real and lifelong conflict with the Orthodox Church. The Holy Synod of the Church of Greece considered action against him in 1955 over *The Last Temptation*; **he was not excommunicated**, and the widely repeated claim that he was is false. The Roman Catholic Church placed *The Last Temptation* on the Index.

**His own answer to the Synod** is often quoted:

> **Μου δώσατε μια κατάρα, Άγιοι πατέρες, σας δίνω μια ευχή: σας εύχομαι να είναι η συνείδησή σας τόσο καθαρή όσο η δική μου και να είστε τόσο ηθικοί και θρήσκοι όσο είμαι εγώ.**

**And his epitaph, in Heraklion**, cut into the stone of the Martinengo bastion:

> **Δεν ελπίζω τίποτα. Δε φοβούμαι τίποτα. Είμαι λέφτερος.**

*I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.*

**What to make of him, as an Orthodox reader.** He is not an Orthodox writer and he is unavoidably a writer formed by Orthodoxy: the Christ of *Ο Χριστός Ξανασταυρώνεται* is the Christ of the village liturgy, the monks of *Αναφορά στον Γκρέκο* are drawn with real love, and his lifelong subject — the struggle of flesh and spirit — is an ascetic's subject handled by a man who would not submit to the ascesis. **Read him as that**, and the arguments about him become interesting rather than tiresome.

**And the practical point**: he is the Greek writer a non-Greek is most likely to have read, which makes him useful conversationally — and Greek opinion of him is genuinely divided, so ask rather than assert.

**Where to read him free.** He is still in copyright in most places, so legal free texts are limited; libraries have him, the Kazantzakis Museum in Myrtia publishes material, and secondhand Greek editions are cheap. **The Greek Wikipedia article on him is long and good**, and reading it is itself useful practice.

**Practice.** Read the first chapter of *Αναφορά στον Γκρέκο* in Greek and see how it feels. Then read his epitaph aloud until you can say it from memory — it is three sentences and every Greek knows them. Then ask one person at church what they think of him.
The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia:
The novelists of the central Greek catastrophe, and the generation that made modern Greek prose — the material closest to the history your parish carries.

**Η Γενιά του '30.** The writers who came of age after the 1922 catastrophe and set out to make a modern Greek literature that was both European and Greek: Seferis and Elytis in poetry, and in prose **Myrivilis, Venezis, Theotokas, Terzakis, Karagatsis, Prevelakis, Politis**. Their programme was explicit — **Ελληνικότητα**, Greekness, found rather than asserted.

**The catastrophe, in one paragraph, because the literature is unreadable without it.** In 1922 the Greek army's advance into Anatolia collapsed; Smyrna burned; and by the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne roughly **1.2 million Orthodox Christians** were expelled from Asia Minor, Pontus and Eastern Thrace to Greece, and about 400,000 Muslims from Greece to Turkey. Greece's population rose by a quarter overnight. **Three thousand years of Greek life in Asia Minor ended in eighteen months.**

**The books:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Η Ζωή εν Τάφω** — Στράτης Μυριβήλης (1924) | *Life in the Tomb* — the Macedonian front, in letters. **The great Greek war book**, and extraordinary. Hard. |
| **Η Παναγιά η Γοργόνα** — Μυριβήλης | the mermaid Madonna — a refugee village on Lesvos, and gentler |
| **Το Νούμερο 31328** — Ηλίας Βενέζης (1931) | *Number 31328* — the author's own experience in the Turkish labour battalions. **Unbearable and essential.** |
| **Αιολική Γη** — Βενέζης (1943) | *Aeolian Land* — childhood in Asia Minor before the end. Lyrical, and the easier way in. |
| **Ιστορία ενός Αιχμαλώτου** — Στρατής Δούκας (1929) | a captive's story, told plainly in the man's own words. **Short, and the best single text to start with.** |
| **Ματωμένα Χώματα** — Διδώ Σωτηρίου (1962) | *Farewell Anatolia* — **the Asia Minor novel most Greeks have read**, and the most readable |
| **Στου Χατζηφράγκου** — Κοσμάς Πολίτης (1962) | Smyrna before the fire, from inside the neighbourhood |
| **Αργώ** — Γιώργος Θεοτοκάς | the Athens of the generation itself |
| **Ο Γιούγκερμαν** — Μ. Καραγάτσης | long, popular, readable, and amoral |
| **Το Χρονικό μιας Πολιτείας** — Παντελής Πρεβελάκης | Rethymno, and Crete |

**Ματωμένα Χώματα is the recommendation** for a learner who wants the subject: narrated plainly in the first person by a villager, in accessible modern Greek, and it has sold more copies in Greece than almost any other novel. **Ιστορία ενός Αιχμαλώτου** is the other — forty pages, in the voice of the man who lived it, and as clean a piece of Greek prose as exists.

**Why this matters for your parish.** The Greek Orthodox communities of Britain, and of everywhere else in the diaspora, are made substantially of three displacements: **1922 from Asia Minor**, the post-war emigration from Greece and Cyprus, and **1974 from northern Cyprus**. The second and third you met in stages 7 and 10. **This is the first**, and it is the deepest layer of the diaspora's memory.

**The vocabulary of it**, which recurs in every one of these books and in conversation:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η Μικρασιατική Καταστροφή** | the Asia Minor Catastrophe |
| **ο ξεριζωμός** | **the uprooting** — the word for the whole event |
| **οι πρόσφυγες** | the refugees |
| **η ανταλλαγή των πληθυσμών** | the exchange of populations |
| **οι χαμένες πατρίδες** | **the lost homelands** |
| **η Σμύρνη, η Πόλη, ο Πόντος, η Καππαδοκία** | Smyrna, Constantinople, Pontus, Cappadocia |
| **ο Μικρασιάτης, ο Πόντιος** | the Asia Minor Greek, the Pontian |
| **η Ρωμιοσύνη** | the Greek Orthodox people, in the Byzantine and Ottoman sense |

**ο ξεριζωμός and οι χαμένες πατρίδες are the two to know**, because they are the terms in which it is still spoken about, and because they are also used of Cyprus in 1974.

**And the music, from stage 7**: rebetiko is the Asia Minor refugees' music, and **Smyrna style** — Σμυρναίικο — is its earlier layer. The whole genre is this history sung.

**Where to read them free.** Mostly in copyright, so libraries and cheap Greek paperbacks; **ebooks.edu.gr** has extracts with notes in the school anthologies, which is the free route; and the Greek Wikipedia articles on the catastrophe and on each writer are substantial.

**Practice.** Read *Ιστορία ενός Αιχμαλώτου* — it is forty pages and it is the best-written short thing in this lesson. Then learn **ο ξεριζωμός** and **οι χαμένες πατρίδες**. Then ask at church whether anyone's family came from Asia Minor, and listen.
The civil war, and the post-war novel:
The second great wound, the literature it produced, and the reason some subjects are still handled carefully in Greek company.

**The history, briefly, because the literature requires it.** Occupation 1941–44 — German, Italian and Bulgarian — with mass starvation in Athens in the winter of 1941–42 and a large resistance, much of it led by the communist EAM/ELAS. Then **the civil war, 1946–49**, between the government and the communist forces, ending in defeat for the left. Then decades of exclusion: the prison islands, the certificates of political reliability, exile. Then the **junta, 1967–74**, and the Polytechnic in November 1973.

**Why it still matters.** The civil war was a war between neighbours, and the division ran through villages and families. **It was not spoken about publicly for decades** — the official silence lasted until the 1980s — and much of the literature is the speaking.

**The books:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Το Κιβώτιο** — Άρης Αλεξάνδρου (1974) | *The Mission Box* — a party member writing his defence from a cell about a box that turns out to be empty. **The great novel of the Greek left's self-destruction**, and one of the finest Greek novels of the century. Hard. |
| **Ακυβέρνητες Πολιτείες** — Στρατής Τσίρκας | *Drifting Cities* — the Greek exiles in Jerusalem, Cairo and Alexandria during the war. Three volumes. |
| **Η Κάθοδος των Εννιά** — Θανάσης Βαλτινός (1963) | *The Descent of the Nine* — nine fighters retreating, told flatly. Short, and devastating. |
| **Το Τρίτο Στεφάνι** — Κώστας Ταχτσής (1962) | *The Third Wedding* — two women talking, across forty years of Greek history. **The most readable great Greek novel**, and very funny. |
| **Τα Ματογυάλια** and the stories of **Δημήτρης Χατζής** | *Το τέλος της μικρής μας πόλης* — the small town and its destruction |
| **Γιώργος Ιωάννου** | *Η Σαρκοφάγος*, *Το δικό μας αίμα* — autobiographical prose about Thessaloniki, the occupation and the refugees. **Beautiful and accessible.** |
| **Ζ** — Βασίλης Βασιλικός (1966) | the Lambrakis assassination, as a novel |

**Το Τρίτο Στεφάνι is the recommendation.** It is two women's voices — a mother and her son's mother-in-law — talking across the whole century, in the most natural spoken Greek in any Greek novel. **It is the best book in this stage for a learner's purposes**: you learn colloquial Greek, you learn the history, and you laugh.

**And Γιώργος Ιωάννου is the other.** Short autobiographical pieces, plain modern Greek, about Thessaloniki, the refugee quarters, the occupation and the Jewish community destroyed in 1943. **Accessible, and he writes about the Church and the feasts with real attention.**

**The vocabulary:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η Κατοχή** | the Occupation |
| **η Αντίσταση** | the Resistance |
| **ο Εμφύλιος** | **the Civil War** — and the word alone is enough |
| **η Χούντα / η Δικτατορία** | the junta / the dictatorship |
| **το Πολυτεχνείο** | the Polytechnic — 17 November 1973, and a national holiday |
| **η εξορία, τα ξερονήσια** | exile, the barren prison islands |
| **ο Δεκέμβρης / τα Δεκεμβριανά** | December 1944, the fighting in Athens |
| **η Μεταπολίτευση** | the restoration of democracy from 1974 |

**The social rule**, as with 1974 in Cyprus: **do not take a side.** The division between left and right over the occupation, the civil war and the junta is live in Greek politics and in families, and a foreigner's opinion about EAM or about the colonels is not wanted. **Ask, listen, and let it go.**

**And the Church is part of this story too**, uncomfortably: the hierarchy's position during the occupation, the civil war and the junta is itself a contested subject, with heroism and compromise both on the record — Archbishop Damaskinos and the rescue of Athenian Jews on one side of the ledger, the Church's accommodations with the colonels on another. **Know that it is contested; do not adjudicate it.**

**Where to read them free.** In copyright, mostly; libraries and cheap paperbacks. **ebooks.edu.gr** has extracts in the school anthologies, and the Greek Wikipedia on the Εμφύλιος and the Πολυτεχνείο is substantial and worth reading as practice.

**Practice.** Read *Το Τρίτο Στεφάνι* — properly, all of it, as the novel of this stage. Then read two pieces by Γιώργος Ιωάννου. Then learn the eight terms above, and do not use them to form an opinion.
Contemporary Greek writing:
What is being written now, which is the part of the literature you can read as it appears — and the part Greeks will actually be talking about.

**The honest framing.** Everything before this lesson is canon, with school editions and settled reputations. This is the live scene, where judgements are open, and where you can read a book the year it comes out and have an opinion worth as much as anyone's.

**The novelists worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πέτρος Μάρκαρης** | the Haritos crime novels — Athens, the crisis, a detective with a dictionary habit. **The easiest literary Greek in print**, and the one to start with. |
| **Ιωάννα Καρυστιάνη** | *Μικρά Αγγλία*, *Κουστούμι στο χώμα* — families, islands, the sea |
| **Ζυράννα Ζατέλη** | *Και με το φως του λύκου επανέρχονται* — strange, dense, northern. Hard and remarkable. |
| **Χρήστος Οικονόμου** | *Κάτι θα γίνει, θα δεις* — short stories from Piraeus in the crisis. **The best Greek prose of the last twenty years, for many readers.** |
| **Σωτήρης Δημητρίου** | Epirus, the border, plain voices |
| **Αμάντα Μιχαλοπούλου** | contemporary Athens, essays and fiction |
| **Έρση Σωτηροπούλου** | *Τι μένει από τη νύχτα* — Cavafy in Paris, as a novel |
| **Θανάσης Βαλτινός** | still working, and formally inventive |
| **Αλέξης Σταμάτης, Νίκος Παναγιωτόπουλος** | and a dozen more |

**Markaris is the practical recommendation**, as stage 8 said: current Athenian Greek, a plot, dialogue, and a recognisable city. **And his crisis trilogy is the best fiction about what Greece went through after 2010.**

**Χρήστος Οικονόμου is the other.** *Κάτι θα γίνει, θα δεις* — *Something Will Happen, You'll See* — is sixteen stories from the Piraeus of the crisis, in stripped-down Greek, and it is as good as contemporary writing in any language.

**The poets now:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κυριάκος Χαραλαμπίδης** | Cypriot, major, and his subject is 1974 and Cypriot antiquity |
| **Τίτος Πατρίκιος** | of the civil-war generation, still publishing into his nineties |
| **Κική Δημουλά** (1931–2020) | **the most loved Greek poet of recent decades** — plain words, grief, grammar used as metaphor. **Very accessible for a learner.** |
| **Μιχάλης Γκανάς** | Epirus, the folk tradition, and much of it set to music |
| **Γιάννης Βαρβέρης, Δημήτρης Δημητριάδης** | and the generation after |
| **The young poets** | publishing in journals and online, and arguing |

**Κική Δημουλά is the one to read.** Her Greek is ordinary vocabulary used strangely; she writes about absence and the death of her husband; she turns grammatical terms into images. **A poem of hers is within your reach now**, which is not true of Elytis.

**Where the conversation happens:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Χάρτης** | **a free online literary monthly** — poetry, prose, essays, and current. The best single free source. |
| **Ο Αναγνώστης** | the free online literary review — reviews of everything as it appears |
| **Νέα Εστία** | the oldest literary journal, founded 1927 |
| **Ποιητική, The Books' Journal** | and the rest of the print journals |
| **Literary blogs and bookshop events** | and the Thessaloniki Book Fair |

**Χάρτης is a genuine recommendation**: free, monthly, substantial, and it will give you current Greek literary prose and poetry every month for nothing.

**What contemporary Greek writing is about**, which tells you something about the country:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The crisis** | 2010 onwards — poverty, emigration, the collapse of the middle class |
| **Migration** | Greece as a frontier, and the boats |
| **Memory** | the civil war, the junta, Asia Minor, still being worked through |
| **The city** | Athens as a subject in itself |
| **The island and the village** | and the people who left them |
| **Family** | which is the permanent Greek subject |

**And what you can do that you could not before.** Read a book the year it is published, read the reviews in Greek, disagree with them, and say so at church. **That is what the whole curriculum was for**, and it is where the stage ends up: not knowing Greek literature, but being a reader among readers.

**Practice.** Read one Markaris novel and one story from *Κάτι θα γίνει, θα δεις*. Then read one poem by Kiki Dimoula. Then read this month's **Χάρτης**, and pick one piece to finish.
Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers:
The twentieth-century Orthodox revival in Greek letters — the writers for whom the Church was not a subject but the ground they stood on. For his purposes, the most important lesson in this stage.

**Φώτης Κόντογλου, 1895–1965.** Born in Aivali — Kydonies — on the Asia Minor coast, and driven out in 1922. An icon painter who **reversed the course of Greek religious art**: he rejected the western-influenced academic painting that had dominated Greek churches since the eighteenth century and returned to the Byzantine tradition, and the entire modern revival of Byzantine iconography in Greece descends from him. He painted the Athens city hall and a number of churches, and he trained a generation.

**And he wrote.** His prose is archaising, rich, deliberately old-fashioned, full of island and Asia Minor vocabulary, and unmistakable.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αϊβαλί, η πατρίδα μου** | Aivali, my homeland — the lost town, written from memory |
| **Ο Θεός Κόνανος** | stories |
| **Ευλογημένο Καταφύγιο** | essays and reflections — **the way into him** |
| **Η Πονεμένη Ρωμιοσύνη** | *The Suffering Greek Orthodox People* — his statement of what Ρωμιοσύνη means |
| **Έκφρασις της Ορθοδόξου Εικονογραφίας** | the technical and theological treatise on iconography |

**Η Πονεμένη Ρωμιοσύνη is the title to understand**, because **Ρωμιοσύνη** is the word at the centre of this whole question: not *Hellenism*, which looks to antiquity, but **Romiosyne** — the Orthodox Christian Greek people of Byzantium and the Ottoman centuries, defined by the Church rather than by the classical past. **Kontoglou's whole argument is that this, not the Parthenon, is what Greece actually is.**

**Νίκος Γαβριήλ Πεντζίκης, 1908–1993.** Thessaloniki's own writer: a pharmacist, a painter, and the author of prose unlike anything else in Greek — associative, liturgical, digressive, stuffed with saints' lives and city topography and botany.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ο Πεθαμένος και η Ανάσταση** (1944) | the dead man and the resurrection |
| **Μητέρα Θεσσαλονίκη** | *Mother Thessaloniki* — the city as a body and a calendar of saints |

**He is difficult and he is the most thoroughly Orthodox imagination in modern Greek prose.** Approach him late, and with patience.

**The Elders, which is the most-read Orthodox writing in Greek by a very wide margin:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γέροντας Παΐσιος ο Αγιορείτης** (1924–1994) | the six volumes of **Λόγοι**, published from the monastery at Souroti. **Transcribed speech: simple vocabulary, short paragraphs, and the easiest Orthodox reading in Greek.** |
| **Γέροντας Πορφύριος ο Καυσοκαλυβίτης** (1906–1991) | *Βίος και Λόγοι* — on love, on prayer, on children |
| **Αρχιμ. Αιμιλιανός Σιμωνοπετρίτης** (1934–2019) | the catechetical talks from Simonopetra — more demanding, and very fine |
| **Γέροντας Σωφρόνιος** (1896–1993) | **and he matters to you particularly**: a Russian who founded the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist at Tolleshunt Knights in **Essex** in 1959 — the main Orthodox monastic centre in Britain. He wrote in Russian; the Greek translations are everywhere. |
| **Μητροπολίτης Ιερόθεος Βλάχος** | of Nafpaktos — accessible dogmatic and ascetic writing, widely read |

**Elder Sophrony's monastery in Essex is worth knowing about as a fact about Britain**: it is where many British Orthodox go on pilgrimage, Saint Sophrony was canonised in 2019, and your parish will have people who have been there.

**Why the Elders are the right reading for you now.** Stage 8 said it and it is worth repeating: transcribed speech, plain vocabulary, short paragraphs, material you want to read anyway, and in print in every church bookshop. **A page of Elder Paisios a day is a serious Greek reading habit that costs almost nothing.**

**And the honest literary note.** The Elders' books are not literature and do not claim to be. Kontoglou and Pentzikis are, and both are hard. **The order to read them in is: Paisios, then Kontoglou's essays, then Pentzikis — the last after the classical curriculum.**

**Where to find them free.** The Elders' texts circulate very widely online, legitimately and otherwise, and most Greek monasteries publish extracts; Kontoglou is partly in copyright; and church bookshops sell all of it cheaply.

**Practice.** Read one page of Elder Paisios in Greek, and notice how easy it is. Then read one essay from Kontoglou's *Ευλογημένο Καταφύγιο* and notice how hard it is. Then learn the word **Ρωμιοσύνη** and what it means, because it is the argument of the next two lessons.
Modern Greek theology:
Where this curriculum and the next one meet: twentieth-century Orthodox theology written in modern Greek, which you can now read — and which is the direct preparation for the classical curriculum.

**What happened in the twentieth century.** Greek academic theology in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was largely written on German Protestant and scholastic models — systematic, confessional, and formally western. From the 1930s onwards a generation set out to recover a theology grounded in the Fathers and in the liturgical and ascetic tradition instead. **That recovery is one of the significant intellectual events of modern Orthodoxy**, and most of it is in modern Greek.

**The figures:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ιωάννης Ρωμανίδης** (1927–2001) | **Το Προπατορικόν Αμάρτημα** — the doctoral thesis that reopened the question of ancestral sin against the Augustinian account. Also **Ρωμαίοι ή Ρωμηοί Πατέρες** and the Ρωμηοσύνη books, arguing that Byzantium was Roman and Orthodox rather than Greek-national. **Influential and genuinely contested.** |
| **Ιωάννης Ζηζιούλας** (1931–2023) | Metropolitan of Pergamon. **Η Ενότης της Εκκλησίας εν τη Θεία Ευχαριστία και τω Επισκόπω** — the Church constituted in the Eucharist around the bishop. His work on personhood and communion is the most internationally cited Greek theology of the century. |
| **Χρήστος Γιανναράς** (1935–2024) | **Η Ελευθερία του Ήθους**, **Το Πρόσωπο και ο Έρως**, **Ορθοδοξία και Δύση στη Νεώτερη Ελλάδα**. A philosopher as much as a theologian, writing on person, eros, and the claim that modern Greece imported a western religiosity alien to its own tradition. **A newspaper columnist too, so his Greek is readable.** |
| **Παναγιώτης Νέλλας** (1936–1986) | **Ζώον Θεούμενον** — *the deified animal*: the human person as called to theosis, read out of the Fathers. Short, dense, and one of the best things on the list. |
| **Νικόλαος Λουδοβίκος** | contemporary — on the Eucharist, on psychoanalysis and theology, and a critic of some of the generation above |
| **Σταύρος Ζουμπουλάκης** | essays on faith and public life; edited *Νέα Εστία* |
| **Γεώργιος Φλωρόφσκι** (1893–1979) | Russian, wrote in Russian and English, and his *Neo-Patristic Synthesis* is the programme the Greeks carried out. Widely translated into Greek. |

**The one to start with is Nellas's *Ζώον Θεούμενον*.** It is short, it is built out of patristic quotation with commentary, and its Greek is clear academic prose of exactly the kind stage 9 taught you to read.

**The vocabulary of Greek theology**, which you need and which is half-ancient:

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **η θέωσις / θέωση** | deification, theosis |
| **η ουσία / η υπόστασις** | essence / hypostasis, person |
| **το πρόσωπο** | the person — **and Yannaras's central term** |
| **η κοινωνία** | communion — and also *society* |
| **οι άκτιστες ενέργειες** | the uncreated energies |
| **το κατ' εικόνα / το καθ' ομοίωσιν** | the image / the likeness |
| **η πτώση** | the fall |
| **το προπατορικό αμάρτημα** | ancestral (not *original*) sin |
| **η νήψη / ο νηπτικός** | sobriety, watchfulness / the hesychast writers |
| **ο νους / η καρδία** | the nous / the heart |
| **η φυσική / υπέρ φύσιν / παρά φύσιν** | according to, above, contrary to nature |
| **η οικονομία** | the divine economy — and also *economy* |
| **η απάθεια, η ταπείνωση, η μετάνοια** | dispassion, humility, repentance |
| **ο Παλαμάς, ο ησυχασμός** | Saint Gregory Palamas, hesychasm |

**Note the forms.** **θέωσις, υπόστασις, καρδία, παρά φύσιν** are ancient and are used unchanged, because the terms are the Fathers' own. **This is the learned register in its proper home**, and it is why the next curriculum exists.

**The honest statement of the limit.** You can read this theology in modern Greek. **What you cannot yet do is read the Fathers it quotes** — and the whole discipline consists of reading the Fathers. Romanides on ancestral sin is an argument about Greek texts of the fourth to fourteenth centuries; Nellas is a commentary on Maximus, Gregory of Nyssa and Palamas; Zizioulas on Ignatius and Cyprian. **Every one of them is a door into the classical curriculum.**

**So this is the lesson where the two curriculums meet**, and the honest summary is: modern Greek takes you to the threshold of Orthodox theology and the older language takes you through it.

**Where to read them free.** A great deal is online: **Pemptousia** and the monastic publishing sites carry articles and extracts; Yannaras's newspaper columns are in the Kathimerini archive; the theological faculties of Athens and Thessaloniki publish some material openly; and the journals **Σύναξη** and **Θεολογία** have online archives.

**Practice.** Learn the fifteen theological terms above. Then read one article on Pemptousia — the register will feel familiar after stage 9's essay lessons. Then read the first chapter of *Ζώον Θεούμενον* if you can get it, and note every Father it quotes.
The essayists, and the lost centre:
Greek criticism and the essay, and one small book that puts the question this whole curriculum raises.

**The essay in Greek**, as a form, is strong — partly because the great poets were also critics and partly because the newspaper column is a serious genre in Greece.

**The essayists:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γιώργος Σεφέρης — Δοκιμές** | two volumes. On Cavafy, on Erotokritos, on the Greek language, on Eliot. **Lucid, and the best prose by a Greek poet.** |
| **Οδυσσέας Ελύτης — Ανοιχτά Χαρτιά** | *Open Papers* — on poetry, light, and his own formation |
| **Ζήσιμος Λορεντζάτος** | **Το Χαμένο Κέντρο**, and the *Μελέτες*. The subject of this lesson. |
| **Τάκης Παπατσώνης** | poet and essayist, Catholic, and a dissenting voice in Greek letters |
| **Κωστής Παπαγιώργης** | *Καλιάρντα*, *Ίμερος και Κλινών* — idiosyncratic, funny, erudite |
| **Στέλιος Ράμφος** | on Orthodoxy, modernity and the Greek self — contested and interesting |
| **Χρήστος Γιανναράς** | the columns, as well as the theology |
| **Νάσος Βαγενάς, Δ. Ν. Μαρωνίτης** | the academic critics, and Maronitis also translated Homer into modern Greek |

**Maronitis's Homer translations deserve the note**: his modern Greek *Iliad* and *Odyssey* are the standard, they are excellent, and **reading Homer in modern Greek translation is a legitimate and useful thing to do before you can read him in Greek.**

**Το Χαμένο Κέντρο, 1961.** Zisimos Lorentzatos's essay, nominally on Seferis, and in fact an argument about the whole of modern Greek literature.

**The argument, briefly.** Modern Greek literature, from Solomos onwards, lost its centre — the religious and spiritual tradition that had held Greek culture together for a millennium and a half — and replaced it with literature itself. The poets became magnificent and had nothing to stand on. **Solomos knew what the centre was and could not reach it; Seferis, Lorentzatos says, is the finest poet of a culture that has forgotten there was one.**

**And his candidate for the writer who kept it is Papadiamantis** — the chanter from Skiathos, writing in the Church's register about the Church's year, dismissed by the literary establishment of his day as a provincial.

**Why this is the right essay to put at the end of this stage.** It is the most serious statement of the question this curriculum has circled from the first lesson: his purpose was **the liturgy, and the Greek people at church**, and the honest answer was that the liturgy is a different language and the modern literature is largely secular. **Lorentzatos's essay is that observation made by a Greek, about Greek literature, from inside.**

**You do not have to agree with him.** It is a contested essay, and the obvious objections — that Elytis built the *Άξιον Εστί* on the Liturgy, that Ritsos wrote in the form of the Lamentations, that Pentzikis and Kontoglou are precisely counter-examples — are all real. **But reading it will organise everything else in this stage.**

**The line of the argument, in his terms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το χαμένο κέντρο** | the lost centre |
| **η παράδοση** | tradition — and the word carries more weight in Greek than in English |
| **η Ρωμιοσύνη** | the Orthodox Greek people, against **ο Ελληνισμός**, which looks to antiquity |
| **ο εκδυτικισμός** | westernisation |
| **η συνέχεια** | continuity — the question of whether modern Greece is continuous with Byzantium, with antiquity, or with neither |

**That last word is the great Greek argument**, and it runs under everything: the language question, the Church's place, Romanides's *Ρωμηοσύνη*, the school curriculum, the name of the country's neighbours, and the way Greeks talk about their own past. **Knowing that the argument exists is most of what a foreigner needs.**

**Where to read them free.** Seferis's *Δοκιμές* and Lorentzatos are in copyright; **both are short and cheap**, and extracts are widely quoted online. The newspaper essays — Yannaras, Ramfos — are in the Kathimerini and Vima archives, free.

**Practice.** Read *Το Χαμένο Κέντρο* — it is a short book and the most useful single thing in this stage for your purposes. Then read Seferis's essay on Cavafy. Then write one paragraph in Greek, using stage 9's argument structure, saying whether you think Lorentzatos is right.
How Greeks talk about their literature:
The last practical lesson: the conversation about literature, so that you can take part in it rather than only read.

**Why this needs a lesson.** Literature occupies a different place in Greek conversation than in British. Poetry is quoted, poets are public figures, the national anthem is a poem, school anthologies are shared memory, and **the argument about the language is a live political subject rather than an academic one.** A foreigner who has read the books but does not know the terms of the conversation will miss most of it.

**The shared references**, which function as common currency:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Lines everybody knows** | *Ιθάκη*; *Τη γλώσσα μου έδωσαν ελληνική*; *Ένα το χελιδόνι*; *Στο περιγιάλι το κρυφό*; the anthem's first stanza |
| **The school anthology** | every Greek adult half-remembers the same poems and stories, from the Ανθολόγιο |
| **The songs** | which carry the poems, so the poetry is known sung |
| **The two Nobels** | Seferis 1963, Elytis 1979 — and both are matters of national pride |
| **Kazantzakis abroad** | and the mixed feelings about being represented by him |

**The arguments you will hear**, with the terms:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Το γλωσσικό ζήτημα** | the language question — demotic against katharevousa, settled in 1976 and still argued about |
| **Η συνέχεια** | continuity: antiquity, Byzantium, modern Greece — one thread or three? |
| **Ελληνισμός against Ρωμιοσύνη** | the classical self-understanding against the Orthodox one |
| **Ο εκδυτικισμός** | westernisation, and whether it was a gain |
| **Η γενιά του '30** | and whether its programme succeeded |
| **Το μονοτονικό** | the 1982 abolition of the polytonic system — **still resented by some**, and a reliable conversational subject |

**Το μονοτονικό is worth knowing as a live grievance.** The three accents and two breathings were abolished for the single accent in 1982. Many older and literary Greeks regard it as a vandalism, some publishers still use the polytonic, and **the Church uses it in liturgical texts.** Saying that you learned the monotonic and find the polytonic beautiful is both true and diplomatic.

**The phrases for talking about books:**

| Greek | English |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι διαβάζεις τώρα;** | what are you reading now? |
| **Έχεις διαβάσει…;** | have you read…? |
| **Μου άρεσε πολύ / Δεν μου άρεσε καθόλου.** | I liked it a lot / not at all |
| **Είναι δυσκολοδιάβαστο.** | it's hard going |
| **Αξίζει;** | is it worth it? |
| **Τι προτείνεις;** | what do you recommend? |
| **Είναι από τα αγαπημένα μου.** | it's one of my favourites |
| **Το έχω αρχίσει και το παράτησα.** | I started it and gave up |
| **Στα ελληνικά το διάβασες;** | did you read it in Greek? — **and this is the question you will be asked** |
| **Με δυσκολία, αλλά το διάβασα.** | with difficulty, but I read it |

**Στα ελληνικά το διάβασες;** is the question, and answering yes is one of the better moments available to a learner of Greek.

**The thing to be careful about.** Literary opinion in Greece is often also political opinion — Ritsos and the left, Kazantzakis and the Church, Romanides and national identity. **Praising a book is sometimes read as taking a side**, and the safe move is the one from stages 10 and 11: ask rather than assert, and be genuinely interested in the answer.

**And the thing in your favour.** A foreigner who has read Papadiamantis is an event. **Mentioning that you are reading him, in Greek, at your parish, will produce a conversation that lasts an hour** — and that conversation is the whole return on this curriculum.

**Practice.** Learn the ten book phrases. Then ask three people at church what their favourite Greek book or poem is, and read one of their answers. Then tell someone what you are reading, in Greek, and see what happens.
Ad astra:
His word from the first question, and the last instruction in the curriculum: what to actually do, for the rest of your life.

**There is no next stage.** This is the point the curriculum was built towards: a language you use, a reading habit that runs on its own, people you talk to, and no course to finish.

**The permanent arrangement, which stage 8 sketched and this lesson settles:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A book on the go, in Greek, always** | and when you finish one, start another that day |
| **Something in your ears** | a podcast, an audiobook, the radio, in the dead time |
| **The daily saint** | four minutes, the floor, every day |
| **The deck** | ten minutes, fed by what you read |
| **Greek at church** | by default, not as an exercise |
| **Something written** | a page a week, in the journal, in Greek |
| **A poem learned** | one a month, four lines at a time |

**That is roughly an hour a day and it does not feel like study.** It is what being able to read a language consists of.

**The four things to keep going deliberately**, because they are the ones that decay:

**1. Speaking.** The ten minutes a week with a person. It will always be the first thing to lapse and the hardest to rebuild. **Protect it.**

**2. Writing.** A page a week. Without it, writing goes stiff within months — and it is the skill that most convinces you, when you reread it, that the years were not wasted.

**3. The accents and spelling.** Reading does not maintain them; writing by hand does. **Copy a paragraph a week.**

**4. Harder material.** Comprehension plateaus at the level of what you read. Every six months, pick up something above you.

**The long projects, each of them years:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The canon** | Papadiamantis, Cavafy, Seferis, Elytis, Ritsos, the folk songs, the *Erotokritos*, Kazantzakis, the Generation of the Thirties. Twenty years of reading, and not a chore. |
| **The theology** | Nellas, Yannaras, Zizioulas, Romanides, and the Elders — and then the Fathers, which needs the next curriculum |
| **The Liturgy** | **and this is the one.** The next curriculum: classical Greek into Koine, Byzantine and liturgical Greek. |
| **Cyprus** | the dialect, deepened by exposure rather than study |
| **The poems learned by heart** | which accumulate quietly and are the most durable thing you will take from this |

**And the classical curriculum, which is where this goes.** His answer to the very first question was **the liturgy, and the Greek people at church**, and this curriculum has honestly given him the second half and the road to the first. The next one is the Liturgy itself: the Koine verb, the ancient cases, the hymnography, the Fathers, the Septuagint, the service books, and katharevousa as the bridge between them and what you now know.

**Nothing gates it.** Begin it whenever stage 8's reading has become comfortable — or before, if you like. The only claim this curriculum makes is that several thousand modern Greek words, the sound system, the case system and the reading stamina make the older language a great deal easier than starting cold.

**The measure, from stage 8's last lesson, restated as the end of the whole route:**

> **Not a level. Whether in five years there is Greek in your ordinary week without your having arranged it — a book by the chair, a voice in the kitchen, a poem you can say, and a conversation after the service that nobody switched out of.**

**And the thing to remember on the bad weeks.** Four minutes of the daily saint is a day with Greek in it. The chain is what matters, and there is no level at which this declares itself finished — which also means there is no level at which falling short of it is failure.

*Ad astra.*

**Practice.** Write out your own version of the permanent arrangement, with your actual week in it. Put the four-minute floor where you will see it. Then open the next book.
