| **Πράξ., Αποκ.** | Πράξεις / Αποκάλυψις | Acts / Revelation |
| **Ψαλμ.** | Ψαλμοί | Psalms |

**Ι.Ν. is the one to recognise first.** Every Greek church notice begins **ΙΕΡΟΣ ΝΑΟΣ** or **Ι.Ν.** followed by the dedication in the genitive: **Ι.Ν. Αγίου Νικολάου**.

**The scripture citation format**, which differs slightly from English:

> **Ματθ. 5, 3–12** or **Ματθ. 5:3–12** — both are used; the comma is more traditional in Greek.

**The organisations you will meet:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ε.Ε.** | European Union |
| **Ο.Η.Ε.** | United Nations |
| **ΕΛ.ΑΣ.** | the Greek police |
| **Ο.Τ.Ε., Δ.Ε.Η.** | the telecoms and electricity companies |
| **ΕΛ.ΣΤΑΤ.** | the statistical service |
| **ΡΙΚ / ΕΡΤ** | the Cypriot and Greek broadcasters |
| **ΑΕΚ, ΠΑΟΚ, ΟΣΦΠ** | the football clubs, which come up more than the rest |

**The spelling convention for acronyms**: full stops between the letters is traditional (**Α.Φ.Μ.**), without them is modern (**ΑΦΜ**), and both are correct. **Acronyms are written in capitals and therefore carry no accents.**

**The one that catches learners**: **κ.** means both **κύριος** and **και** in some older texts, and **κ.ο.κ.** is **και ούτω καθεξής** — *and so on*. Context decides.

**Practice.** Learn the twelve church abbreviations and **π.χ., κ.λπ., δηλ., βλ., π.Χ., μ.Χ., Τ.Κ.** Then find a Greek church notice and read every abbreviation in it. Then find a form and read every official one.
The numerals, in full:
Numbers as words, as digits, and in the alphabetic system — which you will meet on church calendars, in book chapters and on monuments.

**The cardinals, 1 to 20:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** ένας, μία, ένα | **6** έξι | **11** έντεκα | **16** δεκαέξι |
| **2** δύο | **7** εφτά / επτά | **12** δώδεκα | **17** δεκαεφτά |
| **3** τρεις, τρία | **8** οχτώ / οκτώ | **13** δεκατρία | **18** δεκαοχτώ |
| **4** τέσσερις, τέσσερα | **9** εννιά / εννέα | **14** δεκατέσσερα | **19** δεκαεννιά |
| **5** πέντε | **10** δέκα | **15** δεκαπέντε | **20** είκοσι |

**The spelling points**: **τέσσερα** has **σσ**; **εννιά** has **νν**; **εφτά / επτά** and **οχτώ / οκτώ** and **εννιά / εννέα** are each a spoken form and a learned form, both correct.

**The tens and above:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **30, 40, 50** | τριάντα, σαράντα, πενήντα |
| **60, 70, 80, 90** | εξήντα, εβδομήντα, ογδόντα, ενενήντα |
| **100** | εκατό — and **εκατόν** before another number: **εκατόν δύο** |
| **200–900** | διακόσια, τριακόσια, τετρακόσια, πεντακόσια, εξακόσια, εφτακόσια, οχτακόσια, εννιακόσια |
| **1,000** | χίλια — and **χιλιάδες** for *thousands* |
| **1,000,000** | ένα εκατομμύριο |
| **1,000,000,000** | ένα δισεκατομμύριο |

**εκατομμύριο has μμ**, as the double-consonant lesson's list showed.

**The four numerals that decline**, and they are the only ones:

| | M. | F. | N. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **ένας** | **μία / μια** | **ένα** |
| **3** | **τρεις** | **τρεις** | **τρία** |
| **4** | **τέσσερις** | **τέσσερις** | **τέσσερα** |
| **hundreds and thousands** | **διακόσιοι** | **διακόσιες** | **διακόσια** |

> **ένας άντρας, μία γυναίκα, ένα παιδί**
> **τρεις άντρες, τρεις γυναίκες, τρία παιδιά**
> **τέσσερις ώρες, τέσσερα βιβλία**
> **διακόσιοι άντρες, διακόσιες γυναίκες, διακόσια παιδιά**

**And ένας declines for case too**: **ένας / ενός / έναν**, like the article.

**The ordinals:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1st–5th** | πρώτος, δεύτερος, τρίτος, τέταρτος, πέμπτος |
| **6th–10th** | έκτος, έβδομος, όγδοος, ένατος, δέκατος |
| **11th, 12th** | ενδέκατος, δωδέκατος |
| **20th, 30th, 100th** | εικοστός, τριακοστός, εκατοστός |
| **last** | τελευταίος |

**All ordinals are adjectives in -ος / -η / -ο** and decline normally. **In dates they appear abbreviated with a superscript ending**: **1η Μαΐου, 3ος όροφος, 21ος αιώνας**.

**The alphabetic numerals**, which is the system you will meet in church:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **α΄** 1 | **ι΄** 10 | **ρ΄** 100 | **͵α** 1,000 |
| **β΄** 2 | **κ΄** 20 | **σ΄** 200 | |
| **γ΄** 3 | **λ΄** 30 | **τ΄** 300 | |
| **δ΄** 4 | **μ΄** 40 | **υ΄** 400 | |
| **ε΄** 5 | **ν΄** 50 | **φ΄** 500 | |
| **ϛ΄** 6 | **ξ΄** 60 | **χ΄** 600 | |
| **ζ΄** 7 | **ο΄** 70 | **ψ΄** 700 | |
| **η΄** 8 | **π΄** 80 | **ω΄** 800 | |
| **θ΄** 9 | **ϙ΄** 90 | **ϡ΄** 900 | |

**How it works**: units, tens and hundreds each have a letter, and they are added — **ιβ΄** is 10 + 2 = **12**; **κε΄** is 20 + 5 = **25**; **ρν΄** is 150. **A keraia (΄) after the letters marks a numeral**, and a mark before marks thousands.

**And three archaic letters survive only as numerals**: **ϛ** (stigma, 6, also written **στ΄**), **ϙ** (koppa, 90), **ϡ** (sampi, 900). **They are not letters of the alphabet** and exist for counting.

**Where you will meet it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Ode numbers in a canon** | ωδή α΄, γ΄, δ΄… |
| **Tones and modes** | ήχος πλ. δ΄ — plagal fourth |
| **Chapter and book numbers** | Βιβλίο Β΄, Κεφ. ιβ΄ |
| **Church councils** | η Ζ΄ Οικουμενική Σύνοδος — the Seventh |
| **Inscriptions and foundation dates** | and gravestones |
| **School and university years** | Γ΄ Λυκείου, Α΄ Γυμνασίου |
| **Kings and patriarchs** | Κωνσταντίνος ΙΑ΄, Βαρθολομαίος Α΄ |

**The Οικουμενικές Σύνοδοι in alphabetic numerals is the set to know**: **Α΄ to Ζ΄**, Nicaea to Nicaea II.

**Dates, and how Greek writes them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **14 Οκτωβρίου 2026** | the month in the genitive |
| **14/10/2026** | day first, as in Britain |
| **1η Ιανουαρίου** | the ordinal for the first |
| **το 2026** | *in 2026* — with the article |
| **τη δεκαετία του '90** | in the nineties |
| **τον 5ο αιώνα π.Χ.** | in the fifth century BC |

**Practice.** Write the numbers 1 to 20 in words, checking **τέσσερα** and **εννιά**. Then decline **ένας, τρεις, τέσσερις** with nouns in all three genders. Then read the alphabetic numerals **ιβ΄, κε΄, ρν΄, Ζ΄** and find one on a church calendar or in a service book.
Capitalisation, hyphens and syllables:
The remaining mechanical conventions, as a reference — and the syllable rule, which decides where a word can break.

**Capitalisation.** Greek capitalises **less** than English, and the differences are specific:

| | Greek | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Days of the week** | **Δευτέρα, Τρίτη** — capitalised | capitalised |
| **Months** | **Ιανουάριος, Μάιος** — capitalised | capitalised |
| **Nationalities, noun** | **ο Έλληνας, ο Άγγλος** — capitalised | capitalised |
| **Nationalities, adjective** | **ελληνικός, αγγλικός** — **lower case** | capitalised |
| **Languages** | **τα ελληνικά, τα αγγλικά** — **lower case** | capitalised |
| **Religions and their adherents** | **ο χριστιανός, ο ορθόδοξος** — usually lower case | capitalised |
| **Titles before a name** | **ο κύριος Παπαδόπουλος** — lower case for κύριος | capitalised |
| **Book and film titles** | **only the first word** — *Το τρίτο στεφάνι* | most words |
| **After a colon** | lower case | lower case |
| **The first person pronoun** | **εγώ** — lower case | *I* capitalised |

**τα ελληνικά in lower case is the one learners get wrong most**, because English capitalises language names. **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά** — lower case, always.

**The religious capitals**, which matter for your writing:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Capitalised** | **ο Θεός, ο Κύριος, ο Χριστός, η Παναγία, το Άγιο Πνεύμα, η Αγία Τριάδα, η Εκκλησία** (the Church as institution), **η Θεία Λειτουργία, η Αγία Γραφή** |
| **Lower case** | **η εκκλησία** (the building), **ο ιερέας, ο επίσκοπος, η λειτουργία** (a service in general), **η νηστεία** |
| **Pronouns for God** | **capitalised in church usage** — **Αυτός, Σε, Του** — though not universally |
| **Feast names** | **capitalised** — **τα Χριστούγεννα, το Πάσχα, η Ανάσταση, η Κοίμηση, τα Θεοφάνεια** |
| **Saints** | **ο Άγιος Νικόλαος** — both words capitalised |

**And the all-capitals rule, from Spelling 1**: a word in capitals takes **no accents** — **ΚΑΛΗΜΕΡΑ, ΙΕΡΟΣ ΝΑΟΣ** — while a capital at the start of a lower-case word **keeps** its accent: **Άννα, Όλγα, Έλληνας, Ήπειρος**.

**Syllable division**, which decides hyphenation at a line break:

**The rules, in five lines:**

1. **A single consonant between vowels goes with the following vowel**: **πα-τέ-ρας, κα-λός, α-γά-πη**.
2. **Two consonants between vowels go with the following vowel if a Greek word can begin with that pair**: **βι-βλί-ο** (βλ- is possible), **έ-τσι**, **κά-θε**. Otherwise they split: **άν-θρω-πος** (νθ- cannot begin a word), **θάλασ-σα**, **άλ-λος**.
3. **Three consonants go with the following vowel if the first two can begin a word**: **αι-σθη-τός**, otherwise the first stays: **άν-θρω-πος**.
4. **Digraphs and diphthongs never split**: **αι, ει, οι, ου, αυ, ευ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ** stay whole. **παί-ζω**, not **πα-ί-ζω**.
5. **A compound divides at the join when the parts are still felt**: **προσ-ευχή**, **εισ-αγωγή** — though dividing by the ordinary rules is also accepted.

**The two-consonant rule is the useful one**, and the test is simple: **can a Greek word start with this pair?** **βλ, γρ, κτ, πλ, στ, σπ, χθ, φρ, τρ** — yes. **νθ, ρμ, λτ, σμ (sometimes), λλ, σσ** — no.

**Diaeresis**, from Spelling 1, restated as reference: the two dots mark that two vowels are **not** a digraph:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μάιος** | *Má-i-os* — without the diaeresis **αι** would say *e* |
| **παϊδάκια** | *pa-i-dákia* |
| **καΐκι** | *ka-í-ki* |
| **ρολόι** | and here no diaeresis is needed, because the accent on **ό** already separates them |

**The rule**: the diaeresis is needed only when there is no accent to do the separating.

**The apostrophe**, from stage 9's punctuation lesson, as reference: it marks elision — **σ' το λέω, απ' τη δουλειά, παρ' όλα αυτά, μ' αρέσει** — and **κι** takes none, because it is a form rather than a contraction.

**The hyphen in compounds**, which Greek uses sparingly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Joined** | most compounds — **αυτοκίνητο, ποδόσφαιρο, Ελληνοαμερικανός** |
| **Hyphenated** | coordinate pairs and ad-hoc formations — **ελληνο-τουρκικές σχέσεις, κοινωνικο-οικονομικός** |
| **Repetitions** | **σιγά σιγά, λίγο λίγο** — **no hyphen**, just repeated |

**Practice.** Write ten sentences containing a language name, a nationality adjective, a feast and a saint's name, and check every capital. Then divide ten long words into syllables, applying the two-consonant test aloud. Then write five elisions with their apostrophes.
Typing and writing Greek, as reference:
The mechanical reference for both input methods, collected in one place — the keyboard and the hand.

**The Greek keyboard layout**, which stage 1 set up and which this lesson records in full.

**The letters, where they sit on a QWERTY board:**

| Key | Greek | Key | Greek |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **a** | α | **n** | ν |
| **b** | β | **o** | ο |
| **c** | ψ | **p** | π |
| **d** | δ | **q** | **;** (the question mark) |
| **e** | ε | **r** | ρ |
| **f** | φ | **s** | σ |
| **g** | γ | **t** | τ |
| **h** | η | **u** | θ |
| **i** | ι | **v** | ω |
| **j** | ξ | **w** | **ς** (final sigma) |
| **k** | κ | **x** | χ |
| **l** | λ | **y** | υ |
| **m** | μ | **z** | ζ |

**The five to memorise**, because they are not phonetic: **c = ψ**, **j = ξ**, **u = θ**, **v = ω**, **w = ς**, **q = ;**.

**The accent and the diaeresis:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The accent** | press **;** (the semicolon key) then the vowel — **;** then **a** gives **ά** |
| **The diaeresis** | **shift + ;** then the vowel — gives **ϊ, ϋ** |
| **Both together** | **shift + ;** then the vowel after an accent key gives **ΐ, ΰ** |
| **The question mark** | **q** |
| **The άνω τελεία (·)** | **alt gr + w** |
| **The guillemets « »** | **alt gr + [** and **alt gr + ]** |

**On Omarchy and Hyprland**, from stage 1: the layout goes in the Hyprland input block as `kb_layout = us,gr` with `kb_options = grp:alt_shift_toggle`, and **alt + shift** switches. **Keep it one key away**, as the environment lesson said.

**On a phone**: add Greek as a second keyboard in the system settings; the accent is a long press on the vowel.

**The polytonic layout**, which exists and which you need only if you type liturgical texts: most systems offer **Greek (polytonic)** as a separate layout, with the breathings and the three accents on dead keys. **The classical curriculum will need it. This one does not.**

**Handwriting, as reference**, from Spelling 1 and stage 9:

**The letters that descend below the line**: **γ, η, μ, ρ, φ, χ, ψ, ζ, β, ξ**. The next letter starts from the baseline, not from the tail.

**The joins to drill**: **αθα, αδα, αλα, αξα, αζα, ανα, αυα** — the awkward letters between vowels.

**The confusions to keep apart in a fast hand:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ν against υ** | ν pointed, υ round-bottomed |
| **θ against ο** | keep θ's bar short and inside |
| **ζ against ξ** | ξ has two bellies, ζ one and a tail |
| **γ against ψ** | both descend; ψ's fork is above the line |
| **μ against υ** | a hurried μ loses its first leg |
| **ς against σ** | **ς only at the end of a word** — a ς inside a word is a visible error |

**The accent, written as one movement at the end of the word**, not as you pass the vowel.

**The capitals**, which are the printed forms and are written as printed: **Α Β Γ Δ Ε Ζ Η Θ Ι Κ Λ Μ Ν Ξ Ο Π Ρ Σ Τ Υ Φ Χ Ψ Ω**. **No lower-case cursive capitals**, as Latin script has.

**The two sigmas, as reference**: **σ** everywhere, **ς** at the end of a word only, **Σ** as the capital — and a capital sigma at the end of a word is still **Σ**: **ΑΝΘΡΩΠΟΣ**.

**Your signature**: decide how you write your name in Greek letters and write it the same way every time, as stage 9's handwriting lesson said.

**The practical note on fonts and reading**, which belongs here: some Greek printed fonts use a single-storey **α** and others a different **θ** or **φ**; older books use ligatures; and handwritten Greek from an older generation can be genuinely hard. **Reading a Greek grandparent's handwriting is a skill of its own**, and the answer is exposure.

**Practice.** Type one paragraph in Greek with every accent placed, using the **;** key. Then write the same paragraph by hand, placing each accent at the end of its word. Then drill the six awkward joins, a line each.
The spelling checklist, and self-testing:
The last lesson of the track: the whole of Greek spelling reduced to a page you can actually use, and the way to test yourself without a teacher.

**The checklist, in the order that catches most for least effort** — the same twelve steps as stage 9's editing lesson, with the spelling items expanded:

**1. Read it aloud.** First, always. Half the errors are audible.

**2. Count the accents.** One on every word of two syllables or more. Exactly one.

**3. Every *i*: is it an ending?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Third person of a verb** | **-ει** |
| **Feminine singular** | **-η** |
| **Masculine plural** | **-οι** |
| **Neuter singular** | **-ι** |
| **Feminine -ση plural** | **-εις** |
| **Neuter -ος plural** | **-η** |
| **Not an ending** | it is a root — check it, or card it |

**4. Every *o*: verb or noun?** First person of a verb is **-ω**; neuter singular is **-ο**; genitive plural is **-ων**.

**5. Every *e*: active or passive?** **-ετε** is *you* plural active; **-εται** is *it* passive.

**6. Final -ν on τον, την, δεν, μην, έναν** — before a vowel or a stop, keep it.

**7. The agreement chain.** Article, adjective and noun in the same gender, number and case.

**8. The genitive endings.** **-ου, -η, -α** masculine; **-ης, -ας** feminine; **-ου, -ιού, -ατος** neuter; **-ων** plural throughout.

**9. The perfective marker.** Labial → **ψ**; velar → **ξ**; otherwise **σ**; conjugation 2 → **-ήσω** or **-έσω**.

**10. The double consonants**, against your card list.

**11. Punctuation.** **;** for a question, **« »** for quotes, a comma round every vocative.

**12. Read it aloud again.**

**The self-tests, which are the track's real method:**

| Test | What it catches | How often |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dictation, four sentences** | **everything at once** | weekly |
| **Copying a paragraph by hand** | the accents and the joins, without the pressure | weekly |
| **The drill sets** from Spelling 2 and 3 | the endings | twice weekly |
| **Rewriting a paragraph from memory** | the roots | monthly |
| **A paragraph you wrote six months ago** | your progress | quarterly |

**The error log, kept in four columns** — date, error, type, fixed — and read monthly. **The distribution tells you what to study**, and after a year of this track it should look like:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Endings** | near zero. They are grammar, and you know the grammar. |
| **Accents** | occasional, and mostly on unfamiliar words |
| **Roots** | the bulk of what remains, and all of it on cards |
| **Double consonants** | a known list, carded |
| **Final -ν** | near zero |

**That distribution is the target of the whole track** — not perfect spelling, which no Greek has, but **errors confined to the part that is genuinely memory, with that part on cards.**

**The three tools, from stage 8's dictionary lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Triantafyllidis** (greek-language.gr) | the authority, with etymologies — and **the etymology is the mnemonic** |
| **Lexiscope** | any inflected form, with its full table |
| **A corpus search in quotes** | whether Greeks actually write a phrase |

**What this track does not and cannot do.** It cannot make the roots derivable, because they are not. **ποτέ, τύχη, θάλασσα, εκκλησία** are facts, and the only honest method is to meet them, get them wrong, card them, and meet them again. **That is what the deck is for.**

**And the one thing to remember on a bad week.** Greek spelling is hard for Greeks. **Ορθογραφικά λάθη** are a national joke about other people's writing, school children are drilled in exactly these lessons for twelve years, and getting the endings right already puts you ahead of a good deal of what is written online. **The standard is careful writing, not perfection.**

**Where the track leaves you.** Five modules: the sounds, the noun and adjective endings, the verb endings, the roots and prefixes, and the mechanics. **With the checklist above and a deck of root cards, you can write Greek that looks written by someone who was taught** — which was the point.

**Practice.** Run the twelve-item checklist on the longest thing you have written in Greek. Log every error by type. Then look at the distribution and decide which of the five modules to reread. Then do a four-sentence dictation, and put the error log where you will keep using it.
How the Greek verb is organised:
The map of the verb system, before any tables — because the Greek verb is organised on a different axis from the English one, and without the map the tables are unusable.

**The English verb is organised by tense.** Present, past, future, with aspect added by auxiliaries: *I write, I am writing, I wrote, I was writing, I have written*.

**The Greek verb is organised by aspect first and tense second.** Every verb has **two stems**, and the stem is chosen before the tense is:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The imperfective stem** | the action as ongoing, repeated, habitual, attempted — **γράφ-** |
| **The perfective stem** | the action as a single complete whole — **γράψ-** |

**And then the tense and mood are built on whichever stem you chose:**

| | Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Present** | **γράφω** | **—** (there is no perfective present) |
| **Past** | **έγραφα** (imperfect) | **έγραψα** (aorist) |
| **Future** | **θα γράφω** | **θα γράψω** |
| **Subjunctive** | **να γράφω** | **να γράψω** |
| **Imperative** | **γράφε** | **γράψε** |

**That table is the Greek verb.** Everything else is a detail, and the empty cell — **no perfective present** — is logical: you cannot describe something as a completed whole while it is happening.

**The second axis: voice.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Active** | **γράφω** — I write |
| **Passive / mediopassive** | **γράφομαι** — I am written; and for many verbs, a middle sense |

**And the passive has its own two stems too** — **γράφομαι / γραφτώ** — so the full system is **two aspects × two voices × the tenses and moods.**

**The third axis: the compound tenses with έχω.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Perfect** | **έχω γράψει** — I have written |
| **Pluperfect** | **είχα γράψει** — I had written |
| **Future perfect** | **θα έχω γράψει** — I will have written |

**These use έχω plus an invariable form** of the perfective, which never changes for person — **έχω γράψει, έχεις γράψει, έχει γράψει** — so they are the easiest part of the system.

**What there is not**, which matters as much as what there is:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No infinitive** | **θέλω να πάω**, not *θέλω πάω*. The **να** clause does the infinitive's work. |
| **No perfective present** | as above |
| **No separate subjunctive forms** | **να** plus the indicative endings |
| **No progressive auxiliary** | the imperfective aspect does it |
| **No sequence of tenses** | reported speech keeps the original tense |

**The two conjugations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Conjugation 1** | stress on the stem — **γράφω, διαβάζω, παίρνω** |
| **Conjugation 2** | stress on the ending — **αγαπώ / αγαπάω**, and **μπορώ** |

**And conjugation 2 splits into two types**, 2a (**-άω**) and 2b (**-ώ**), which take different endings — the Spelling track's second module laid them out.

**How to use the rest of this module.** Each lesson is a complete table for one part of the system, meant as reference rather than as reading. **The way to use a table is not to read it but to produce from it**: cover the forms, say them, check.

**And the one thing to carry from this lesson into every table that follows:** when you meet a Greek verb form, ask the two questions in order. **Which stem? Which tense and mood?** That is how the system is indexed, and it is how a dictionary and Lexiscope will answer you.

**Practice.** Take five verbs you know and fill in the five-by-two table above for each, from memory. Then find ten verb forms in today's reading and name, for each, the stem and the tense. Then check three in Lexiscope.
The two conjugations, in full:
The complete present active of all three types, as the reference table — and the test of which conjugation a verb belongs to.

**Conjugation 1 — stress on the stem:**

| Person | **γράφω** | **διαβάζω** | **παίρνω** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | γράφ**ω** | διαβάζ**ω** | παίρν**ω** |
| **εσύ** | γράφ**εις** | διαβάζ**εις** | παίρν**εις** |
| **αυτός** | γράφ**ει** | διαβάζ**ει** | παίρν**ει** |
| **εμείς** | γράφ**ουμε** | διαβάζ**ουμε** | παίρν**ουμε** |
| **εσείς** | γράφ**ετε** | διαβάζ**ετε** | παίρν**ετε** |
| **αυτοί** | γράφ**ουν** | διαβάζ**ουν** | παίρν**ουν** |

**The endings: -ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν.** Six forms, no variation, and this is the largest class in the language.

**Conjugation 2a — stress on the ending, -άω type:**

| Person | **αγαπώ** | Alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | αγαπ**ώ** | αγαπ**άω** |
| **εσύ** | αγαπ**άς** | |
| **αυτός** | αγαπ**ά** | αγαπ**άει** |
| **εμείς** | αγαπ**άμε** | αγαπ**ούμε** |
| **εσείς** | αγαπ**άτε** | |
| **αυτοί** | αγαπ**ούν** | αγαπ**άνε** |

**Both columns are correct.** The **-άω / -άει / -άνε** forms are commoner in speech, the **-ώ / -ά / -ούν** forms in writing.

**Conjugation 2b — stress on the ending, -ώ type:**

| Person | **μπορώ** | **θεωρώ** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | μπορ**ώ** | θεωρ**ώ** |
| **εσύ** | μπορ**είς** | θεωρ**είς** |
| **αυτός** | μπορ**εί** | θεωρ**εί** |
| **εμείς** | μπορ**ούμε** | θεωρ**ούμε** |
| **εσείς** | μπορ**είτε** | θεωρ**είτε** |
| **αυτοί** | μπορ**ούν** | θεωρ**ούν** |

**The endings: -ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν.**

**The test for which conjugation**, in two questions:

1. **Where is the stress in the first person?** On the stem → conjugation 1. On the ending → conjugation 2.
2. **What is the second person?** **-άς** → 2a. **-είς** → 2b.

**And you cannot derive which** — it is a fact about the verb, listed in the dictionary. **Lexiscope will tell you in one lookup.**

**The members, as a reference list:**

| 2a (**-άς**) | 2b (**-είς**) |
| --- | --- |
| αγαπώ, μιλώ, ρωτώ, περνώ, γελώ | μπορώ, θεωρώ, τηλεφωνώ, συμφωνώ |
| πεινώ, διψώ, ξεχνώ, χαλώ | αργώ, προχωρώ, οδηγώ, ευχαριστώ |
| σταματώ, κρατώ, πετώ, φυλώ | καλώ, μισώ, νικώ, τιμώ, ζω |
| βαστώ, γερνώ, κερνώ, ακουμπώ | αποτελώ, εκτελώ, μεταφέρω (conj. 1) |

**Several verbs take both sets**, notably **ζητώ, κρατώ, βοηθώ, τραβώ** — and both are correct.

**The irregulars, which are their own paradigms:**

| | είμαι | έχω | πάω | λέω | τρώω |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **είμαι** | έχω | πάω | λέω | τρώω |
| **εσύ** | **είσαι** | έχεις | πας | λες | τρως |
| **αυτός** | **είναι** | έχει | πάει | λέει | τρώει |
| **εμείς** | **είμαστε** | έχουμε | πάμε | λέμε | τρώμε |
| **εσείς** | **είστε / είσαστε** | έχετε | πάτε | λέτε | τρώτε |
| **αυτοί** | **είναι** | έχουν | πάνε | λένε | τρώνε |

**είμαι is the only verb in the language with passive-shaped endings and no active**, which is why it looks like a deponent and is not.

**How to use this table.** Cover the right-hand columns, say the six persons of each verb aloud, and uncover to check. **Thirty seconds a verb, three verbs a day**, and the whole present is automatic in a month.

**Practice.** Produce all six persons of **γράφω, αγαπώ, μπορώ, είμαι, έχω, λέω** from memory, aloud. Then take ten verbs from today's reading and assign each to conjugation 1, 2a or 2b, checking three in Lexiscope.
The imperfect, in full:
The past imperfective — the background tense of every narrative — in all three conjugations, with the augment rule.

**Conjugation 1:**

| Person | **γράφω** | **διαβάζω** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **έγραφα** | **διάβαζα** |
| **εσύ** | **έγραφες** | **διάβαζες** |
| **αυτός** | **έγραφε** | **διάβαζε** |
| **εμείς** | **γράφαμε** | **διαβάζαμε** |
| **εσείς** | **γράφατε** | **διαβάζατε** |
| **αυτοί** | **έγραφαν / γράφανε** | **διάβαζαν** |

**The endings: -α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν.**

**The augment**, from the Spelling track: the stress must fall on the third syllable from the end. **γράφ-** has one syllable, so **έ-** is prefixed to make three — **έ-γρα-φα**. In **γράφαμε** there are already three, so no augment. **διαβάζω** has enough syllables throughout, so the stress simply moves.

**So the augment appears in persons 1, 2, 3 and 6, and vanishes in 4 and 5** — for short stems only.

**Conjugation 2a and 2b — both take -ούσα:**

| Person | **αγαπώ** | **μπορώ** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **αγαπούσα** | **μπορούσα** |
| **εσύ** | **αγαπούσες** | **μπορούσες** |
| **αυτός** | **αγαπούσε** | **μπορούσε** |
| **εμείς** | **αγαπούσαμε** | **μπορούσαμε** |
| **εσείς** | **αγαπούσατε** | **μπορούσατε** |
| **αυτοί** | **αγαπούσαν** | **μπορούσαν** |

**Both conjugation-2 types converge in the imperfect**, which removes a decision — and **-ούσα** is long enough that no augment is ever needed.

**Some 2a verbs also take -αγα**: **αγαπάγα, μιλάγα, ρωτάγα** — spoken, regional, and correct.

**The irregular imperfects**, which must be learned:

| Verb | Imperfect |
| --- | --- |
| **είμαι** | **ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν, ήμαστε, ήσαστε, ήταν** |
| **έχω** | **είχα, είχες, είχε, είχαμε, είχατε, είχαν** |
| **θέλω** | **ήθελα** |
| **ξέρω** | **ήξερα** |
| **πάω** | **πήγαινα** |
| **λέω** | **έλεγα** |
| **τρώω** | **έτρωγα** |
| **πίνω** | **έπινα** |
| **έρχομαι** | **ερχόμουν** |
| **βλέπω** | **έβλεπα** |
| **πηγαίνω** | **πήγαινα** |

**ήμουν and είχα are the two to know cold**, because every narrative uses them and every compound tense uses **είχα**.

**What the imperfect is for**, from stage 4 and stage 9's narrating lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Background** | **Ήταν Κυριακή και έβρεχε.** |
| **Habit** | **Πήγαινα κάθε Κυριακή.** — *I used to go* |
| **Ongoing, interrupted** | **Διάβαζα όταν χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο.** |
| **Description in the past** | **Ήταν ψηλός και φορούσε παλτό.** |
| **An attempt** | **Του έλεγα, αλλά δεν άκουγε.** — *I kept telling him* |
| **Politeness** | **Ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω κάτι.** — *I wanted to ask* |

**The last one is worth noting**: the imperfect of **θέλω** and **μπορώ** is a politeness device, exactly as English uses *I was wondering*.

**The contrast with the aorist, in one pair:**

> **Έγραφα ένα γράμμα.** — I was writing a letter. (It may not be finished.)
> **Έγραψα ένα γράμμα.** — I wrote a letter. (Done.)

**And the imperfective future and subjunctive**, which use the same stem with **θα** and **να**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα γράφω** | I will be writing, I will write habitually |
| **να γράφω** | that I write, keep writing |
| **θα αγαπώ** | I will love — and here the imperfective is the natural choice, because loving is not an event |

**Practice.** Produce the full imperfect of **γράφω, διαβάζω, αγαπώ, μπορώ, είμαι, έχω** from memory. Mark where the augment appears. Then write six sentences, one for each use in the table above.
The imperfective future, subjunctive and:
The remaining imperfective forms, which need no new endings at all — because Greek builds them from particles plus what you already know.

**The imperfective future: θα + present.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα γράφω** | I will be writing / will write habitually |
| **θα γράφεις, θα γράφει, θα γράφουμε, θα γράφετε, θα γράφουν** | |
| **θα αγαπώ, θα μπορώ** | conjugation 2, unchanged |
| **θα είμαι, θα έχω** | the irregulars, unchanged |

**θα is invariable and unaccented.** That is the whole of the imperfective future.

**When to use it rather than the perfective future**, from stage 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα γράφω** | repeatedly, habitually, continuously — **Θα σου γράφω κάθε μέρα.** |
| **θα γράψω** | once, completed — **Θα σου γράψω αύριο.** |
| **θα είμαι, θα έχω, θα μπορώ, θα ξέρω** | **these verbs have no perfective future**, being states |

**The state verbs are worth the note**: **είμαι, έχω, ξέρω, θέλω, αγαπώ** describe conditions rather than events, so their future is naturally imperfective and several of them have no perfective stem at all.

**The imperfective subjunctive: να + present.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **να γράφω** | that I write, that I keep writing |
| **θέλω να γράφω** | I want to be writing |
| **πρέπει να γράφω** | I must write, habitually |
| **μπορώ να γράφω** | I can write |
| **ας γράφω** | let me keep writing |
| **να μην γράφω** | the negative — **μην**, not **δεν** |

**The endings are identical to the present**, and there is no separate subjunctive form in modern Greek. **The Spelling track's lesson on this is the one that matters: να γράφει, never να γράφη.**

**The three particles:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **να** | after verbs of wanting, needing, being able; purpose; and as the infinitive's replacement |
| **θα** | future and conditional |
| **ας** | let — **ας πάμε**, *let's go* |

**And the one that is both**: **θα** plus the imperfect makes the conditional — **θα έγραφα**, *I would write* — which stage 6 taught as the politeness tense.

**The imperfective imperative**, which has its own two forms:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2 sg.** | **γράφε** — keep writing |
| **2 pl.** | **γράφετε** — identical to the present second plural |

**Conjugation 2:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2 sg.** | **αγάπα, μίλα, ρώτα** — 2a; **—** for most 2b verbs |
| **2 pl.** | **αγαπάτε, μιλάτε** |

**The imperfective imperative is uncommon** — you use it for *keep doing* or for a general instruction — and **the perfective imperative is the ordinary one**, which the next module covers.

**The negative imperative, which has no form of its own:**

> **Μην γράφεις.** — Don't write / stop writing.
> **Μην μιλάς.** — Don't talk.

**μην plus the ordinary present.** There is no negative imperative in Greek, so this is the only way to say it.

**The full imperfective system for one verb, as a single reference:**

| | **γράφω** |
| --- | --- |
| **Present** | γράφω, γράφεις, γράφει, γράφουμε, γράφετε, γράφουν |
| **Imperfect** | έγραφα, έγραφες, έγραφε, γράφαμε, γράφατε, έγραφαν |
| **Future** | θα γράφω … |
| **Subjunctive** | να γράφω … |
| **Conditional** | θα έγραφα … |
| **Imperative** | γράφε, γράφετε |
| **Negative imperative** | μην γράφεις, μην γράφετε |

**That is one stem, six constructions, and only two sets of endings** — the present's and the past's. **The imperfective half of the verb is genuinely small**, and the perfective half uses the same endings on a different stem, which is the next module.

**Practice.** Write the full reference table above for **διαβάζω**, **μιλώ** and **μπορώ**. Then write six sentences distinguishing **θα γράφω** from **θα γράψω**, and three using **μην** with the present.
είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs:
The handful of verbs that behave differently, in full — because they are the commonest verbs in the language and none of them is derivable.

**είμαι, in every form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Present** | **είμαι, είσαι, είναι, είμαστε, είστε (είσαστε), είναι** |
| **Imperfect** | **ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν, ήμαστε (ήμασταν), ήσαστε (ήσασταν), ήταν** |
| **Future** | **θα είμαι** … |
| **Subjunctive** | **να είμαι** … |
| **Conditional** | **θα ήμουν** … |
| **Imperative** | **να είσαι, να είστε** — *be* |
| **Participle** | **όντας** — *being*, learned and rare |

**είμαι has no aorist, no perfective and no passive.** It is a state, and states have no perfective aspect. **Where English says *I was*, Greek says ήμουν** — the imperfect — and there is nothing else to choose.

**And its endings look passive** — **-μαι, -σαι, -ται… -μαστε, -στε** — which is a historical accident. **είναι is the third person for both singular and plural**, which is unique in the language.

**έχω, in every form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Present** | **έχω, έχεις, έχει, έχουμε, έχετε, έχουν** |
| **Imperfect** | **είχα, είχες, είχε, είχαμε, είχατε, είχαν** |
| **Future** | **θα έχω** … |
| **Subjunctive** | **να έχω** … |
| **Conditional** | **θα είχα** … |
| **Imperative** | **να έχεις** |

**έχω also has no aorist in ordinary use.** And **είχα** is doing double duty: it is **έχω**'s own imperfect **and** the auxiliary of the pluperfect — **είχα γράψει**, *I had written*.

**The state verbs, and what they lack:**

| Verb | Perfective | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **είμαι** | **none** | |
| **έχω** | **none** in ordinary use | |
| **ξέρω** | **none** | aorist **ήξερα** is imperfective in sense |
| **θέλω** | **none** | aorist **ήθελα** likewise |
| **μπορώ** | **μπορέσω** | and it means *manage to* |
| **πρέπει** | **none** | impersonal, third person only |
| **αξίζει** | **none** | impersonal |
| **υπάρχω** | **υπάρξω** | rare |
| **ανήκω** | **none** | |
| **κάνει** (weather) | — | **κάνει ζέστη**, impersonal |

**The pattern: a verb that describes a condition rather than an event has no perfective**, because there is nothing to complete. **That is a grammatical fact with a logical reason**, which makes it easy to remember.

**And μπορώ's perfective is instructive**: **μπορώ** is *I am able*; **μπόρεσα** is *I managed*, which is an event. **The aspect difference is the difference between a capacity and an occasion.**

**The impersonal verbs**, which exist only in the third person singular:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πρέπει** | it is necessary — **πρέπει να πάω** |
| **μπορεί** | it may be — **μπορεί να βρέχει** |
| **αξίζει** | it is worth |
| **χρειάζεται** | it is needed |
| **φαίνεται** | it seems |
| **συμβαίνει** | it happens |
| **απαγορεύεται, επιτρέπεται** | it is forbidden, permitted |
| **κάνει ζέστη / κρύο** | it is hot / cold |
| **βρέχει, χιονίζει** | it is raining, snowing |

**Their past is the ordinary third singular**: **έπρεπε, μπορούσε, άξιζε, χρειαζόταν, φαινόταν, έβρεχε.**

**έπρεπε is worth its own line**, because it carries an English modal distinction Greek handles by aspect:

> **Έπρεπε να πάω.** — I had to go / I should have gone. **Both**, and context decides.
> **Πρέπει να πήγε.** — He must have gone. **πρέπει** plus a past, for inference.

**The verbs with two different meanings by aspect**, which is the subtlest thing in the Greek verb:

| Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- |
| **ξέρω** — I know | — |
| **μαθαίνω** — I learn, I am learning | **μάθω** — I find out |
| **βλέπω** — I see, I watch | **δω** — I catch sight of |
| **μπορώ** — I can | **μπορέσω** — I manage |
| **θυμάμαι** — I remember (state) | **θυμηθώ** — I recall, it comes back to me |
| **καταλαβαίνω** — I understand | **καταλάβω** — I realise |
| **έχω** — I have | **—** |

**That table is worth more than it looks.** **Να το θυμηθώ** is *let me recall it*; **να το θυμάμαι** is *let me keep it in mind*. The aspect is carrying a distinction English makes with different verbs entirely.

**Practice.** Produce **είμαι** and **έχω** in all six constructions from memory. Then write ten sentences using the impersonal verbs. Then write a pair of sentences for each row of the last table, showing the two senses.
How to use a conjugation table:
The method lesson for this module, because a table read is worth nothing and a table produced from is worth a great deal.

**The three uses of a conjugation table, which are different skills:**

**1. Recognition — reading a form you have met.** You have **ανακοινώθηκε** in front of you and you want to know what it is.

**The procedure, four questions in order:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Is it active or passive?** | **-θηκε** is a passive ending → passive |
| **2. Which tense?** | **-θηκε** is the aorist passive → past, perfective |
| **3. Which person?** | **-ε** → third singular |
| **4. What is the verb?** | strip to **ανακοινών-** → **ανακοινώνω** |

**Answer: aorist passive, third person singular, of ανακοινώνω** — *it was announced*.

**And the tool for when that fails is Lexiscope**, which takes the inflected form and gives you the lemma and the full table.

**2. Production — making a form you need.** You want *they had written*.

**The procedure, in reverse:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Which verb?** | γράφω |
| **2. Which tense?** | pluperfect → **είχα** + the invariable perfective |
| **3. Which person?** | third plural → **είχαν** |
| **4. Assemble.** | **είχαν γράψει** |

**Production is the skill that matters**, and it is the one that reading a table does not develop.

**3. Drilling — making the forms automatic.** Which is what the rest of this lesson is about.

**The cover-and-say drill**, which is the whole method of this track:

1. **Cover the forms**, leaving the persons visible.
2. **Say all six aloud**, at speed.
3. **Uncover and check.**
4. **Redo any you missed, three times each.**

**Thirty seconds per verb per tense.** Three verbs a day, five tenses, is seven minutes.

**The substitution drill**, which is harder and better:

**Take one sentence and change one thing at a time.**

> **Γράφω ένα γράμμα.**
> → past: **Έγραψα ένα γράμμα.**
> → imperfect: **Έγραφα ένα γράμμα.**
> → future: **Θα γράψω ένα γράμμα.**
> → plural: **Θα γράψουμε ένα γράμμα.**
> → negative: **Δεν θα γράψουμε ένα γράμμα.**
> → subjunctive: **Θέλω να γράψουμε ένα γράμμα.**
> → perfect: **Έχουμε γράψει ένα γράμμα.**
> → passive: **Το γράμμα γράφτηκε.**
> → pluperfect passive: **Το γράμμα είχε γραφτεί.**

**Nine transformations from one sentence**, each one a different cell of the table, and all of them said aloud. **That is the single most productive verb drill in the curriculum**, and it takes two minutes.

**What to drill, in priority order**, because you cannot drill everything:

| Priority | Forms |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | the present, both conjugations |
| **2** | the aorist and the imperfect |
| **3** | **θα** and **να** with both stems |
| **4** | **είμαι, έχω, πάω, λέω, τρώω** |
| **5** | the aorist passive **-θηκα / -τηκα** |
| **6** | the perfect with **έχω** |
| **7** | the participles |
| **8** | everything else, as it arises |

**The reference tools, for when drilling is not the answer:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Triantafyllidis** (greek-language.gr) | gives every verb's full inflection |
| **Lexiscope** | takes any inflected form and names it |
| **Greek Wiktionary** | full conjugation tables, free, patchy coverage |
| **This track** | the tables, in one place |

**And the honest point about tables.** They are reference, and reference is consulted rather than memorised. **What should be memorised is the pattern**, so that a new verb slots into it — and that is what the drills build.

**The weekly habit for the Forms track, settled:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Twice a week, twenty minutes** | one module's tables, cover-and-say |
| **Daily, two minutes** | one substitution drill on a sentence from your reading |
| **Continuously** | the deck, with every verb carded as an **aspect pair** |

**The aspect pair rule, from stage 6, restated because it belongs here**: a verb carded without its perfective stem is half a verb. **γράφω / γράψω** on one card.

**Practice.** Do the nine-transformation substitution drill on a sentence from today's reading. Then cover-and-say the present and aorist of five verbs. Then put one inflected form you cannot identify through Lexiscope and read its table.
The perfective stem, formed:
How the second stem is built — the rules, which cover most verbs, and the list, which covers the rest.

**What the perfective stem is for**, from Forms 2: the aorist, the perfective future (**θα γράψω**), the perfective subjunctive (**να γράψω**) and the perfective imperative (**γράψε**). **Four constructions, one stem.**

**And how it is cited**: dictionaries give the perfective as the **first person perfective subjunctive without να** — **γράψω** — which is the form this track uses throughout.

**The formation, for conjugation 1: a marker is added to the stem**, and which marker depends on the stem's final consonant.

| Stem ends in | Marker | Result | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **π, β, φ, πτ, φτ, εύ** | **ψ** | **-ψω** | γράφω → **γράψω**; κρύβω → **κρύψω**; κόβω → **κόψω**; δουλεύω → **δουλέψω**; βάφω → **βάψω** |
| **κ, γ, χ, γγ, χν, ζ** | **ξ** | **-ξω** | ανοίγω → **ανοίξω**; τρέχω → **τρέξω**; πλέκω → **πλέξω**; δείχνω → **δείξω**; αλλάζω → **αλλάξω** |
| **ζ, σ, θ, τ, δ, ν, and vowels** | **σ** | **-σω** | διαβάζω → **διαβάσω**; αγοράζω → **αγοράσω**; ακούω → **ακούσω**; λύνω → **λύσω**; πείθω → **πείσω** |

**The three groups are the ancient ones:** labials give **ψ**, velars give **ξ**, everything else gives **σ**. **It is the same rule that makes English *scribe / script*** — a consonant assimilating to a following sibilant.

**ζ is the one that goes both ways**, and it is a fact about each verb:

| **-σω** | **-ξω** |
| --- | --- |
| διαβάζω → διαβάσω | αλλάζω → αλλάξω |
| αγοράζω → αγοράσω | παίζω → παίξω |
| αρχίζω → αρχίσω | στενάζω → στενάξω |
| γνωρίζω → γνωρίσω | κοιτάζω → κοιτάξω |
| νομίζω → νομίσω | σφάζω → σφάξω |
| ετοιμάζω → ετοιμάσω | τινάζω → τινάξω |

**The rough tendency: -ίζω verbs take σ, -άζω verbs often take ξ** — and there are exceptions in both directions (**αγοράζω → αγοράσω**, **ετοιμάζω → ετοιμάσω**), so the dictionary decides.

**For conjugation 2, the marker is -ήσ- or -έσ-:**

| Type | Perfective | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2a (-άω)** | **-ήσω** | αγαπώ → **αγαπήσω**; μιλώ → **μιλήσω**; ρωτώ → **ρωτήσω**; σταματώ → **σταματήσω**; περπατώ → **περπατήσω** |
| **2b (-ώ)** | **-ήσω** or **-έσω** | τηλεφωνώ → **τηλεφωνήσω**; μπορώ → **μπορέσω**; καλώ → **καλέσω**; αργώ → **αργήσω** |
| **2a, some** | **-άσω** | χαλώ → **χαλάσω**; γελώ → **γελάσω**; περνώ → **περάσω**; ξεχνώ → **ξεχάσω** |
| **2b, some** | **-ήσω** with a changed stem | θεωρώ → **θεωρήσω**; προχωρώ → **προχωρήσω** |

**The -άσω group is small and common**: **χαλάσω, γελάσω, περάσω, ξεχάσω, κρεμάσω, χορτάσω** — and the **α** is the spelling point.

**The verbs whose perfective adds nothing**, which are a real group: some verbs have the same form for both stems, and the aspect is carried by context alone. They are few, and **μένω → μείνω** shows the commoner pattern of a **vowel change instead of a marker**:

| Imperfective | Perfective | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **μένω** | **μείνω** | the stem vowel |
| **στέλνω** | **στείλω** | the stem vowel |
| **πλένω** | **πλύνω** | the stem vowel |
| **φέρνω** | **φέρω** | the **-ν-** dropped |
| **παίρνω** | **πάρω** | the **-ν-** dropped and the vowel changed |
| **σέρνω** | **σύρω** | both |
| **γέρνω** | **γείρω** | the vowel |

**The -νω verbs are the group to watch**, because many of them form the perfective by dropping the **-ν-** rather than adding a marker.

**The method for an unknown verb**, in three steps:

1. **Find the stem's final consonant** and apply the three-group rule.
2. **If the verb is conjugation 2**, try **-ήσω**.
3. **If either guess looks wrong, check it.** The Triantafyllidis dictionary and Lexiscope both give the perfective.

**And the carding rule, from stage 6 and Forms 2**: **every verb is carded as a pair.** **γράφω / γράψω** on one card, front and back. A verb without its perfective is half a verb.

**Practice.** For thirty verbs from today's reading, form the perfective by the three-group rule and check each one. Then list the **-νω** verbs you know and work out each perfective. Then card any you got wrong, as pairs.

**The six monosyllabic perfectives — δω, πω, βρω, μπω, βγω, πιω** — are the strangest forms in the language and the most used. They conjugate normally:

| | **δω** | **πω** | **βρω** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **να** | δω | πω | βρω |
| | δεις | πεις | βρεις |
| | δει | πει | βρει |
| | δούμε | πούμε | βρούμε |
| | δείτε | πείτε | βρείτε |
| | δουν | πουν | βρουν |

**And their aorists are irregular in a different way**: **είδα, είπα, βρήκα, μπήκα, βγήκα, ήπια** — with **ει** or **η** in the stem, which is the spelling point from the Spelling track.

**The -αίνω group**, which is large and regular within itself:

| Imperfective | Perfective | Aorist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **μαθαίνω** | **μάθω** | **έμαθα** |
| **παθαίνω** | **πάθω** | **έπαθα** |
| **καταλαβαίνω** | **καταλάβω** | **κατάλαβα** |
| **ανεβαίνω** | **ανεβώ** | **ανέβηκα** |
| **κατεβαίνω** | **κατεβώ** | **κατέβηκα** |
| **πεθαίνω** | **πεθάνω** | **πέθανα** |
| **μπαίνω** | **μπω** | **μπήκα** |
| **βγαίνω** | **βγω** | **βγήκα** |
| **τυχαίνω** | **τύχω** | **έτυχα** |

**The pattern: -αίνω drops the -αιν- and the perfective is short.** That is a usable regularity within an otherwise irregular group, and the **αι** spelling is the one the Spelling track flagged.

**The compounds, which inherit their simple verb's perfective** — and this is the labour-saving fact of this lesson:

| Simple | Compound | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **βάζω → βάλω** | **ανεβάζω, κατεβάζω, προβάλλω** | **ανεβάσω, κατεβάσω, προβάλω** |
| **δίνω → δώσω** | **αποδίδω, παραδίδω** | **αποδώσω, παραδώσω** |
| **βλέπω → δω** | **προβλέπω, επιβλέπω** | **προβλέψω, επιβλέψω** |
| **λέω → πω** | **προλέγω, αντιλέγω** | **προλέξω / προβλέψω** by sense |
| **έρχομαι → έρθω** | **επανέρχομαι, προσέρχομαι** | **επανέλθω, προσέλθω** |
| **φέρνω → φέρω** | **αναφέρω, προσφέρω, μεταφέρω** | **αναφέρω, προσφέρω, μεταφέρω** |

**So learning thirty simple verbs gives you several hundred compounds**, which is the best return available in Greek morphology.

**The learned compounds in -έλθω** are worth recognising: **προσέλθω, επανέλθω, διέλθω, εξέλθω, εισέλθω** — all from **έρχομαι**, all formal, and all in official and church Greek.

**How to learn this list.** As cards, as **pairs**, ten at a time, over a fortnight. **The front is the imperfective, the back is the perfective and the aorist** — three forms on one card, because they come as a set.

**Practice.** Card the thirty in three batches of ten. Then for each of the six monosyllables, write all six persons of **να** plus the form. Then take ten compound verbs from today's reading and work out each one's perfective from its simple verb.
The aorist, in full:
The past perfective — the narrative tense of Greek — in every conjugation, with its endings and its stress.

**The endings, which are the same for every verb in the language:**

| Person | Ending |
| --- | --- |
| **1 sg.** | **-α** |
| **2 sg.** | **-ες** |
| **3 sg.** | **-ε** |
| **1 pl.** | **-αμε** |
| **2 pl.** | **-ατε** |
| **3 pl.** | **-αν** (or **-ανε**) |

**Identical to the imperfect's endings.** The difference between **έγραφα** and **έγραψα** is the stem alone, which is why the perfective stem matters so much.

**Conjugation 1:**

| Person | **γράφω** | **διαβάζω** | **ανοίγω** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **έγραψα** | **διάβασα** | **άνοιξα** |
| **εσύ** | **έγραψες** | **διάβασες** | **άνοιξες** |
| **αυτός** | **έγραψε** | **διάβασε** | **άνοιξε** |
| **εμείς** | **γράψαμε** | **διαβάσαμε** | **ανοίξαμε** |
| **εσείς** | **γράψατε** | **διαβάσατε** | **ανοίξατε** |
| **αυτοί** | **έγραψαν** | **διάβασαν** | **άνοιξαν** |

**Conjugation 2:**

| Person | **αγαπώ** | **μπορώ** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **αγάπησα** | **μπόρεσα** |
| **εσύ** | **αγάπησες** | **μπόρεσες** |
| **αυτός** | **αγάπησε** | **μπόρεσε** |
| **εμείς** | **αγαπήσαμε** | **μπορέσαμε** |
| **εσείς** | **αγαπήσατε** | **μπορέσατε** |
| **αυτοί** | **αγάπησαν** | **μπόρεσαν** |

**The stress rule, which is the whole difficulty**: the aorist's stress falls on the **third syllable from the end**, which means it **moves** between the singular and the plural:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **α-γά-πη-σα** | stress on the third from the end |
| **α-γα-πή-σα-με** | and it moves forward one |
| **έ-γρα-ψα** | the augment supplies the third syllable |
| **γρά-ψα-με** | three syllables already, so no augment |

**So the augment is a consequence of the stress rule, not a separate thing to remember.** Short stems get an **ε-**; long ones do not need one.

**The irregular aorists**, from the last lesson, with their stress:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **είδα, είδες, είδε, είδαμε, είδατε, είδαν** | the stress stays on **εί-** throughout |
| **είπα, είπες, είπε, είπαμε, είπατε, είπαν** | same |
| **πήγα, πήγες, πήγε, πήγαμε, πήγατε, πήγαν** | same |
| **πήρα, πήρες, πήρε, πήραμε, πήρατε, πήραν** | same |
| **βρήκα, βρήκες, βρήκε, βρήκαμε, βρήκατε, βρήκαν** | same |
| **ήρθα, ήρθες, ήρθε, ήρθαμε, ήρθατε, ήρθαν** | same |
| **έφαγα, έφαγες, έφαγε, φάγαμε, φάγατε, έφαγαν** | **and here the augment behaves normally** |
| **ήπια, ήπιες, ήπιε, ήπιαμε, ήπιατε, ήπιαν** | |

**The group whose stress does not move — είδα, είπα, πήγα, πήρα, βρήκα, ήρθα, μπήκα, βγήκα** — is a real relief, because they are the commonest verbs and their aorists are invariant in stress.

**What the aorist is for**, from stage 4 and stage 9's narrating lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A single completed event** | **Έγραψα το γράμμα.** |
| **A sequence of events** | **Μπήκα, κάθισα, άρχισα να διαβάζω.** |
| **A state entered** | **Κατάλαβα.** — *I understood*, i.e. *it dawned on me* |
| **A period seen as a whole** | **Έζησα δέκα χρόνια στην Αθήνα.** |
| **The narrative spine** | with the imperfect supplying the background |

**And the contrast with the imperfect, in the pair that teaches it:**

> **Διάβαζα όταν χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο.**
> *I was reading* — imperfect, background — *when the phone rang* — aorist, event.

**The two things learners get wrong:**

1. **Using the aorist for description.** **Ήταν ψηλός** is right; **—** an aorist there would mean he became tall.
2. **Using the imperfect for a completed event.** **Πήγα στην εκκλησία** is *I went*; **πήγαινα** is *I used to go* or *I was on my way*.

**The perfective future, subjunctive and imperative**, which use the same stem and need no new endings:

| | **γράφω** |
| --- | --- |
| **Aorist** | **έγραψα** … |
| **Future** | **θα γράψω, θα γράψεις, θα γράψει, θα γράψουμε, θα γράψετε, θα γράψουν** |
| **Subjunctive** | **να γράψω** … |
| **Imperative** | **γράψε** (sg.), **γράψτε** (pl.) |

**The future and subjunctive take the present's endings** — **-ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν** — on the perfective stem. **That is the whole of it.**

**Practice.** Produce the full aorist of **γράφω, διαβάζω, αγαπώ, μπορώ** and six irregulars, aloud, marking where the stress moves. Then write five pairs of sentences contrasting the aorist with the imperfect.
The perfective future, subjunctive and i:
The three remaining perfective constructions, which need no new endings — and the imperative, which is the one place with its own forms.

**The perfective future: θα + perfective stem + present endings.**

| Person | **θα γράψω** | **θα διαβάσω** | **θα πω** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | θα γράψ**ω** | θα διαβάσ**ω** | θα π**ω** |
| **εσύ** | θα γράψ**εις** | θα διαβάσ**εις** | θα π**εις** |
| **αυτός** | θα γράψ**ει** | θα διαβάσ**ει** | θα π**ει** |
| **εμείς** | θα γράψ**ουμε** | θα διαβάσ**ουμε** | θα π**ούμε** |
| **εσείς** | θα γράψ**ετε** | θα διαβάσ**ετε** | θα π**είτε** |
| **αυτοί** | θα γράψ**ουν** | θα διαβάσ**ουν** | θα π**ουν** |

**The perfective subjunctive: να, and the identical endings.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **να γράψω, να γράψεις, να γράψει, να γράψουμε, να γράψετε, να γράψουν** | |
| **θέλω να γράψω** | I want to write |
| **πρέπει να γράψεις** | you must write |
| **μπορώ να σε βοηθήσω;** | can I help you? |
| **για να καταλάβεις** | so that you understand |
| **πριν φύγεις** | before you leave — **and πριν takes the perfective subjunctive without να** |
| **να μην ξεχάσεις** | don't forget — the negative, with **μην** |

**When the perfective rather than the imperfective**, which is the aspect decision from stage 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Once, completed** | **θα σου γράψω** — I'll write to you |
| **Repeatedly** | **θα σου γράφω** — I'll write to you regularly |
| **A specific occasion** | **να φάμε μαζί** — let's eat together (this once) |
| **Generally** | **πρέπει να τρώμε καλά** — we should eat well (in general) |
| **After πριν, μόλις, αφού, όταν (once)** | perfective — **όταν φτάσεις** |
| **After όταν (whenever), ενώ, όσο** | imperfective — **όταν φτάνεις** |

**The imperative, which has its own endings — the only place in the verb that does.**

| | Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2 sg.** | **γράφε** | **γράψε** |
| **2 pl.** | **γράφετε** | **γράψτε** |

**Conjugation 2:**

| | Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2 sg.** | **αγάπα, μίλα** | **αγάπησε, μίλησε** |
| **2 pl.** | **αγαπάτε, μιλάτε** | **αγαπήστε, μιλήστε** |

**The perfective plural -τε is the form you will use most**: **γράψτε, διαβάστε, μιλήστε, περιμένετε, ελάτε, πείτε, δώστε.**

| **τρώω** | **φάε** | **φάτε** |
| **πίνω** | **πιες** | **πιείτε** |
| **μπαίνω** | **μπες** | **μπείτε** |
| **βγαίνω** | **βγες** | **βγείτε** |
| **βρίσκω** | **βρες** | **βρείτε** |
| **ανεβαίνω** | **ανέβα** | **ανεβείτε** |
| **κατεβαίνω** | **κατέβα** | **κατεβείτε** |
| **βάζω** | **βάλε** | **βάλτε** |
| **βγάζω** | **βγάλε** | **βγάλτε** |

**Note ελάτε, πείτε, δείτε, πιείτε, μπείτε, βγείτε, βρείτε take ει**, which the Spelling track flagged.

**The negative imperative, which does not exist as a form:**

> **Μην γράφεις.** / **Μην γράψεις.**
> **Μην πεις τίποτα.**
> **Να μην ξεχάσεις.**

**μην plus the ordinary present or perfective subjunctive.** Both aspects are available and the distinction holds: **μην γράφεις** is *stop writing*, **μην γράψεις** is *don't write (this)*.

**And the polite imperative**, which is the plural used to one person:

> **Περιμένετε, παρακαλώ.** — *Please wait.* (to one person, politely)
> **Καθίστε.** — *Sit down.* (polite)

**The whole perfective system for one verb, as one reference:**

| | **γράφω / γράψω** |
| --- | --- |
| **Aorist** | έγραψα, έγραψες, έγραψε, γράψαμε, γράψατε, έγραψαν |
| **Future** | θα γράψω … |
| **Subjunctive** | να γράψω … |
| **Imperative** | γράψε, γράψτε |
| **Negative** | μην γράψεις, μην γράψετε |
| **Perfect** | έχω γράψει … |

Drilling the pairs:
The method lesson for this module: how to make the two stems automatic, which is the single thing that most improves spoken Greek at this level.

**Why it is worth a lesson.** The aspect choice is made **before** the tense, in the instant of speaking, and if the perfective stem is not automatic you will hesitate on every past, future and subjunctive. **Fluency in Greek is largely fluency in the two stems.**

**Drill 1 — the pair drill.** See one stem, say the other.

> γράφω → **γράψω** · ανοίγω → **ανοίξω** · διαβάζω → **διαβάσω** · μιλώ → **μιλήσω** · βλέπω → **δω** · παίρνω → **πάρω**

**Thirty pairs in two minutes**, both directions, daily. **This is the highest-value two minutes in the Forms track.**

**Drill 2 — the four-form drill.** For each verb, say four things:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Present** | γράφω |
| **Aorist** | έγραψα |
| **Perfective future** | θα γράψω |
| **Perfective subjunctive** | να γράψω |

**Ten verbs, forty forms, three minutes.**

**Drill 3 — the aspect-choice drill**, which is the hardest and most useful. A sentence, and you choose:

| Sentence | Answer and reason |
| --- | --- |
| Κάθε μέρα **θα σου γράφω / θα σου γράψω**. | **θα σου γράφω** — *every day*, so habitual |
| Αύριο **θα σου γράφω / θα σου γράψω**. | **θα σου γράψω** — one occasion |
| Όταν **φτάνεις / φτάσεις**, τηλεφώνησέ μου. | **φτάσεις** — a single future event |
| Όταν **φτάνεις / φτάσεις** στο σπίτι, βάζεις τα κλειδιά εκεί. | **φτάνεις** — *whenever*, habitual |
| Πρέπει να **τρώμε / φάμε** καλά. | **τρώμε** — generally |
| Πρέπει να **τρώμε / φάμε** τώρα. | **φάμε** — this once |
| Πριν **φεύγεις / φύγεις**, πες μου. | **φύγεις** — **πριν** always takes the perfective |
| Ενώ **διάβαζα / διάβασα**, χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο. | **διάβαζα** — background, so imperfective |
| **Έμενα / Έμεινα** δέκα χρόνια στην Αθήνα. | **Έμεινα** — a period seen as a whole |
| **Πήγαινα / Πήγα** κάθε Κυριακή. | **Πήγαινα** — habitual |

**The particles that decide the aspect for you**, which is worth having as a list:

| Always perfective | Always imperfective |
| --- | --- |
| **πριν** | **ενώ** |
| **μόλις** | **όσο** |
| **αφού** (after) | **καθώς** |
| **ώσπου** | **όταν** (whenever) |
| **όταν** (once, future) | **πάντα, συνήθως, κάθε** |
| **αμέσως μόλις** | **συνέχεια, συχνά** |

**That list removes the decision in a large number of sentences**, and learning it is faster than learning the aspect by feel.

**Drill 4 — the transformation drill**, from Forms 2, which exercises everything:

> **Διαβάζω το βιβλίο.**
> → aorist: **Διάβασα το βιβλίο.**
> → imperfect: **Διάβαζα το βιβλίο.**
> → perfective future: **Θα διαβάσω το βιβλίο.**
> → imperfective future: **Θα διαβάζω το βιβλίο.**
> → subjunctive, both: **Θέλω να διαβάσω / να διαβάζω το βιβλίο.**
> → perfect: **Έχω διαβάσει το βιβλίο.**
> → pluperfect: **Είχα διαβάσει το βιβλίο.**
> → imperative, both: **Διάβασε / Διάβαζε το βιβλίο.**
> → negative imperative: **Μην διαβάσεις το βιβλίο.**

**Ten forms from one sentence**, two minutes, and every cell of the verb exercised.

**Drill 5 — mining your own reading.** Take any past-tense verb in what you are reading and ask: **is it aorist or imperfect, and why did the author choose it?** **That is the drill that builds judgement** rather than knowledge, and it costs nothing.

**The weekly habit, settled for the whole Forms track:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Daily, two minutes** | the pair drill, thirty pairs |
| **Daily, two minutes** | one transformation drill on a sentence from your reading |
| **Twice a week, twenty minutes** | one module's tables, cover-and-say |
| **Continuously** | the deck, every verb as a pair |

**Six minutes a day and two twenty-minute sessions a week.** That is the whole track, and it is less than the Spelling track.

**The marker that it has worked.** You can say any of the ten forms of a verb without pausing, and you choose the aspect without thinking about it. **At that point the Greek verb is finished as a problem**, and what remains is vocabulary.

**Practice.** Do the pair drill on thirty verbs, both directions. Then the aspect-choice drill above, saying the reason aloud. Then one transformation drill. Then learn the two particle lists.
The passive present and imperfect:
The passive's own endings, which are unlike the active's and which the deponent verbs use as their only forms.

**The present passive, conjugation 1:**

| Person | **γράφομαι** | **πλένομαι** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | γράφ**ομαι** | πλέν**ομαι** |
| **εσύ** | γράφ**εσαι** | πλέν**εσαι** |
| **αυτός** | γράφ**εται** | πλέν**εται** |
| **εμείς** | γραφ**όμαστε** | πλεν**όμαστε** |
| **εσείς** | γράφ**εστε** | πλέν**εστε** |
| **αυτοί** | γράφ**ονται** | πλέν**ονται** |

**The endings: -ομαι, -εσαι, -εται, -όμαστε, -εστε, -ονται.** All six spelt as the Spelling track's passive lesson gave them, with **-αι** on three of them.

**The present passive, conjugation 2a — type αγαπιέμαι:**

| Person | Form |
| --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **αγαπιέμαι** |
| **εσύ** | **αγαπιέσαι** |
| **αυτός** | **αγαπιέται** |
| **εμείς** | **αγαπιόμαστε** |
| **εσείς** | **αγαπιέστε** |
| **αυτοί** | **αγαπιούνται** |

**The present passive, conjugation 2b — type θεωρούμαι:**

| Person | Form |
| --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **θεωρούμαι** |
| **εσύ** | **θεωρείσαι** |
| **αυτός** | **θεωρείται** |
| **εμείς** | **θεωρούμαστε** |
| **εσείς** | **θεωρείστε** |
| **αυτοί** | **θεωρούνται** |

**θεωρείται is the form to know**, because stage 9's impersonal list is built on this type: **θεωρείται, πιστεύεται, υποστηρίζεται, αναμένεται, προβλέπεται, απαγορεύεται, επιτρέπεται, συνιστάται.**

**And the pair that must never be confused**, from the Spelling track: **θεωρείτε** (*you consider*, active, second plural) against **θεωρείται** (*it is considered*, passive, third singular).

**The imperfect passive:**

| Person | **γράφομαι** | **θεωρούμαι** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **γραφόμουν** | **θεωρούμουν** |
| **εσύ** | **γραφόσουν** | **θεωρούσουν** |
| **αυτός** | **γραφόταν** | **θεωρούνταν** |
| **εμείς** | **γραφόμαστε** | **θεωρούμαστε** |
| **εσείς** | **γραφόσαστε** | **θεωρούσαστε** |
| **αυτοί** | **γράφονταν / γραφόντουσαν** | **θεωρούνταν** |

**The endings: -όμουν, -όσουν, -όταν, -όμαστε, -όσαστε, -ονταν.** **All with ο and ου, no *i* sounds** — easy to spell and awkward to say, which is why the compound forms are often preferred in speech.

**Note that the first person plural is identical in the present and the imperfect** — **γραφόμαστε** — which is a genuine ambiguity the language lives with.

**The three senses of the Greek passive**, which is why it is called the mediopassive:

**1. True passive** — something is done to the subject:

> **Το γράμμα γράφτηκε.** — The letter was written.
> **Η απόφαση ανακοινώθηκε.** — The decision was announced.

**2. Reflexive** — the subject acts on itself:

> **Πλένομαι.** — I wash (myself).
> **Ντύνομαι.** — I dress.
> **Ετοιμάζομαι.** — I get ready.
> **Σηκώνομαι.** — I get up.
> **Κάθομαι.** — I sit.

**3. Reciprocal** — the subjects act on each other:

> **Αγαπιόμαστε.** — We love each other.
> **Φιλιόμαστε.** — We kiss.
> **Μιλιόμαστε.** — We're on speaking terms.

**The reflexive sense is the commonest in everyday speech**, and it is why so many ordinary verbs of daily routine are passive in form: **σηκώνομαι, πλένομαι, ντύνομαι, χτενίζομαι, ξυρίζομαι, ετοιμάζομαι, κουράζομαι, ξεκουράζομαι, κοιμάμαι.**

**And that is the point to hold on to**: a passive-looking Greek verb is more often reflexive or deponent than truly passive. **The agent construction is rare in speech** and belongs to writing, where stage 9 showed its purpose is to hide the agent.

**The agent, when it is named**, takes **από**:

> **Το βιβλίο γράφτηκε από τον Παπαδιαμάντη.**

**And in the learned register, υπό with the genitive**: **υπό του συγγραφέως** — which you read and do not write.

**Practice.** Produce the present and imperfect passive of **γράφομαι**, **αγαπιέμαι** and **θεωρούμαι** in full. Then write five sentences in each of the three senses. Then write ten **-ετε / -εται** pairs and name which is which.
The aorist passive:
The passive's perfective stem and its past tense — the form you will write most often in Greek, because formal writing runs on it.

**The formation: a -θ- or -τ- is inserted, and the endings are -ηκα.**

| Person | Ending |
| --- | --- |
| **1 sg.** | **-ηκα** |
| **2 sg.** | **-ηκες** |
| **3 sg.** | **-ηκε** |
| **1 pl.** | **-ήκαμε** |
| **2 pl.** | **-ήκατε** |
| **3 pl.** | **-ηκαν** |

**Every one with eta**, as the Spelling track insisted: **-θηκα, -τηκα, -χτηκα, -στηκα** — never iota.

**The four groups, by what the stem ends in:**

| Group | Marker | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Conjugation 2, and -ώνω / -άζω / -ίζω verbs** | **-ήθηκα / -ώθηκα / -άστηκα / -ίστηκα** | αγαπώ → **αγαπήθηκα**; ανακοινώνω → **ανακοινώθηκα**; ετοιμάζω → **ετοιμάστηκα**; γνωρίζω → **γνωρίστηκα** |
| **Labial stems (π, β, φ)** | **-φτηκα / -φθηκα** | γράφω → **γράφτηκα**; κόβω → **κόπηκα**; κρύβω → **κρύφτηκα** |
| **Velar stems (κ, γ, χ)** | **-χτηκα / -χθηκα** | ανοίγω → **ανοίχτηκα**; διώχνω → **διώχτηκα**; δείχνω → **δείχτηκα** |
| **Others** | **-θηκα / -στηκα** | λύνω → **λύθηκα**; χάνω → **χάθηκα**; πλένω → **πλύθηκα**; στέκομαι → **στάθηκα** |

**The -θηκα and -φθηκα / -χθηκα doublets are register**: **γράφτηκε** is the ordinary modern form, **εγράφη** the learned one, and **-φθηκε / -χθηκε** sit between — commoner in writing, especially in official and church Greek. **All are correct; the plainer ones are safer.**

**The forms you will meet constantly in written Greek:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ανακοινώθηκε** | it was announced |
| **αποφασίστηκε** | it was decided |
| **εγκρίθηκε** | it was approved |
| **απορρίφθηκε** | it was rejected |
| **δημοσιεύτηκε** | it was published |
| **υπογράφηκε** | it was signed |
| **πραγματοποιήθηκε** | it took place |
| **διαπιστώθηκε** | it was ascertained |
| **ιδρύθηκε** | it was founded |
| **χτίστηκε / οικοδομήθηκε** | it was built |
| **γεννήθηκε** | he was born |
| **βαφτίστηκε** | he was baptised |
| **χειροτονήθηκε** | he was ordained |
| **ονομάστηκε** | he was named |
| **κοιμήθηκε** | he fell asleep — **and εκοιμήθη in the Church's own register** |

**That last pair is the stage-7 learned-fossil point in its natural place**: **κοιμήθηκε** is the modern aorist passive; **εκοιμήθη** is the ancient one, kept because it is the Church's word for a saint's death.

**The perfective passive subjunctive and future**, which drop the **-ηκα** and take the present endings on the **-θ-** stem:

| Person | **να γραφτώ** | **να ανακοινωθώ** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | γραφ**τώ** | ανακοινω**θώ** |
| **εσύ** | γραφ**τείς** | ανακοινω**θείς** |
| **αυτός** | γραφ**τεί** | ανακοινω**θεί** |
| **εμείς** | γραφ**τούμε** | ανακοινω**θούμε** |
| **εσείς** | γραφ**τείτε** | ανακοινω**θείτε** |
| **αυτοί** | γραφ**τούν** | ανακοινω**θούν** |

**The endings: -ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν** — conjugation 2b's endings, on the passive perfective stem.

**να ανακοινωθεί and θα ανακοινωθεί are among the most-written forms in formal Greek**, and the **-θεί** is epsilon-iota, never **-θή**.

> **Θα ανακοινωθεί αύριο.** — It will be announced tomorrow.
> **Πρέπει να εγκριθεί πρώτα.** — It must be approved first.
> **Αναμένεται να υπογραφεί.** — It is expected to be signed.

**The deponents' aorists**, which look passive and mean active:

| Verb | Aorist |
| --- | --- |
| **έρχομαι** | **ήρθα** — irregular |
| **κάθομαι** | **κάθισα** — active-shaped |
| **σκέφτομαι** | **σκέφτηκα** |
| **αισθάνομαι** | **αισθάνθηκα** |
| **φοβάμαι** | **φοβήθηκα** |
| **θυμάμαι** | **θυμήθηκα** |
| **χρειάζομαι** | **χρειάστηκα** |
| **εργάζομαι** | **εργάστηκα** |
| **κοιμάμαι** | **κοιμήθηκα** |
| **γίνομαι** | **έγινα** — irregular |
| **εξομολογούμαι** | **εξομολογήθηκα** |
| **προσεύχομαι** | **προσευχήθηκα** |

**And their subjunctives**: **να σκεφτώ, να θυμηθώ, να φοβηθώ, να κοιμηθώ, να προσευχηθώ** — all with the **-θώ** ending.

**να θυμηθώ is worth noting** because it is the one on the aspect table from Forms 2: **θυμάμαι** is to hold in mind; **θυμηθώ** is for something to come back to you.

**Practice.** Produce the aorist passive of **γράφω, ανοίγω, ανακοινώνω, ετοιμάζω** in full. Then write the **να** and **θα** forms of five of them. Then write out the twelve deponent aorists from memory.
The perfect tenses:
The three compound tenses, which are the easiest forms in the Greek verb because the second word never changes.

**The construction: έχω plus the invariable perfective.**

**The invariable form** is the third person singular of the perfective subjunctive without **να** — **γράψει, διαβάσει, πει, δει, πάει** — and it is the same for every person.

**The perfect:**

| Person | Form |
| --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | **έχω γράψει** |
| **εσύ** | **έχεις γράψει** |
| **αυτός** | **έχει γράψει** |
| **εμείς** | **έχουμε γράψει** |
| **εσείς** | **έχετε γράψει** |
| **αυτοί** | **έχουν γράψει** |

**Only έχω conjugates.** **γράψει** never changes — not for person, not for number, not for gender.

**The pluperfect: είχα plus the same.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **είχα γράψει, είχες γράψει, είχε γράψει, είχαμε γράψει, είχατε γράψει, είχαν γράψει** | |

**The future perfect: θα έχω plus the same.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα έχω γράψει, θα έχεις γράψει…** | and it is rare in speech |

**And the conditional perfect: θα είχα plus the same** — which stage 6's third conditional needed:

> **Αν το είχα μάθει, θα είχα έρθει.** — If I had found out, I would have come.

**The passive perfect**, which uses the passive invariable:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έχω γραφτεί** | I have been written |
| **έχει ανακοινωθεί** | it has been announced |
| **είχε εγκριθεί** | it had been approved |
| **θα έχει ολοκληρωθεί** | it will have been completed |

**The invariable passive form is -θεί / -τεί** — the same **-θεί** as the subjunctive.

**The alternative perfect, with -μένος**, which is a different construction and means something different:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έχω γράψει το γράμμα.** | I have written the letter. — **the event** |
| **Το γράμμα είναι γραμμένο.** | The letter is written. — **the resulting state** |
| **Έχω φάει.** | I have eaten. |
| **Είμαι χορτάτος.** | I am full. — the state |

**And a third, which is genuinely useful:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έχω γραμμένο το γράμμα.** | I have the letter written — I have it ready |
| **Έχει βαμμένα τα μαλλιά της.** | Her hair is dyed. |

**έχω plus a declined -μένος participle** agrees with the object and describes a state the subject possesses. **It is common in speech and no textbook teaches it clearly.**

**When Greek uses the perfect, which is the real question.**

**The honest answer, from stage 6: far less than English.** Greek prefers the aorist where English would use the perfect:

| English | Greek, naturally |
| --- | --- |
| *I have already eaten.* | **Έφαγα ήδη.** — aorist |
| *Have you seen the film?* | **Είδες την ταινία;** — aorist |
| *I have been here for ten years.* | **Είμαι εδώ δέκα χρόνια.** — **present** |
| *I have never been to Greece.* | **Δεν έχω πάει ποτέ στην Ελλάδα.** — **perfect, and here it is right** |
| *He has died.* | **Πέθανε.** — aorist |

**So the perfect is used for:**

1. **Experience over a lifetime** — **Έχω πάει τρεις φορές.**
2. **Something never done** — **Δεν έχω δει αυτή την ταινία.**
3. **Emphasising completion against expectation** — **Το έχω τελειώσει!**
4. **In writing, where precision about sequence matters.**

**And the pluperfect is used normally**, exactly as English uses *had*: for an event before another past event. **It is far commoner than the perfect in narrative**, which stage 9's narrating lesson used.

**The one thing that catches learners.** English present perfect with *for* and *since* — *I have lived here for ten years* — is **present** in Greek:

> **Μένω εδώ δέκα χρόνια.**
> **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά εδώ και δύο χρόνια.**

**Present tense, because the action is still going on.** This is one of the most reliable learner errors, and the fix is a rule: **if it is still happening, use the present.**

**Practice.** Produce the perfect, pluperfect and future perfect of **γράφω** and **ανακοινώνω** (passive). Then write five sentences where English would use the perfect and Greek uses the aorist. Then write three with **μένω / μαθαίνω** plus a time span, in the present.
The participles:
Both participles, in full — the indeclinable active one and the declinable passive one — with the forms and the rules.

**The active participle: -οντας / -ώντας.** Indeclinable: one form, for every gender, number and case.

| Conjugation | Formation | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | stem + **-οντας** | **γράφοντας, διαβάζοντας, παίρνοντας, τρέχοντας** |
| **2a** | stem + **-ώντας** | **αγαπώντας, μιλώντας, ρωτώντας, περπατώντας** |
| **2b** | stem + **-ώντας** | **μπορώντας, θεωρώντας, οδηγώντας** |
| **Irregular** | | **λέγοντας** (λέω), **πηγαίνοντας** (πάω), **τρώγοντας** (τρώω), **βλέποντας** (βλέπω), **έχοντας** (έχω), **όντας** (είμαι) |

**The spelling point: -οντας with omicron for conjugation 1, -ώντας with omega for conjugation 2** — and the omega is because the stress is on it.

**It is formed from the imperfective stem only.** **There is no perfective active participle** in modern Greek — **γράψοντας** does not exist.

**What it does**, from stage 9: replaces a subordinate clause.

| Clause | Participle |
| --- | --- |
| **Όταν έφτασα…** | **Φτάνοντας…** |
| **Επειδή δεν ήξερα…** | **Μη γνωρίζοντας…** |
| **Ενώ μιλούσε…** | **Μιλώντας…** |
| **Αν λάβουμε υπόψη…** | **Λαμβάνοντας υπόψη…** |
| **Αφού τελείωσα…** | **Έχοντας τελειώσει…** — the compound |

**The compound participle: έχοντας + the invariable perfective.**

> **Έχοντας διαβάσει το βιβλίο, κατάλαβα.** — Having read the book, I understood.
> **Έχοντας ολοκληρώσει τις σπουδές του, επέστρεψε.**

**That is how Greek expresses a completed prior action participially**, since the simple participle has no perfective.

**The negative is μη, not δεν**: **μη γνωρίζοντας, μη έχοντας, μη θέλοντας.**

**The iron rule, restated from stage 9 because it is the one error everybody makes:** the participle's subject must be the main clause's subject.

> **Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, η πόρτα ήταν ανοιχτή.** ✗
> **Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, βρήκα την πόρτα ανοιχτή.** ✓

**The passive participle: -μένος / -μένη / -μένο.** Declinable, like any **-ος** adjective.

| | M. | F. | N. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | **γραμμένος** | **γραμμένη** | **γραμμένο** |
| **Gen. sg.** | **γραμμένου** | **γραμμένης** | **γραμμένου** |
| **Nom. pl.** | **γραμμένοι** | **γραμμένες** | **γραμμένα** |

**The formation**, which varies by the stem:

| Stem | Participle | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Labial** | **-μμένος** | γράφω → **γραμμένος**; κρύβω → **κρυμμένος**; κόβω → **κομμένος** |
| **Velar** | **-γμένος** | ανοίγω → **ανοιγμένος**; πλέκω → **πλεγμένος**; βρέχω → **βρεγμένος** |
| **Dental / σ** | **-σμένος** | διαβάζω → **διαβασμένος**; κλείνω → **κλεισμένος**; χάνω → **χαμένος** |
| **Conjugation 2** | **-ημένος / -ωμένος** | αγαπώ → **αγαπημένος**; κουράζω → **κουρασμένος**; ανακοινώνω → **ανακοινωμένος** |
| **-ν- stems** | **-μένος** | πλένω → **πλυμένος**; δίνω → **δοσμένος** |

**The double μμ in γραμμένος, κρυμμένος, κομμένος** is the double-consonant point from the Spelling track, and it is caused by the labial assimilating.

**Its two uses:**

**1. As an adjective:**

> **ένα γραμμένο κείμενο, μια κλεισμένη πόρτα, τα κουρασμένα παιδιά, αγαπημένος φίλος**

**2. As a state, with είμαι:**

> **Η πόρτα είναι κλειστή.** — and note **κλειστή**, the short stative adjective, not **κλεισμένη**.

**The stative adjective against the participle**, which is a real distinction:

| State | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **κλειστός** — closed | **κλεισμένος** — having been closed |
| **ανοιχτός** — open | **ανοιγμένος** — having been opened |
| **γεμάτος** — full | **γεμισμένος** — having been filled |
| **κρυφός** — hidden, secret | **κρυμμένος** — having been hidden |
| **σβηστός** — off, extinguished | **σβησμένος** — having been put out |

**The short form describes how a thing is; the -μένος form implies someone did it.** That is the whole difference, and it is worth knowing because the wrong one is comprehensible and slightly odd.

**The learned participles**, which you read and do not write:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-ων / -ούσα / -ον** | the ancient active — **ο παρών, οι ενδιαφερόμενοι, ο υπογράφων, τα υπάρχοντα** |
| **-θείς / -θέντος** | the ancient aorist passive — **ο αποβιώσας, τα αναφερθέντα, ο εκλεγείς** |
| **-όμενος** | the ancient present passive — **ο ενδιαφερόμενος, τα λεγόμενα, ο εργαζόμενος** |

**The -όμενος group is largely naturalised** and several members are ordinary nouns: **ο εργαζόμενος** (the employee), **ο ενδιαφερόμενος** (the interested party), **τα λεγόμενα** (what was said), **ο προϊστάμενος** (the superior), **τα δεδομένα** (the data), **το περιεχόμενο** (the content). **Those you can use.**

**Practice.** Form both participles for twenty verbs. Then decline **γραμμένος** in full. Then write five sentences with the active participle, checking each one's subject against the main verb. Then write the five stative-against-participle pairs in sentences.
The full verb, on one page:
Every form of one verb in one table — the reference page of this track, and the thing to copy out by hand once.

**γράφω / γράψω / γράφομαι / γραφτώ — *write*.**

| **Future** | θα γράφω, θα γράφεις, θα γράφει, θα γράφουμε, θα γράφετε, θα γράφουν |
| **Subjunctive** | να γράφω … |
| **Conditional** | θα έγραφα … |
| **Imperative** | γράφε, γράφετε |
| **Participle** | γράφοντας |

**ACTIVE, PERFECTIVE**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Aorist** | έγραψα, έγραψες, έγραψε, γράψαμε, γράψατε, έγραψαν |
| **Future** | θα γράψω, θα γράψεις, θα γράψει, θα γράψουμε, θα γράψετε, θα γράψουν |
| **Subjunctive** | να γράψω … |

| **Invariable** | γράψει |

| | |
| --- | --- |

| **Pluperfect** | είχα γράψει … |

**PASSIVE, IMPERFECTIVE**

| | |
| --- | --- |

| **Imperfect** | γραφόμουν, γραφόσουν, γραφόταν, γραφόμαστε, γραφόσαστε, γράφονταν |

**PASSIVE, PERFECTIVE**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Aorist** | γράφτηκα, γράφτηκες, γράφτηκε, γραφτήκαμε, γραφτήκατε, γράφτηκαν |
| **Future** | θα γραφτώ, θα γραφτείς, θα γραφτεί, θα γραφτούμε, θα γραφτείτε, θα γραφτούν |

| | |
| --- | --- |
